One loopable Aux envelope and three LFOs, each able to modulate many parameters, including each other. LFOs can run free or sync, and LFOs 2 and 3 can modulate in stereo.

Same design as the other envelopes, routed to two of 29 destinations through the A and B choosers, each with an amount.

Frontmatter Definition

In this garden, Frontmatter Definition pages model a custom frontmatter property that one entity type adds for its instances — the property's meaning, its permitted values, and how instances set it. Global, cross-type conventions stay on Logseq/Frontmatter; a Frontmatter Definition is scoped to a single entity type.
What counts as an instance
A page whose job is to define one custom property belonging to a single entity type: what the property means, which values are permitted, and how an instance uses it.

Not an instance: a shared convention on Logseq/Frontmatter (those apply to every page, not one type); a Logseq/Entity/Definition page (that defines an entity type, not a property); an individual permitted value.
Naming and namespace
Ownership follows the namespace: Logseq/Entity/<Type>/Frontmatter/<key> belongs to Logseq/Entity/<Type>. A separate ownership property or body section would repeat that relationship.

A Frontmatter Definition lives under its owning type at Logseq/Entity/<Type>/Frontmatter/<key>, where <key> is the literal frontmatter key it defines, in kebab-case to match the :: property (for example dotfiles-dep-stage).
The /Frontmatter/ segment is the boundary: above it is the entity definition; at and below it are that type's frontmatter schema and values.
Permitted values

When the property draws from a closed set, enumerate the permitted values as child pages Logseq/Entity/<Type>/Frontmatter/<key>/<Value>. An instance references a value page, which gives autocomplete and turns each value page's linked references into the list of instances currently holding that value.

Value pages are permitted values, not definitions and not entities: they carry no logseq-entity::. An ordered vocabulary uses a leading number so the sequence sorts in order, for example 1 - Incubating.
Frontmatter
On instances, set logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Frontmatter/Definition]] so this type page collects a backlink to every custom frontmatter property in the garden.

On instances, set alias:: [[<key>]] to the literal key the page defines, as alias:: [[logseq-entity-hierarchy-type]] on . Clicking a key in <key>:: <value> opens the page [[<key>]], and the alias makes that page the definition.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
Page shape (body)

Logseq Flavored Markdown. Suggested sections: the property's meaning, its permitted values (link the value pages, in order), any rules between values, and ownership when the namespace does not already identify it.
Relationships to other types
Logseq/Entity/Definition — defines entity types; a Frontmatter Definition defines one property a type adds. A type page links its Frontmatter Definitions from its own ## Frontmatter section.
— a Frontmatter Definition is a schema: a declared shape a property's value must satisfy to count as valid.

29.42.1.1 Singing Synthesizer
1. Put Vocoder on the vocal track — a recorded clip, or a live mic chosen as the track input.
2. Put a synth such as Ableton/Live/UG/31 Instrument Reference/01 Analog on another track, played from a clip or live.
3. Set Carrier to External and pick the synth track in Audio From (Post FX in the lower chooser works best).
4. For live input, arm both tracks.
5. Play the synth while speaking: the speech rhythm comes through with the synth's tone. Solo the voice track to hear only the vocoded sound.
Bright, harmonically rich patches, such as saw-based ones, make the words clearer; Unvoiced and Enhance add more clarity.

29.30.2 Bit Reduction
The bit reduction controls are on the right. Fewer bits mean less dynamic range, more noise and distortion; at extremes everything becomes jagged square waves.
Bits — bits used for the output
Shape — the quantizer curve; higher values keep quiet parts finer than loud parts. The result depends on the input's dynamic range.

Melodic Minor Scale

Also called jazz minor and, in its ascending form, the acoustic collection. On C, ascending: C D E♭ F G A B. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 2 2 1. The classical descending form is Music/Scale/Minor/Natural.
History

The classical form records voice leading. Raising both sixth and seventh on the way up avoids the augmented second of Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic while keeping the leading tone. Lowering both on the way down lets the line fall toward the dominant.
Baroque lines follow the harmony more than the direction. Over a dominant chord, 's descending lines keep the raised sixth and seventh.

jazz theory uses the ascending form in both directions and treats each of its modes as a chord-scale. 's Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization ( ) brought Lydian-based thinking into that theory.
Use
Its modes cover much of jazz harmony beyond the diatonic system:

29.20 Gate
Gate passes only signal above a threshold. It removes noise between sounds, such as hiss or hum, or shapes sounds by cutting off reverb or delay tails and natural decays.
The display shows input in light gray and output in darker gray with a white outline, so the gating can be seen.
Threshold — sensitivity; a blue line in the display that can be dragged
Return (hysteresis) — gap between the opening level and the closing level, shown as an orange line. More return stops the gate chattering open and shut near the threshold.
Flip — reverses the gate so only signal below the threshold passes
Lookahead — 0, 1 or 10 ms of delay so the gate can open on time
Attack — time to open; very short can click, long softens the attack
Hold — time the gate stays open after the signal falls below the threshold; then Release sets how long it takes to close
Floor — how much a closed gate turns the signal down; −∞ dB mutes, 0 dB does nothing

10.5.12 Editing Velocities

Velocity, roughly a note's loudness, shows as color saturation: paler notes are softer. Edit it in the Velocity Editor by dragging a note's marker; the value shows in the lane header, and hovering a note highlights its marker.
Shift-click to select several markers. Drag a group to the top or bottom to make them equal, then set the value.

Cmd-drag (Mac) / Alt-drag (Win) a selected note vertically to change velocity without the lane. Or select a marker, type a value and press Enter; Cmd (Mac) / Ctrl (Win) with up and down change it by 10, with Shift for fine steps.

17.3 Controlling external and modular gear

Arturia's MicroBrute, MiniBrute, and MatrixBrute helped renew interest in analog synthesizers. Many musicians also use Eurorack modules to build individual instruments; Arturia's RackBrute provides a Eurorack case.
The MicroFreak follows Arturia's other products with interfaces for modular equipment. Its Pitch, Velocity, and Pressure outputs can control external Eurorack modules.

MIDI also controls external synthesizers and modular systems. Connect the MicroFreak to a MIDI-equipped synthesizer with a MIDI cable. To control Eurorack modules over MIDI, use a module that converts MIDI from the MicroFreak into Pitch and Gate signals.
MIDI can also control external synthesizer parameters such as filters and envelope generators, if the synthesizer has a MIDI input.

06.02 The Parameter Controls
The parameter controls bring the Digital Oscillator to life in different ways.

Type selects an oscillator model, each with its own character. Type can also be modulated: changing models rapidly with the LFO creates abrupt changes in timbre. The Envelopes, keyboard pressure, Sequencer, and Arpeggiator can modulate Type too.
Changing Type shows that model and its current values on the display.

Each model has three sound-shaping parameters: Wave, Timbre, and Shape. Their effects depend on the model. Turning a knob shows its current function on the display; the oscillator overview uses those display names and puts the model's screen name in parentheses.
Wave, Timbre, and Shape can each be a modulation destination in the Matrix, so a sound can change as the modulation changes.
06.03.19 Scan grains
Scan grains oscillator model

The Scan grains oscillator plays short slices (grains) of a loaded sample. Each grain has a volume envelope for a smooth sound, and the oscillator scans from the sample's start to its end at a user-defined speed.
Scan: The Wave knob sets scan speed by moving the grain start position.
Density: The Timbre knob sets how often a grain is generated.
Chaos: The Shape knob adds randomness to density, size, pitch, and other parameters.
Sample browsing and parameter adjustment work like the Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/03 Types/18 Sample.

10.5.3 Find and Select Notes

The Find and Select Notes toggle shows note filters that select matching notes, to edit all notes of one pitch or length at once. Filters can be combined, and each has an Invert toggle and a Select button to reapply it.
The eight filters:
Pitch: chosen pitches in every octave.
Time: a range with Start and Length in beats, repeating every Repeat beats.
Chance: a probability or range.
Condition: active notes, notes under 100% probability, or notes with velocity deviation.
Count: every nth note or chord, with Offset; Quantized counts each grid step as one, so every third sixteenth on a 1/16 grid.
Duration, Scale (the clip's scale or a chosen one), and Velocity.
Notes are selected as you adjust a filter, and a yellow dot marks active filters. Clicking in the editor clears all filters and the selection.
With filters showing, Shift-click a piano key to add that key's notes, or Shift-drag to make evenly repeated time selections.

Todi Thaat
In sargam: S r g M' P d N. On C: C D♭ E♭ F♯ G A♭ B. Steps in semitones: 1 2 3 1 1 3 1.
History
One of 's ten Hindustani thaats, named for raga Todi. See Music/Scale/Marwa for how a thaat relates to the ragas inside it.
The principal raga is Miyan ki Todi. Its name ties it to Miyan Tansen, the singer at Akbar's court in the .
The Carnatic equivalent parent scale is Shubhapantuvarali, melakarta 45.
Use
Miyan ki Todi is a late-morning raga. Pa is weak or skipped in ascent, and the lowered Re, Ga and Dha are sung slightly flat of their equal-tempered pitches, with slow oscillation.
Gujari Todi drops Pa entirely; Bilaskhani Todi takes its notes from the Bhairavi thaat yet keeps the Todi name.
Quirks
The name points to two different scales. Carnatic Todi, Hanumatodi or melakarta 8, has the notes of Music/Scale/Phrygian, while Hindustani Todi has a raised fourth and a raised seventh.
Its step pattern, 1 2 3 1 1 3 1, contains two augmented seconds, like Music/Scale/Minor/Hungarian, from which it differs only in the second degree.

Clip envelopes can automate or modulate mixer and device controls. Automation sets a control's absolute value; modulation only changes that value relatively, so both can act on one parameter.

10.3 Glide
The Glide knob controls how quickly pitch moves between notes. It smooths the abrupt pitch change from one key to another, with a time from off to about 10 seconds.
The Glide Knob
Glide appears in musical styles around the world. Indian vocal phrases and sitar string bends use it; in Western music, this kind of phrasing is called melisma.

In Time mode, glide ranges from zero to 10 seconds. Synced mode offers 1/32T, 1/32, 1/16T, 1/16, 1/8T, 1/8, 1/4T, 1/4, 1/2T, 1/2, and 1/1. In Rate mode, the time to glide within an octave ranges from immediate at 0 ms to more gradual at 10 ms.

Pressure can modulate Glide: set Glide as a Matrix destination and Pressure as the source, then adjust the Matrix attenuator. Different LFO waveforms produce different glide intensity and slope. With LFO Sync on, each note gets a different glide shape; changing the LFO rate changes the synchronized rate and the glide speed.

29.3 Auto Pan-Tremolo
Auto Pan-Tremolo uses LFOs to move a signal across the stereo field or vary its level: auto-panning, tremolo and gating.
Modes:
Panning — two LFOs shift level between left and right
Tremolo — one LFO varies level
The display shows the wave and, below it, the live pan position or level.
Waveform — Sine, Triangle, Shark Tooth, Saw Up, Saw Down, Square, Random, Wander, S&H
Time modes — Rate (Hz), Time (100 ms to 200 s, for long cycles), Synced, Dotted, Triplet, 16th
Stereo offset:
Phase — offsets the left and right waves in degrees; 180° is fully opposite
Spin — runs the two channels at rates that differ by a percentage
Random, Wander and S&H allow Phase only.
Phase Offset, in the beat-based time modes, moves each LFO's start against the beat grid. With Random, Wander or S&H it widens the stereo spread instead.
Invert flips the wave. With ramp waves, inverted gives ducking and normal gives gating.
Tremolo-only options:
Harmonic — splits the signal at a fixed 600 Hz and modulates highs and lows in alternation
Vintage — adds a non-linear curve for a warmer, grittier tremolo
Controls below the display:
Amount — modulation depth
the rate control, labeled Freq, Time or Rate depending on time mode. Amount and rate are shared by both modes.

Shape — in Panning, pushes the waves toward their limits for harder switches between channels; in Tremolo, rounds or sharpens the peaks. At the extremes it makes ramps for gating (Invert off) or pumping (Invert on).
Attack Time — how long after a transient the modulation reaches full depth, so attacks stay centered or keep their punch
Dynamic Frequency Modulation — louder input speeds up the LFO (positive) or slows it (negative)

01 Welcome and Introduction
Congratulations on your purchase of the Arturia MicroFreak!
The MicroFreak is a compact, versatile, semi-modular synthesizer with many distinctive features. It lets you experiment with modular sound construction without patch cords.

The standard MicroFreak and MicroFreak Vocoder Edition share the instrument's core features. The Vocoder Edition has a white casing and a gooseneck microphone; see Microfreak/UG/19 Appendix B Vocoder for its specific features.

Its digital oscillator and analog filter combine a broad range of digital sounds with a warm analog character. A cycling envelope adds modulation options associated with high-end modular systems, and the modulation matrix routes sources to many destinations.
The pressure-sensitive touch keyboard, paraphonic playing, arpeggiator, and assignable modulation destinations make the MicroFreak suited to expressive performance.
The MicroFreak is a USB MIDI Class Compliant device and can connect to compatible devices without installing drivers. Connecting an iPad may require a camera connection or USB-to-Lightning cable.
Two paraphonic sequencers can record and play up to four voices at once, sharing one filter; each sequencer has four modulation tracks.
Check the Arturia website for current firmware, MIDI Control Center, tutorials, and FAQs.

In this garden, Record Label pages model a label or imprint that releases music recordings.
What counts
A record label is the business or imprint named on a release. A label page collects the Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording pages it released.

31.1.2 Oscillators
Modeled oscillators, so no aliasing. Each has an on switch (Osc 1, Osc 2) and a level slider.
F1/F2 — balance between Filter 1 and Filter 2; centered sends equally.
Shape — sine, sawtooth, rectangular or white noise. Rectangular enables Pulse Width (100% is a square with odd harmonics only; low values sound thin), which an LFO can modulate.
Octave, Semi, Detune — tuning; Detune moves in cents, up to 300 cents either way.

Pitch Mod — LFO amount, and Key: how far pitch follows the keyboard. 100% is equal temperament, 0% ignores note pitch. C3 always plays the same frequency, so oscillators with different Key values move further out of tune with each other the farther you play from C3.
Pitch Env — Initial pitch and the Time to glide to the final pitch.

Sub/Sync — Sub adds an oscillator an octave down (square for saw or rectangle, sine for sine, off for noise) at a set Level. Sync restarts the waveform from a hidden oscillator whose rate rises with Ratio; 0% has no effect. Mapping Ratio to a mod wheel is a suggested use.

40.4 Variables Outside of Live’s Control
Timestamps only exist inside the computer. External hardware acts on MIDI as soon as it arrives.
MIDI cables are serial, so a chord's notes travel one after another; dense passages can smear timing.
Older synths may scan their own keyboards slowly, adding jitter. Problems multiply as more devices join the chain.
Live has to trust incoming timestamps and the handling of outgoing events, and can verify neither.
Tests and Results

Input test: a MIDI source feeds a zero-latency splitter. One branch records into a MIDI clip; the other goes through a MIDI-to-audio converter into an audio clip. The offset between matching events measures Live's accuracy.
Ableton tested three combined audio/MIDI interfaces, A, B and C, at about 50% CPU, on macOS and Windows, at 44.1 and 96 kHz and three buffer sizes: 36 configurations.

Results: most jitter fell within ±1 ms on every interface. Worst cases ranged from ±4 ms (Windows, A) to ±10 ms (Windows, C at 44.1 kHz / 1024 samples) and ±11 ms (macOS, A and B at 44.1 kHz / 1152 samples). Interface C on macOS stayed within ±1 ms in every test.
Output tests gave results comparable to input.

06.03.12 Modal Resonator (Modal)
Modal Resonator Oscillator Model

Description: A modal resonator imitates how an object's shape amplifies some harmonics and dampens others when it vibrates. This lets it mimic instrument bodies such as woodwinds, strings, and drums. It needs an exciter signal to produce sound, as a real instrument needs a bow, drumstick, or breath. Its harmonic structure and the instrument shape it mimics can change as a knob turns or a Matrix source such as the LFO or Envelope modulates it.
The resonator also controls how quickly the sound fades. Its damping can change with a knob or a Matrix source.
Inharm: Sets inharmonicity, or material selection.
Timbre: Sets excitation brightness and dust density.
Decay: Sets damping and decay time, which controls energy absorption.
Freaky idea: The MicroFreak is paraphonic. Arpeggiate or sequence chords while modulating damping to selectively dampen steps in the sequence or arpeggio.

31.2.7 Sound Design Tips
For a realistic marimba, follow the physical chain: the Mallet strikes a tuned bar (Resonator 1), and a tube (Resonator 2) amplifies it, in serial 1 > 2.
For unrealistic sounds:
Use the Noise exciter with long envelopes for washy, near-granular textures, or effects like bowed vibraphone and crystal glasses.
Try the parallel 1 + 2 structure.
Modulate with the LFOs and MIDI or MPE controllers.
The models are idealized and can respond far more strongly than real objects. Some settings jump sharply in volume, so keep levels low while experimenting.

31.3.7 Global Section
Mode — voice mode:
Poly — one voice per note, up to 32.
Mono — one note at a time drawn with four voices; Thickness raises the three extra voices from silent at 0. A new note chokes a held one.
Stereo — two voices per note panned apart by Spread.
Unison — four voices per note detuned by Strength.
Voices — total voices. At 32: Poly plays 32 notes, Stereo 16, Unison 8.
Drift — scales each voice's own random offsets to oscillators and filter; more sounds more out of tune.
Legato (Mono) — new notes change pitch without restarting envelopes; Glide sets the slide time.
Volume and Vel > Vol — level and how much velocity affects it.
Transpose — ±48 semitones. Note PB — per-note pitch bend on or off, so an MPE controller can be used without finger position changing pitch. PB Range — pitch bend range.
29.29 Phaser-Flanger
Phaser-Flanger combines a phaser, a flanger and a doubler in one device, with two LFOs and an envelope follower.
Modes, chosen in the display:

Phaser — modulated all-pass filters feed a phase-shifted copy back in, creating moving notches. The display shows the notches. Notches sets how many; Center their center frequency; Spread their spacing (all-pass Q); Blend routes modulation between Center (0.0) and Spread (1.0).
Flanger — a modulated, fed-back delay gives a moving comb filter. Time sets the delay; in the display, moving right shortens the delay and left lengthens it.
Doubler — modulated delays imitate stacked takes. Time sets the delay; modulation is bipolar, so right lengthens and left shortens.
The title bar button unfolds the device, showing more LFO options, LFO2, the envelope follower, Safe Bass and an LFO display.
Main LFO:
Freq/Rate — in Hz or synced, chosen with the Modulation Sync buttons

LFO Waveform — Sine, Triangle (default), Saw Up, Saw Down, Rectangle, Random, Random S&H, plus Triangle Analog (a filtered square that changes shape and level with rate), Triangle 8 and Triangle 16 (stepped in 8 or 16)
LFO Stereo Mode — Phase (left/right offset; 180° is inverted) or Spin (different rates per side)
Duty Cycle — squeezes the wave toward the start (100%) or end (−100%) of its cycle, like pulse width; no effect on Random and Random S&H
LFO2 is always a triangle. LFO2 Mix blends it with the main LFO (0% main only, 100% LFO2 only); LFO2 Freq/Rate sets its speed, free or synced with Modulation Sync 2.
Global:
Amount — modulation depth for both LFOs

Feedback — output fed back for a stronger comb-filter sound; in Doubler it also keeps echoing after playback stops. Ø inverts it for a hollow sound. High feedback can jump in level quickly — protect ears and equipment.
Env Fol with Envelope Amount (negative inverts) turns input level into modulation; Attack and Release set its response.
Safe Bass — high-pass from 5 Hz to 3000 Hz that keeps the effect off the lows
Output, Warmth (slight distortion and filtering), Dry/Wet (100% on a return track)

08.2.1 LFO Retriggering
LFO retriggering restarts the LFO each time you press a keyboard key or the arpeggiator or sequencer generates a gate signal. This can make the LFO add a small pitch rise at the start of each note.
To enable retriggering, open Utility and set Preset > LFO Retrig to ON.
32.2 Using Max for Live Devices

The Core Library includes Max for Live instruments, audio effects, MIDI effects and Modulators. They appear under the matching labels in the browser. Modulators control other parameters in Live with modulation signals.

The browser's Max for Live label lists every Max for Live device: built-in ones, ones from installed third-party Packs, and ones you have saved. It also holds Max for Live MIDI Tools, which transform or generate notes in MIDI clips.
Many Max for Live devices come with presets that behave like Live's own device presets.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: As of September 26, 2026, I found no official Ableton MCP server, CLI, or external agent API for Live 11, and no company-backed equivalent from Anthropic, OpenAI, or another major software vendor. Ableton does officially document two relevant integration mechanisms, but only one is a real public API for Live 11:

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Max for Live's Live API / Live Object Model is an official, documented way for Max devices to query objects, set properties, invoke functions, and observe changes in Live. It is exposed through live.object, live.path, live.observer, and the JavaScript LiveAPI object.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: MIDI Remote Scripts / Control Surfaces are officially supported as things users can install and select in Live, but Ableton's public documentation is essentially installation documentation, not a supported Python SDK. Projects built this way import Live's embedded Python modules such as Live, _Framework, and ableton.v2.control_surface directly—the same general machinery used by hardware control surfaces.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: The new Ableton Extensions SDK is not an answer for Live 11: Ableton says Extensions were introduced with Live 12.4.5 and its SDK is aimed at Live 12 Suite Beta 12.4.5 or later.

content.text: These security grades are the report’s threat-model assessment, not security audits. They weigh network exposure, arbitrary-code execution, telemetry, supply-chain hygiene, tool scope, transparency, and provenance.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: The most important distinction is that “uses the official Live Object Model” does not by itself mean “uses an official integration API.” Producer Pal reaches the LOM through Ableton's documented Max for Live API. Most of the other projects reach roughly the same world of Live objects through the embedded Python Control Surface machinery. Ableton supports installing those scripts, but the Python modules they consume are not presented by Ableton as a public application-development SDK. AbletonOSC makes the distinction unusually visible in source: it subclasses ableton.v2.control_surface.ControlSurface, imports _Framework.EncoderElement, and imports Live directly.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
What the Live 11 integration landscape actually looks like
content.text: For Live 11, there are effectively three architectural strategies.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
What the Live 11 integration landscape actually looks like
content.text: Max for Live LiveAPI is the cleanest supported programmatic substrate. Ableton's documentation explicitly describes the Live API as access to the Live Object Model and supports property access, function calls, observation, and device-parameter control. JavaScript in Max gets a LiveAPI object, while Max patchers can use live.path, live.object, and live.observer. A project can therefore put a Max device into the set, use Max's JavaScript or Node-for-Max facilities as a bridge, and expose an external HTTP/MCP interface. is the notable open-source implementation of this architecture.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
What the Live 11 integration landscape actually looks like
content.text: Remote Scripts are the pragmatic but unsupported-at-the-API-level alternative. Ableton explicitly tells users how to install third-party Remote Scripts into the User Library and select them as a Control Surface. The scripts can execute Python inside Live and interact with Live's internal object model. This is very powerful, and hardware-control-surface implementations have depended on it for years, but it creates exactly the engineering problem you alluded to with devices such as the Launchpad: projects are coupling themselves to Python modules and behaviors that are not documented by Ableton as a stable general-purpose SDK. AbletonOSC's source is representative: ControlSurface, _Framework, and Live are imported directly.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
What the Live 11 integration landscape actually looks like
content.text: The practical consequence is that Live-version compatibility is empirical. Wouter Stierhout's project is a good example: its September 17, 2026 release had to handle a Live-11-specific difference involving the embedded Python 3.7 environment and socket.timeout. That is precisely the sort of compatibility edge one expects when building against the Remote Script runtime rather than a conventional supported external SDK.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
What the Live 11 integration landscape actually looks like
content.text: OSC/MIDI layers can hide that coupling rather than remove it. AbletonOSC gives external programs a pleasant OSC interface and PyLive wraps that from Python, but AbletonOSC itself is still a MIDI Remote Script operating inside Live. Its README says its goal is to expose the Live Object Model through OSC, and explicitly requires Live 11 or later. This is nevertheless useful architectural separation: an agent can be restricted to sending defined OSC messages instead of receiving a generic Python-evaluation primitive.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
What the Live 11 integration landscape actually looks like
content.text: That last distinction matters enormously for agent safety. A coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex already has substantial authority on the host, depending on how you configure its sandbox and approvals. Giving that agent 100–300 narrowly typed Ableton mutations increases its authority over the DAW; giving it an eval endpoint inside the Live process introduces an additional general-purpose code-execution boundary.

content.text: Comparison of the viable offerings

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: is the standout because it is not another Remote Script clone. Its Max for Live device hosts a bridge built around Node for Max and Max's JavaScript/ v8 side, which then accesses the documented Live API. The project exposes both MCP and a REST API, so a coding agent does not even need MCP if it can issue ordinary local HTTP requests. The project is GPL-3.0 and explicitly positions itself as free/open-source with no subscription or paywall.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Its repository also looks substantially more like maintained software than a weekend MCP wrapper: source, Max device, examples, documentation, web UI, developer/contribution documentation, a security policy, lockfiles, and release machinery are all present. The author, , publicly describes himself as a software engineer with more than 20 years of full-stack experience, lists Playlab on his GitHub profile, and has multiple Ableton/music-software projects. That is the strongest creator-maturity signal I found among the Live-11-specific agent integrations.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Producer Pal's security work is unusually serious for this niche. Its security document states that released tools are scoped to Live rather than arbitrary filesystem/process operations; a generated-JavaScript execution facility exists in development source but is removed from release builds; release checks block dangerous flags; child_process, eval, and new Function are lint-blocked in shipped code; dependencies are pinned; a release cooldown is used; GitHub Actions are pinned to commit hashes; Dependabot and CodeQL are used; and signed commits/tags are the normal release practice starting with the 2.x line.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: But there is a surprisingly important counterweight: Producer Pal's local server is unauthenticated and, by the project's own security documentation, listens on port 3350 on all network interfaces rather than loopback only. The author explicitly calls this a known limitation and frames the threat model as a trusted local environment rather than an adversarial one. That means I would trust the software-development process more than most competitors while simultaneously disliking its default network boundary. On a laptop connected to an untrusted Wi-Fi or a home LAN containing less-trusted IoT devices, that matters.

content.text: It is also one of the projects with particularly clear Codex/Claude Code ergonomics: its documentation gives pinned commands such as uvx mcp-server-ableton-live@1.8.1, including direct codex mcp add and claude mcp add examples. Pinning the package version in the recommended install is a small but meaningful supply-chain improvement over documentation that simply executes whatever the current package version happens to be. Version 1.8.1, released September 17, 2026, specifically addressed a Live 11 embedded-Python compatibility issue, which is stronger evidence than a generic “Live 11 supported” badge.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: The creator, Wouter Stierhout, has a comparatively sparse GitHub footprint; public professional search results associate him with Hypersolid, but I found no evidence that Hypersolid publishes, supports, or endorses this project. I therefore regard the project as an individual developer's new open-source project, not a company-supported product. The abletonmcp.com marketing page is more confident than the project’s age warrants; the repository is a stronger trust signal. The phrase about there being no repository to clone appears to be trying to say that users can install the PyPI package with uvx, not that no source repository exists. The underlying design really is local: stdio MCP → loopback TCP → Live Remote Script.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: ahujasid/ableton-mcp is the adoption leader among the purpose-built MCPs I found. The inspected repository had roughly 3,100 stars, hundreds of forks, dozens of commits, active issues and pull requests, and straightforward support for Claude Code through uvx ableton-mcp. Its README says Live 10 or newer, so Live 11 is squarely in scope. Architecturally it is the classic approach: an MCP server talks over JSON/TCP to a Python MIDI Remote Script running as a Live Control Surface.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: The current Remote Script has a good network default: its source explicitly sets HOST to 127.0.0.1, warns in comments that the socket accepts unauthenticated DAW-control commands, and requires an explicit ABLETON_MCP_HOST override to widen the listener. That is a meaningful positive signal because it shows the maintainer has thought about the LAN threat rather than merely happening to use localhost.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Its biggest privacy caveat is telemetry. Anonymous usage telemetry is enabled by default and includes an installation identifier, per-run identifier, tool invocations, success/failure, and duration. The project says it does not include prompts, MIDI, clip/track names, or device settings. A separate dataset-recording feature can collect prompts, MIDI, names, and settings for a potential open training dataset, but that feature is off by default and requires opt-in. The project documents ABLETON_MCP_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true to disable the former as well. On a security/privacy-sensitive workstation, I would set that flag before first use.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: The creator, Siddharth Ahuja, has much stronger open-source credibility than a raw GitHub-profile count might suggest: his GitHub profile is centered on open-source AI integrations for creative software, and his Blender MCP project has accumulated very large adoption in addition to the Ableton project. I did not find strong enough evidence to assert a current employer or company backing, so I would classify his provenance as established independent open-source developer, rather than “engineer at a known company.”

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: AbletonOSC + PyLive deserves special treatment because it predates the agent/MCP rush and is arguably the most credible underlying open-source API stack. AbletonOSC has hundreds of commits and substantial community adoption, explicitly supports Live 11+, and exposes a broad Live Object Model-like surface over OSC. It even includes a simple run-console.py interactive CLI, so an agentic coding tool capable of operating a terminal can drive Live without MCP at all. PyLive provides a higher-level standalone Python interface on top of AbletonOSC and similarly targets Live 11+.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: For someone comfortable writing a thin adapter, this is attractive: instead of trusting 150–350 MCP tools and all their glue, you could give Codex/Claude Code a small Python package or a deliberately tiny MCP server implementing only the operations you need. The underlying creator, Daniel Jones / ideoforms, has a long public creative-technology/open-source history, dozens of GitHub repositories, and describes himself as an artist-researcher and technologist; both AbletonOSC and PyLive are established rather than AI-boom projects.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Unfortunately, AbletonOSC has the clearest network-security defect I found in a mature project. The actual server constructor defaults to local_addr = ('0.0.0.0', OSC_LISTEN_PORT), and its own source explains that this listens on every available local IPv4 interface. The UDP socket is then bound directly to that address. There is no authentication layer in the OSC protocol shown here. Because AbletonOSC provides mutating operations—track creation, parameter changes, playback, clip manipulation, and more—that means another machine able to reach UDP 11000 can potentially control the running Live instance. The README's statement that it “listens on port 11000” understates this important distinction.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: For my own system I would not run stock AbletonOSC on an untrusted network. I would change the listener to 127.0.0.1, firewall UDP 11000, or put it inside an OS-level networking sandbox. With that modification, AbletonOSC/PyLive becomes one of the options I like most because its conceptual surface is simple and mature.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Simon Kansara's ableton-live-mcp-server essentially turns AbletonOSC into an MCP stack. It uses an MCP server plus an OSC-facing daemon and requires AbletonOSC; the MCP-facing components default to localhost. Its repository had meaningful community interest but only around 18 commits when inspected, so much of its real maturity comes from the older AbletonOSC layer below it rather than from the MCP wrapper itself. The security trap is that putting a localhost MCP server in front does not fix AbletonOSC's own 0.0.0.0:11000/UDP binding. I found no comparably strong professional-maintainer provenance for this wrapper, so I would choose it for convenience, not because it improves the trust story.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: uisato/ableton-mcp-extended explicitly advertises Live 11+ and adds significantly more functionality around the same general Remote Script/socket design, including optional higher-performance UDP communication. The inspected project had nontrivial adoption, but its creator's public GitHub footprint is essentially centered on this project and I found no established-company affiliation comparable to the stronger examples above. Its optional ElevenLabs integration is outside the “free-only” criterion when it requires a paid external service, so I would evaluate only the core Ableton integration. More network transports and more tools are not inherently insecure, but they enlarge the amount of code and protocol surface one has to audit. Given that ahujasid and Wouter already cover this architecture with stronger security signals, I see little security-driven reason to prefer the extended version.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: AbletonBridge is the technically most expansive community project I found. Its current README describes 359 tools, with roughly 340 core tools, a Control Surface Remote Script over TCP/UDP, an optional Max for Live bridge for deeper access, an HTTP status dashboard, and explicit Live 10/11/12 fallbacks. It also claims 214 tests and documents measures such as input validation, size limits, concurrency controls, hard tool timeouts, bounded worker pools, and chunked communications. Those are better engineering signals than the project's modest GitHub popularity might suggest.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: On the other hand, this is an enormous authority surface. Its architecture includes TCP 9877, UDP 9882, optional OSC/UDP 9878/9879, and a web dashboard; the README explicitly shows the dashboard on 127.0.0.1, but in the material I inspected I did not find an equivalent security statement establishing authentication or loopback-only defaults for every Remote Script transport. The creator's own GitHub profile says they would like to work for Ableton or Anthropic, which is useful evidence that this is not an Ableton- or Anthropic-affiliated project. I would call it an impressive experimental project, not a trust-minimized production choice.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Finally, Ben Schoepke's ableton-live-mcp is worth knowing about precisely because its design illustrates what I would not expose to an autonomous coding agent on an important machine. The project's README explicitly says the agent can evaluate arbitrary Python running inside Ableton, while also providing optimized tools for common operations. That gives it extraordinary flexibility but largely destroys capability isolation: instead of “the agent may create a clip and set a parameter,” the primitive is effectively “the agent may execute Python in the DAW's embedded interpreter.” The author also warns users to back up sets, and the version I examined documented testing on Live 12 rather than Live 11, so I do not count it as a verified Live-11 option.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Interestingly, Schoepke has one of the better corporate-engineering provenance signals: in a public Swift discussion he previously identified himself as a UI developer on Microsoft's Windows team. I could not verify that as his current employment in 2026, so it should be treated as historical professional evidence rather than a current Microsoft affiliation. This is a useful reminder that creator pedigree and security architecture are separate axes: I would still reject arbitrary in-Live eval for a production agent integration.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Security and provenance findings

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: The most surprising result is that the projects with the best security stories are not necessarily the projects using the “most official” Ableton interface.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Producer Pal has the most mature security-development story. Its maintainer has published a real threat model, disabled dangerous execution paths in release builds, uses dependency and CI hardening, documents data flows, supports private vulnerability reporting, and explicitly acknowledges known limitations. Yet its all-interface unauthenticated port 3350 means its network default is weaker than Wouter's or the current ahujasid Remote Script. I would not conflate “excellent security process” with “safe defaults.”

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Wouter Stierhout's project has the best default capability/network combination I found. It exposes explicitly typed operations rather than Python eval, validates inputs, binds the Live-side socket to loopback, documents the lack of authentication, supplies pinned package invocation examples, backs up replaced scripts, maintains a server/Remote-Script version handshake, and runs tests and linting in CI. The reason I stop short of calling it the overall safest choice is maturity: roughly 20 commits and a tiny user population cannot tell you as much about weird edge cases as years of use can.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: ahujasid has the strongest crowd signal among direct MCPs. Thousands of GitHub stars do not prove security, but the combination of substantial adoption, active contribution, another highly successful creative-software MCP, explicit loopback binding, protocol size limits, and comments documenting the threat of widening the listener is meaningful. Its default telemetry is the reason I would harden the configuration before use.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: AbletonOSC has the strongest age/community-maturity signal but the weakest surprising default among the mature options. Nearly 300 commits, extensive API coverage, and a long creative-coding lineage make it much less “random AI-generated GitHub project” than most MCPs. But the 0.0.0.0 unauthenticated UDP endpoint is unambiguous in source. This is exactly the kind of thing I would catch before granting an agent access to it.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: There is also an important supply-chain distinction between cloning source and running package managers as an agent integration. uvx is convenient, but an MCP configuration becomes an implicit executable dependency. Wouter's examples pin mcp-server-ableton-live@1.8.1, whereas ahujasid's quickstart uses unversioned uvx ableton-mcp. For a workstation that matters, I would pin exact versions or Git commit hashes, review the corresponding source, and upgrade deliberately rather than allowing each launch to resolve an uncontrolled newer release. That is my recommendation based on the documented invocation patterns, not a claim that either package has experienced a compromise.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: The same goes for cloud versus local agents. A local Codex CLI/IDE or Claude Code process can reach loopback directly. Wouter's documentation explicitly notes that cloud execution cannot simply reach Live's loopback bridge. The right answer is usually to keep the DAW-control plane local, not to expose an unauthenticated DAW port or casually create a public tunnel. Producer Pal itself warns that tunnel URLs should be treated as secrets.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: For an AI agent, I would prioritize capability-limited tools over a generic interpreter even though Codex or Claude Code can themselves execute shell commands. These are different trust boundaries. A coding agent's host execution can be controlled with sandboxing and approval policies; an unrestricted eval endpoint inside Ableton places the Live process, Live's embedded runtime, and whatever that runtime can reach directly behind a model-selected tool call. Schoepke's explicit arbitrary-Python design therefore carries qualitatively more risk than the typed-tool approach used by Wouter and ahujasid.

content.text: Recommended shortlist

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: For Live 11 + an agentic coding tool + security sensitivity, I would narrow the landscape to four approaches.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Best overall architecture if Max for Live is available: Producer Pal. It is the only strong candidate I found that stays on Ableton's documented Max for Live API path rather than reaching into the Control Surface Python runtime. Its creator provenance, security documentation, release hygiene, MCP support, and REST API are all unusually good. I would, however, treat the default 0.0.0.0-equivalent network exposure on port 3350 as something to mitigate immediately with a host firewall or other local-network isolation. The project's own security policy acknowledges that it is unauthenticated and LAN-reachable. With that mitigated, this is my preferred option.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Best out-of-the-box network posture without Max for Live: wstierhout/ableton-live-mcp. It is the one I would test first with Codex CLI or Claude Code on a security-conscious workstation: loopback-only socket, no arbitrary Python tool, explicit security documentation, pinned installation examples, version-matched Live bridge, safe-ish installer behavior, and actual Live-11-specific compatibility work. The price is novelty. I would review the source and pin a known commit/version rather than assigning it the trust normally earned by years of deployment.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Best mature ready-made MCP ecosystem: ahujasid/ableton-mcp. It has vastly more adoption than Wouter's project and a creator with a demonstrated record of successful creative-application MCPs. Its current loopback binding is good. I would launch it with telemetry explicitly disabled and pin the package version rather than use the bare uvx ableton-mcp example.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: Best option for building your own minimal interface: AbletonOSC/PyLive, after fixing network exposure. For an AI architect, this may actually be the most appealing long-term design. AbletonOSC is older, smaller conceptually, Live-11-native, well understood, and already has both a programmatic OSC API and interactive console. Put it on loopback instead of its default 0.0.0.0, expose only a dozen commands through a tiny local stdio MCP server or CLI, and you have a much smaller reviewable trusted-computing base than a 300-tool agent framework. The stock wildcard bind is the part I would not accept.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: I would not make AbletonBridge or ableton-mcp-extended my first trust-sensitive choice despite their capabilities; both add a lot of code and interface surface without a corresponding improvement in maintainer provenance or security documentation over the top three. I would also exclude bschoepke's arbitrary-eval bridge from a security-conscious deployment and from the verified-Live-11 shortlist, notwithstanding the author's credible professional background.

ancestors: Open-source options for controlling Ableton Live 11 from Codex, Claude Code, and other agents
content.text: The broader conclusion is encouraging: Live 11 is not stranded for agentic control, but the strongest choices are community bridges rather than supported external automation APIs. If minimizing dependence on Ableton's private Python internals matters most, Producer Pal is in a class by itself because it builds on the documented Max for Live API. If minimizing network and arbitrary-code exposure matters most, Wouter's typed loopback MCP currently has the cleanest default design, albeit with very little age behind it. If longevity and auditability matter most, AbletonOSC/PyLive plus a small custom, loopback-only agent adapter is arguably the most conservative engineering foundation—provided you correct AbletonOSC's unsafe wildcard listener first.

Logseq Entity

This page is the general conceptual model for entities in this knowledge garden: what an entity is, how a page is marked as one, and how entity definition pages are named. The entity definitions are child pages of this page.
Terms

Entity — a single thing that has its own page in the garden: one person, one software project, one book, etc. A page models one or more entities. When it models more than one, it must satisfy the shape requirements of each.

Entity definition — the documentation page for a category of entities that share the same modeling rules. Each entity definition page describes how to recognize, name, and create instances of that kind; individual pages that meet those rules are its instances. Each entity definition page is itself an entity, modeled by Logseq/Entity/Definition.
Entity and type

When you write about the entity system, call each thing an entity and each page that describes one an entity definition. Use type only to compare the entity system with a type system, as does. When one entity descends from another, call them two entities in one lineage.

The entity system borrows ideas from type systems, and a page may differ from its entity definition while codekiln's idea of that entity is still changing. When codekiln first described the entity system in type-system terms, AI agents checked pages against their definitions like a type checker and asked "are you sure?" over every difference. codekiln brings pages into line with their definitions over time. An agent filing a new page follows its definition, and leaves an older page that differs as it was filed until codekiln asks for a change. and already say this about pages filed under older paths.
Finding the entity definitions

Each kind of entity has its own definition page under the Logseq/Entity/ namespace — one page per kind. The set of those pages is the list of entity definitions the garden models; there is no separate catalog to maintain on this page.

Every entity definition page carries logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Definition]], so the list of entity definitions is the backlinks of Logseq/Entity/Definition — queryable rather than hand-maintained.
The first line under an entity definition page's heading is its short description, so the definition pages together read as a self-describing index.
How we mark a page as an entity

Naming entity definition pages
All entity definition pages under Logseq/Entity/ use Title Case nouns. Multi-word names use nested namespace segments, for example Logseq/Entity/Software/Project.

Exception: tools and executables that are conventionally lowercase (e.g. tmux, git) may stay lowercase on their own topic pages, but entity definition pages are modeling nouns and use Title Case, for example .
Do not use kebab-case segments (e.g. software-project, color-theme) for entity definition page names.
Plural or contextual reference forms belong in alias:: on the entity definition page; instance naming follows Logseq/Frontmatter/alias.

10 The Keyboard Section

One of the first capacitive keyboards appeared on the EMS Synthi AKS. In 1972, Don Buchla introduced the Buchla Easel, whose touch-sensitive keys did not move and could produce accurate pressure and voltage-controlled portamento. The capacitive keyboard became a hallmark of the Easel, though few people could afford one. Decades later, the Arturia MicroFreak brought the capacitive keyboard back.
The MicroFreak has 25 capacitive keys. Hundreds of copper-colored dots on the surface register touch as either aftertouch or velocity, according to the Utility setting at Preset → Press.
The Touch Capacitive Keyboard
A Key in Close-Up

A capacitive keyboard makes the player part of its electrical circuit. Changing how much skin touches a key changes its resistance and the pressure signal it sends. Finger contact alone can reach about 30% of the pressure range; pressing more of the finger onto the key can reach 100%. This touch response helps make the MicroFreak a performance instrument.

The keyboard sends gate, pitch, and pressure signals. The Matrix can route these signals to any destination in its top row, and the outputs are also available on the back of the MicroFreak for modular gear or another synthesizer with voltage inputs.
Tip: Clean the keyboard occasionally with a soft, damp cloth. Avoid abrasives that could damage its surface. A dirty keyboard may produce unexpected musical results.

08.1 LFO Shape
The Shape button selects one of six waveforms: sine, triangle, rising sawtooth, rectangle (square), random (sample and hold), or random gliding (smoothed random).

The Random wave creates random modulations. For a familiar science-fiction computer sound, select Random, set the LFO speed to about 4 Hz, choose the LFO-to-Pitch crossing in the Matrix, then set the modulation amount to about 30.

Random gliding is a slewed random wave. Its pitch changes gradually between random values, unlike the abrupt changes of the Random wave. Routing it to oscillator pitch makes the modulation amount easier to fine-tune before applying it to another target.
The bottom half plays scale notes in real time; pressing a pad plays it and selects it for sequencing. Hold Select to choose without playing.
Pad colours: track colour for the root, lighter track colour for selected, green for playing, white for other scale notes.

Set Global Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Menu/Quantization to anything but None so clips are cut on time.
Arm the tracks; empty slots on armed tracks show Clip Record buttons.
Session Record records into the selected scene on every armed track; the new clips' launch buttons turn red. Press it again to switch straight to looped playback.
Or click one Clip Record button to record a single slot, and press the clip's Launch button to loop it.
A slot's Clip Stop button, or the Control Bar's Stop, stops the clip.
The New button stops clips on armed tracks and selects a scene ready for a new take, adding a scene if needed. It only appears in Key Map and MIDI Map modes, for mapping.

40.2 MIDI Timing Problems
Two problems keep computer MIDI from the ideal:

ancestors: Two problems keep computer MIDI from the ideal:
content.text: Latency — a constant delay. Audio has to be buffered on its way in and out of an interface. Players adapt to small delays as long as they stay the same; even a piano has some delay between key and string.

ancestors: Two problems keep computer MIDI from the ideal:
content.text: Jitter — a random, varying delay. MIDI, audio and the interface run as separate processes with separate clocks, and moving events between them depends on the operating system and drivers. Jitter, far more than latency, makes timing feel loose.

29.37 Spectral Time

Spectral Time combines spectral freezing and spectral delay. Filters, delays and frequency shifting resynthesize the input: sustain a sound forever, add timed fades, smear frequencies over time, or add metallic echoes.
Two sections, Freezer and Delay, used alone or in series (freezer into delay), switched with Freezer On and Delay On.
The spectrogram shows dry (yellow) and wet (blue) signals and can be hidden.
Zero Dry Signal Latency in the context menu passes the dry signal with no delay instead of aligning it with the effect — useful when playing an instrument through it live.

ancestors: 06.01 The oscillator as a sound generator
content.text: When you hear a sound, you hear air vibrating against the eardrum of your ear. As humans, we can hear frequencies in the range of 20 to 20,000 Hz. As you age your ability to hear high frequencies will gradually diminish. At 65 you'll probably hear only frequencies up to 6000 Hz. But that is enough to be able to enjoy timbral variations in music.

ancestors: 06.01 The oscillator as a sound generator
content.text: The ear can perceive sound around 50 Hz as bass (think huge organ pipes), but around 30 Hz it's difficult for the ear to hear a sound as a pitch; it's perceived as a low rumble. In electronic music, low-frequency sounds are often used as voltage or control signals to modulate another module. An LFO is an oscillator specifically designed to generate frequencies in this range. The LFO in the MicroFreak can generate signals in the range from 0.1Hz to 100Hz. Please refer to Microfreak/UG/08 LFO for details.

15 Using Scales

Scales can shape the emotion of a melody. Adding chord notes from the melody's scale strengthens its character: major notes may sound forceful and happy, while minor notes may sound sad. Responses to major and minor scales vary across musical cultures.

The chromatic scale contains twelve notes: C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F, F♯, G, G♯, A, A♯, B. A scale selects notes from those twelve. Most scales use eight notes; pentatonic scales use five, and blues scales use six, combining five pentatonic notes with one chromatic note.
C major, also called C Ionian, uses the white piano keys: C, D, E, F, G, A, B. The gaps between selected notes are whole tones or semitones. From C to D is a whole tone; from E to F is a semitone.
C major follows the interval pattern tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone.
C Major Intervals
Starting on D and playing only white keys gives the pattern tone, semitone, tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone. Applying that pattern from C produces a Dorian scale.
C Major Scale, Root D
C Dorian Scale
Starting a C major scale on its fifth step gives a Mixolydian scale. Building scales by starting on different steps creates the church modes, now widely used in western music.

Preset metadata over USB
Direct preset renaming is feasible through MIDI SysEx over USB. Elektroid implements the write sequence; the garden already has Python/RtMidi readers and full-preset backup support.
Investigation date: . Source inspection establishes write feasibility; Microfreak/CLI/Validation/26-10-03 slot 397 records successful hardware reads. Hardware writes remain untested.
Existing implementation
Elektroid MicroFreak connector provides preset listing, renaming, downloading and uploading. Its preset operation tables do not implement deletion.
Garden preset inventory and reconciliation reads saved names, categories and initialized status using python-rtmidi. Its writes update garden pages; it does not write presets to the instrument.

Garden full-preset download captures the header and sound data, with a manifest and checksums. The raw backup is a custom format, not an MCC-compatible .mfp or .mbp file. Initialized slots are rejected by this downloader, so backup support needs extending before a general CRUD tool can cover every slot.

Existing mise entry points are microfreak:sync, microfreak:download, microfreak:inspect and microfreak:compare. Inspection and comparison support examining exported preset data; they do not provide device writes.
Rename protocol
microfreak_preset_rename reads a saved preset header with operation 0x19, mode 0. The response uses operation 0x52.

The function edits the name in the returned header, sends the complete header using operation 0x52, then sends operation 0x52 with the preset address and mode 1. It finishes with a MIDI program change to select the renamed preset.
Rename sends the header without transferring the sound-data packets. A custom CLI should preserve every header field except the explicitly edited name or category.

Device slot addresses are zero-based; user-facing slots are 1–512. Name storage supports 14 characters. Elektroid accepts spaces, letters, digits, period, underscore and hyphen, replaces unsupported characters with periods, and truncates long names. A custom CLI could reject invalid input and show the accepted name before writing.

The protocol includes a sequence counter, response operation and payload length. The garden downloader already validates these and uses bounded response waits. A writer should additionally validate acknowledgments, slot identity and readback results.

Elektroid's rename selects the preset afterward. That can replace an unsaved edit in the active sound; device validation should determine whether selecting the preset is required for persistence or only for refreshing the display.
CRUD scope
Read: names, categories and initialized status are already decoded by the garden inventory script.
Update name: directly supported by Elektroid's header write sequence.
Update category: the category field is present in the same writable header, making the rename sequence a plausible implementation. A category-only write and readback need testing on the instrument.
Create: import a complete preset or copy an existing preset into a chosen slot. Elektroid implements full preset upload; slots are fixed storage locations rather than newly allocated records.

Delete: reset a slot to an initialized preset. Elektroid can serialize and upload initialized presets, but its preset connector exposes no delete operation. The reset behavior and persistence need device testing before exposing deletion.
Notes, tags and provenance: retain these in the garden. The inspected header and connector expose no arbitrary text metadata fields for these annotations.
Proposed CLI
Extend the garden's Python/RtMidi code with list, show, rename, update-category, backup and restore commands. Add copy/import and reset after the upload and initialized-preset paths have been tested.
Example command shapes: microfreak list --json, microfreak rename 395 "Evening Pad", microfreak update 395 --category Pad. These are proposed interfaces, not installed commands.

Before changing a populated slot, capture a complete backup and show the proposed metadata changes. After writing, download the preset again and check the requested metadata and unchanged sound data. Preserve backups for explicit restoration after a partial failure.

For bulk changes, use an explicit slot-to-change manifest and verify each completed slot. A failed transfer should report the uncertain slot and stop further writes; it should not blindly repeat a write.

Reconcile garden metadata after successful device verification. The existing sync script identifies presets by slot and name, so a rename can retire the old page and create a new page; preserving notes through a device rename needs an explicit migration path.
Podcast workflow
Workflow and implementation TODOs: Microfreak/CLI/Episode patch workflow.

episodes need a record of the saved MicroFreak slots created during recording, followed by renaming after the episode. Episode-linked capture and batch rename are the immediate prototype scope; general preset CRUD can follow as needed.

During recording, list each saved slot on the episode page, with its session order and an optional audio clip or recording timestamp. A capture task should attach the current name, a full preset backup and a fingerprint of the sound data, excluding mutable name/category metadata.

A slot number identifies a storage location whose contents can change. Before renaming after the episode, compare the saved sound fingerprint against the connected device. A mismatch requires identifying the original patch or choosing a restoration target before a write.

Prototype as thin mise file tasks over the existing Python/RtMidi code. Proposed interfaces: microfreak:episode-capture records selected slots against an episode page; microfreak:episode-rename previews convention-based names, then applies and verifies the selected changes. These tasks are not implemented.

Device name convention suggested by the existing export examples: GitP.YY.MM.DD.A, with the suffix following the episode's recorded patch order. GitP.24.11.23.A fits the 14-character device limit. GitP.2024.11.23.A is too long for device storage but can remain an export filename. Multiple sessions on the same date and suffixes beyond A–Z need an explicit naming rule.

The garden contains historical device names such as Microfreak/Preset/360 TMF.24.11.18.A. Episode links, patch backups and recording timestamps should remain attached to the same patch when its device name changes.

Preserve an episode patch identity independently of its current slot and name. Include the patch's episode order, captured sound fingerprint, original name, current device name, backup location and audio reference. The existing garden sync identifies a preset by slot and name, so note-preserving reconciliation needs extending for this workflow.

Future creative naming: associate a representative audio excerpt with each captured patch, generate candidate names with an audio-capable model, and select a name before applying it to the device. The excerpt's patch association must be recorded; filenames such as mf1 or mf ALL alone do not establish which saved preset produced the audio.

Retain the episode/date identity in garden metadata and export filenames when a creative device name uses the limited display space. Decide whether the preferred device display is the convention-based name, the creative name, or a compact combination before implementing automatic naming.

Audio-model selection and naming quality have not been evaluated. An excerpt records a performance, effects and recording conditions as well as the patch, so suggested names describe the recorded sound rather than proving a unique preset identity.

The local GitP script gitp-tools/gitp_tools/rename_tmf_to_gitp.py currently replaces GitP with GitP in filesystem names and text content. It does not implement a TMF-to-GitP conversion or device communication. It was inspected without execution.
Device validation

Test against the connected instrument's firmware. The inspected Elektroid connector requires firmware major version 5; this is an implementation constraint, not proof that other versions cannot support the protocol.

Microfreak/UG/04 Presets/02 Save Presets describes name/category editing and saving on the instrument. Microfreak/UG/14 Config/01 Utility & MCC/02 Global documents Mem Protect: Off permits overwrites, Factory Only protects factory presets, and On protects all presets.

Use a backed-up test slot to validate rename, category changes, restoration and initialized-slot handling. Verify the displayed result and persistence after reconnecting or restarting the instrument, as well as unchanged sound data after metadata edits.
Close MIDI Control Center during testing to avoid competing SysEx transactions. The garden reader already recommends this when a response times out.

USB renaming does not require controlling MIDI Control Center's UI. The remaining uncertainty is behavior on the connected instrument, especially category-only writes, resets and active-preset refresh.

29.1 Amp
Amp models seven classic guitar amplifiers, built with Softube using physical modeling. Every model uses the same controls.
Models:
Clean — the "Brilliant" channel of a 1960s amp associated with the British Invasion
Boost — the "Tremolo" channel of the same amp; edgy rock riffs
Blues — a bright 1970s amp popular in country, rock and blues
Rock — a classic 45-watt 1960s amp
Lead — the "Modern" channel of a high-gain metal amp
Heavy — the "Vintage" channel of that amp; metal and grunge
Bass — a rare 1970s PA with strong lows and fuzz at high volume
Gain drives the preamp and is the main distortion control. Volume sets the power amp stage; on Blues, Heavy and Bass, high Volume adds distortion too.
Bass, Middle and Treble shape the tone. As on real amps they interact with each other and with the rest of the amp in non-linear ways; raising EQ can add distortion.
Presence — extra mid/high tone control in the power amp stage, adding or removing edge; its effect varies by model
Output — mono or stereo (Dual); Dual uses twice the CPU
Dry/Wet — balance of processed and dry signal

A slow MicroFreak improvisation that moves from harmonic tones into a blurred, pitch-bent drone and closes with a virtual analog sound. Recorded in Ableton Live without spoken commentary.
Session notes

recalls MicroFreak presets 401 and 402, sequencer patterns A and B, short five-step sequences, paraphonic playing, and a change from the Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/03 Types/04 Harmo to Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/03 Types/06 VAnalog. The log does not pin either preset to an exact passage.

The Launchpad/UG/05 Session Mode controlled Live's pan, send, volume, record arm, stop clip, click, device, tap tempo, and fixed-length recording. The Launchpad/UG/09 Sequencer was not used; the sequences came from the Microfreak/UG/13 Sequencer.
00:00–03:30 · Harmonic opening

Sparse notes give way to sweeps of filter cutoff (CC 23, reaching 91), resonance (CC 83, reaching 74), filter amount (CC 26, reaching 84), and oscillator timbre, wave, and shape (CC 12, 10, 13); see Microfreak/UG/21 Appendix D - CC Values. The note count thins after 02:00 while those oscillator controls keep moving. The session log identifies the opening sound as Harmo, though the MIDI does not encode the loaded preset.
03:30–10:00 · Sequences and texture

Cycling envelope rise (CC 102) appears around 03:33. LFO sync rate (CC 94) changes around 04:33; the log recalls changing the LFO shape from sine to saw, but that waveform choice is not present in the CC capture. Spice (CC 2) begins around 06:24 and moves through values up to 82 during a denser run of notes. Around 09:34, a brief group of sequencer sync-rate changes (CC 92, up to 102) accompanies the transition into a quieter passage. See Microfreak/UG/13 Sequencer/01 Use/01 Select & Play for switching patterns A and B.
10:00–17:30 · Pitch motion

Pitch-bend messages return around 10:00 and continue through the middle of the recording. Cycling envelope amount (CC 24) enters around 12:10 and reaches 127. The log recalls routing cycling envelope and keyboard pressure to pitch through the Microfreak/UG/05 Connections/02 Matrix and Encoder/01 Sources and Destinations; the MIDI records the bend and envelope controls but cannot establish that internal routing. Oscillator type (CC 9) changes around 14:49, while the saved sound at that instant is unknown. Around 17:00, cycling envelope fall (CC 103), hold (CC 28), and rise (CC 102) changes join the filter sweeps.
18:00–26:53 · Drone and closing gestures

Long passages of cutoff and resonance movement, continuing pitch bend, and fewer notes make the middle more droning. From about 22:00, the note activity increases along with Spice, oscillator shape, timbre, and wave changes. Glide (CC 5) appears at 23:44 and rises as high as 31 in the final minutes. A further oscillator-type change (CC 9) occurs near 26:30; the log says the session ended on V.Analog, but the CC value alone does not identify that oscillator model.

These times follow the Ableton arrangement at a constant 56.818 BPM. The captured MIDI contains note and controller events from the “mf MIDI ALL” track. Microfreak/UG/21 Appendix D - CC Values identifies the controls; the GitP/A/Session/26/10/11-Sun/Asset/MIDI/Full/mid preserves their recorded values for inspection.

29.25 Looper

Looper is modeled on hardware looping pedals: record audio and overdub endlessly in sync with the Set. With the Set stopped, it can detect the tempo of what was played and set Live's tempo, or fit a recording to a chosen number of bars. Audio can be dragged in as a bed for overdubs, or out as a new clip.
The large display turns red while recording, then shows position and loop length in bars and beats.
Transport buttons:
Record — records until another button is pressed, replacing what was there
Overdub — adds layers the length of the first recording
Play — plays the buffer without recording
Stop — stops
With Live playing, Looper behaves like a clip and follows launch Quantization. With Live stopped, buttons act immediately.
Clear — erases the buffer. In Overdub with Live playing, tempo and length are kept; otherwise they reset.
Undo — removes everything overdubbed since Overdub was last turned on, keeping earlier passes; it then becomes Redo.

04.05 Understanding Digitally-Controlled Analog
Every MicroFreak module, including the analog filter, is controlled digitally. This combines the warmth and direct control of analog sound with the ability to save and recall presets and settings.
Knobs and sliders send instructions to the digital circuitry; they do not control voltages directly. After loading a preset, the physical control positions may not match the stored settings.
MIDI Control Center offers three ways to match a control's position to its stored value:

ancestors: MIDI Control Center offers three ways to match a control's position to its stored value:
content.text: Hook: Move the control until it reaches the stored position; it has no effect before then.

ancestors: MIDI Control Center offers three ways to match a control's position to its stored value:
content.text: Jump: The value jumps to the control's position as soon as it moves.

ancestors: MIDI Control Center offers three ways to match a control's position to its stored value:

3.14 The Mixer
A clip's signal passes through the track's device chain from left to right and then into the mixer, which Session and Arrangement share.
Device-to-device connections are always stereo; inputs and outputs can be set to mono in the Audio Settings.

23.2.2 Device A/B Comparison
Every built-in device holds two states, A and B, with separate parameter values, for comparing edits — useful for presets, EQ and compression.
On loading, A and B are the same. Edits go to A while B keeps the starting values.
Compare: Copy A to B (Edit menu, context menu or Show Options) copies values across; Compare: Switch to B, or P, switches state. The title bar shows "(B)" while B is active.
Not available for Racks, Max for Live devices or plug-ins.
Automation belongs to one state: switching disables it, and switching back doesn't re-enable it. Use Re-Enable Automation in the parameter's context menu in the state you want.
Copying a device, or saving it as a preset, takes only the active state's values and uses them for both A and B.

13.3.3. Second Experiment: Hoketus
Hoketus keeps one pitch while changing timbre, articulation, and rhythm. On the MicroFreak, use modulation tracks to change parameters while the sequence repeats that pitch.

Create a 16-step sequence with the same pitch at every step. Add rests and ties for rhythm, then press Record while playback is stopped. Turn a control to capture its position, use Rate/Swing to move to the next step, and repeat. Up to four controls can change across the pattern.
Variation: To imitate a monochord, use one or two modulation tracks to introduce nearby pitches around the repeated central pitch.
