6.8 Audio Clip Fades and Crossfades
Audio clips have fades at their start and end; neighbouring clips on a track can crossfade.
Hover over a clip, in a tall enough track, to see the fade handles as small squares at its edges. In Automation Mode, hold F over an automation lane to show them.
Fade In Start and Fade Out End handles change a fade's length without moving its peak; the Fade Curve handle shapes it.
Selecting time that includes a clip's start or end and choosing Create → Create Fade In/Out, Cmd+Option+F (Mac) / Ctrl+Alt+F (Win), sets the fade to that length.
Crossfade by dragging a fade handle over the neighbouring clip's edge, or select across the boundary and choose Create Crossfade. The slope handle shapes it.
Delete removes a selected fade, unless Create Fades on Clip Edges is on in Record, Warp & Launch Settings; then it resets to 4 ms, and adjacent clips get automatic 4 ms crossfades to prevent clicks.
Fades can't cross a clip's loop boundaries, and a clip's two fades can't overlap. A dotted line shows a selected handle's limit.
Fades belong to clips, not tracks, and are separate from automation.

An analysis file (Ableton/File/.asd) sits next to its sample with the same name. It improves warping quality, detects the tempo of long samples, and speeds up waveform drawing. Long samples stay grayed out and unplayable until analysis finishes.
.asd files don't show in the browser; a checkmark on a sample's icon means one exists.

The Save Default Clip button in a clip's title bar stores the clip's settings, such as Warp Markers, in the .asd, so the sample loads that way in future Sets. It doesn't change clips already in other Sets, and unlike a Live Clip it stores no devices.
A sample with an .asd isn't analyzed again. Long samples aren't analyzed when Auto-Warp Long Samples is off.
Create Analysis Files = Off in File & Folder Settings stops writing .asd files, so samples are analyzed on every load. Existing files stay, and Save Default Clip still writes one.

In this garden, Series pages model an ordered sequence of another entity type — a named run of works that should cluster together, and appear in intended order, when paths are sorted .
Combined with another entity
Series is not a standalone kind of work. A page that belongs to a sequence declares both types, primary entity first: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Book]], [[Logseq/Entity/Series]].
The hub that names the sequence may declare Series alone, or Series plus the member type when the sequence is also treated as one work.
Any entity type that has ordered installments can combine with Series: books, podcast episodes, talks, courses, essay runs, software version lines, and others.

Music Performance
In this garden, Music Performance pages model a particular event or session in which a musical work is performed.
What counts
A performance is an occurrence, not the abstract work and not a recording of the occurrence.
A live rendition at a concert or awards show is a performance. An improvised studio or home session may also be modeled as a performance when it has a distinct identity worth revisiting.
An audio or video capture of the event is a separate Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording when the recording itself needs a page.
Naming and placement
Place a performance under its principal performer as Person/<Performer>/Music/Performance/<Date or Event>/<Work>.
Use the event date or a stable event name to distinguish repeated performances of the same work.
A session of several works may use one event page with an ordered set of work:: links.
Relationships
Use work:: for the performed work, performer:: for performers as defined at Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording/Frontmatter/performer, and recording:: for a recording page that documents the event.
Link an event or venue when its page exists. A performance's date-created:: is the date of the event when known.
Instance shape
Start each performance page with logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Music/Performance]] and one H1 naming the performance.
Add the event date, work::, performers, and a source link when available.

25.5.4 Chain Select Zones
Chain select zones let one parameter, the draggable Chain selector above the 0–127 scale, choose which chains can play. Only chains whose zone overlaps the selector's value produce output.

Probability is the chance a note plays on each pass. The Chance Editor lane is hidden by default; show it from the Lane Selector menu.

Press Pattern to generate a semi-random arpeggio from keys played legato. Each new key press generates a new pattern.

31.8.9 Filters
Filter A and Filter B have their own on switches, a Frequency knob, 17 types and two macros per type, most often Q (emphasis at cutoff) and Drive (input saturation).
Types:
SVF 12dB / 24dB — state variable; L-B-H-N morphs low-pass, band-pass, high-pass and notch.
MS2 — low- and high-pass from a Sallen-Key design in a well-known Japanese semi-modular mono synth, with soft clipping on resonance.
OSR — band-pass from a rare British mono synth, resonance limited by a hard-clipping diode.
LP Crunch 12dB — feeds its own distortion back in.
LP Switched Res — resistors replaced by fast switches for downsampling artifacts; Lofi high is crushed, low is smoother.
Filther — low-pass with hard diode clipping in and soft saturation out.
Eq Peak / Eq Notch — Boost or Cut around the cutoff.
Phaser — six-stage with Feedback and notch Spread.
Redux — resampler and bitcrusher; Crush sets bit depth, Lofi mixes filtered downsampled signal with raw artifacts.
Vowel — formant filter; Morph moves between vowels.
Comb + / Comb - — feedforward and feedback combs with Feedback and Damp.
Plate Resonator — 32 modes of a rectangular plate; size, resonance and ratio. Scale-aware.
Membrane Resonator — 32 modes of a round membrane; size, resonance and high-frequency damping. Scale-aware.

Bebop Dorian Scale
Also called the bebop minor scale. On C, in the form most reference lists give: C D E♭ E F G A B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 1 1 2 2 1 2. Music/Scale/Dorian with an added chromatic passing tone.
History
The bebop scales are a teaching abstraction of the eighth-note lines of , and their contemporaries. 's method books from the popularized the family: bebop dominant, bebop major and bebop minor.
The names came decades after the music. They describe a habit of chromatic passing tones that pedagogy later fixed into eight-note collections.
Use
An eight-note scale run in eighth notes from a chord tone on the beat puts chord tones on every downbeat.

With the added major third, the collection equals the bebop dominant scale a fourth above (F G A B♭ C D E♭ E). A line descending from F puts F, E♭, C and A on the beats, so one line serves both chords of a ii–V in B♭, Cm7 and F7.
With the added major seventh, a line descending from C puts C, B♭, G and E♭ on the beats, the chord tones of Cm7 itself.
The added note is a passing tone, never a resting point.
Quirks
Sources disagree on which note to add. The major-seventh form, C D E♭ F G A B♭ B, matches the MicroFreak manual's spelling of its "Minor" setting in Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings.
The Launchpad manual names a "Bebop Dorian" setting without listing its pitches.

31.12.2 String Tab
The string's physical properties and how it is played.
31.12.2.1 The Exciter Section
With the Exciter off, only the damper can move the string. With Exciter and Damper both off there is no sound.
31.12.2.2 Exciter Types
Bow — sustained vibration from stick-and-slip friction, as on violin, viola and cello. Damping is unavailable.
Hammer — strikes from below once and falls away, as in a piano.
Hammer (bouncing) — dropped from above and may bounce, as on a hammered dulcimer.
Plectrum — snaps the string, as on a guitar or harpsichord.
31.12.2.3 Exciter Parameters
Type-specific: Bow has Force (more is scratchier) and Friction (more gives a faster attack); the Hammers have Mass and Stiffness; Plectrum has Protrusion (less is thinner) and Stiffness.

Shared: Velocity — how fast the exciter hits. Position — 0% at the termination, 50% at the midpoint. Damping — how much impact force the exciter absorbs; for the bouncing hammer it sets the stiffness of its spring, and more makes a shorter, louder, brighter contact.
Fix. Pos — keeps the contact point fixed regardless of string length, like a guitar pick. Leave it off for a piano, whose hammers strike about 1/7 of the length.
Vel and Key modulate by velocity and pitch. Some combinations produce no sound.
31.12.2.4 The Damper Section
Dampers mute the string, like felt in a piano or a player's fingers, and make sounds of their own.
Mass — how hard it presses; more mutes faster. Stiffness — felt to metal. Very high values can shorten the string and change its tuning.
Velocity — how fast the damper lands at key release and lifts at key press; very high values can make a loud release. Works only with Gated on; with Gated off the damper stays on the string.
Position, Fix. Pos and Key sliders as in the Exciter.
Damping — overall absorption. Above 50% the damper gets stiff enough to bounce, which lengthens decay again; try it on one repeated key.
The String Section
Decay with < Key. Ratio — shortens release decay relative to onset decay.
Inharm — real strings are inharmonic, more so when thicker; raising it detunes upper partials.
Damping with < Key — more high partials at higher values.
The Vibrato Section
An LFO on pitch: Delay, Attack, Rate, Amount, < Mod (mod wheel depth relative to Amount) and Error (random variation of rate, amount, delay and attack).
31.12.2.5 The Termination Section
Models finger, fret and string, which set the string's working length. Finger Mass (with Vel and Key), Finger Stiff and Fret Stiff.
31.12.2.6 The Pickup Section
An electromagnetic pickup. Position 0% at the termination is brighter and thinner; toward 50% is fuller.
The Body Section
The body radiates and filters the string's energy; some, like guitars, have an air cavity that boosts lows.
Body Type after real instruments, Body Size XS to XL (larger is lower), Decay, Str/Body (dry string versus body; fully left bypasses the body), Low Cut and High Cut.
Volume sets the overall output and is also on the Filter/Global tab.

06.03.14 BASS Oscillator (Bass)
BASS Oscillator Model

Description: The BASS model is a quadrature oscillator with Sine and Cosine inputs. The Sine oscillator feeds a balanced modulator, and its output mixes with the modulated Cosine oscillator. Saturate, Fold, and Noise control the modulation model.
Saturate: Sets the saturation of the Cosine oscillator.
Fold: Applies a two-stage asymmetric fold that adds harmonics by folding parts of the wave that fall outside set boundaries back onto the wave. Don Buchla pioneered wavefolding in the early 1970s.
Noise: Sets the noise level. Noise phase-modulates the two oscillators in opposite phases and is added between the fold stages.

30.6 Random
Random changes the pitch of incoming notes at random.
Chance is how likely each note is to be changed, like a dry/wet for randomness.

Choices (1–24) and Interval multiply to give the spread of possible pitches above, below or around the played note. With Chance 50%, Choices 1 and Interval 12, repeated C3s play C3 or C4. With Choices 12 and Interval 1, they play C3 or any note from C to C4. (Both examples use Random mode and Add.)
Mode:
Random — pitches in no order

Alt — steps through the possible pitches in a fixed cycle. Chance 100% always moves to the next pitch; 0% always plays the incoming note. With Choices 12 and Interval 1, repeated C3s climb a semitone at a time to C4 and start over; with Choices 2 and Interval 2, they alternate C3 and D3 — useful for up-bow/down-bow or left/right hand samples.
Sign:
Add — only higher pitches
Sub — only lower pitches
Bi — either
LEDs beside Chance flash +, 0 or - for a higher, unchanged or lower note.

04.03 Tweaking the Preset Configurations
Utility contains settings that change how the current preset behaves. Each preset saves its own settings, so presets can differ in voice mode, pressure response, sequence length, and other behavior.

Changing Utility > Preset settings can reshape a sequence. For example, change Glide Mode from Time to Rate, turn on Envelope Reset for a snappier sequence, or change Seq (1–4) Smooth to hear how smoothing affects its mood.
The following preset parameters can be edited in Utility. None can be edited in MIDI Control Center.
Voice
Bend Range [0–24]: Sets the range from zero to two octaves.
Glide Mode [Time, Sync, Rate]: Selects time-based, tempo-synced, or rate-based glide for the Glide knob.
Unison Spread [0.001–12.000]: Sets the spread between the four voices.
Unison Count [2–4]: Sets how many voices take part in Unison mode.
Modulations
Envelope Legato [Off, On]: Resets the envelope on a keyboard trigger.
Envelope Snap [Off, On]: Creates a sharper envelope decay.
LFO Retrig [Off, On, Legato]: Sets whether the LFO retriggers, retriggers on a keyboard trigger, or does not retrigger during legato playing.
Press Mode [Aftertouch, Velocity]: Selects the pressure mode.
Key/Arp Mode [Linear, Random]: In Random mode, generates a new random value for each key pressed.
Velo Amp Mod [0–10]: Sets how velocity affects the output volume.
Preset Volume
Preset Volume [−12 to +12]: Sets the preset's relative volume.
Scale
Scale: Selects Global, Off, Major, Minor, Harmominor, Dorian, Mixolydian, Blues, or Penta.
Root Note: Selects C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F, F♯, G, G♯, A, A♯, or B.
Seq/Arp
Seq Length [4–64]: Sets the sequence length.
Default Gate Length [5–85]: Sets the default sequencer or arpeggio gate length; the default is 45.
Seq 1 Smooth [Off, On]: Smooths the sequencer MOD track 1.
Seq 2 Smooth [Off, On]: Smooths the sequencer MOD track 2.
Seq 3 Smooth [Off, On]: Smooths the sequencer MOD track 3.
Seq 4 Smooth [Off, On]: Smooths the sequencer MOD track 4.
Vocoder
Vocoder Hiss Mode [Off, Switched, Pass]: Sets whether hiss is heard while using the vocoder.
Vocoder Hiss Volume [−20 to 0]: Sets the vocoder hiss volume.

3.7 Tracks
Tracks hold clips and manage signal flow: recording, synthesis, effects and mixing.
Session and Arrangement share one set of tracks, shown as columns in the Session and as stacked rows in the Arrangement.
A track plays one clip at a time, so clips that alternate go in the same Session column, and clips that play together go across a row, called a scene.

A track plays a Session clip or an Arrangement clip, never both, and Session clips win. A track that switched to a Session clip stays off the Arrangement until you press Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View/Button/Back to Arrangement, found in the Main track in Session View, at the top right of the scrub area, and on each Arrangement track.
Pressing Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Button/Arrangement Record from Session View captures the Session into the Arrangement.

Synth Preset
In this garden, Synth Preset pages model saved synthesizer sounds and the evidence needed to describe or restore them.
Identity and notes

A saved sound includes the settings and sequences stored by its instrument. A device slot is its current location. Stable page titles preserve links from composition and performance logs when metadata changes.

The name appears once in the filename and once in its instrument-specific name property. The body starts with - # Notes and holds listening observations, performance notes and links to music logs. Empty notes remain a heading without generated descriptions.

Sync owns documented device metadata in frontmatter and preserves handwritten body content. Sound descriptions require listening or verified parameters; a category and name cannot establish a signal chain.
Frontmatter
An instance’s logseq-entity:: links to its data definition, using the narrowest known type such as Logseq/Entity/Preset/Synth/Microfreak. Shared properties follow Logseq/Frontmatter.

Keys start with the owning type’s lowercase, hyphen-separated path: Preset/Synth gives preset-synth-; Preset/Synth/Microfreak gives preset-synth-microfreak-. Each property is documented under its owner’s Frontmatter/<literal-key> page as a Logseq/Entity/Frontmatter/Definition.

Each property definition has the literal key as an alias, connecting the clickable property name to its namespaced dictionary. Logseq Properties describes property pages; Logseq aliases describes alias references. Existing standalone pages with the same key need reconciliation before adding an alias.

Categorical values are explicit links to the definition’s child value pages; numeric and Boolean values retain their scalar types. A linked instrument model can supply an existing categorical vocabulary.

Numbered collections use and for adjacent populated slots. A page absent from the device has neither navigation property.
Preserving a sound

Human-readable properties describe verified parameters. Exact exports preserve data that may still lack a decoded dictionary. A complete reconstruction also needs referenced samples or wavetables, applicable global settings and the firmware context.

New parameter definitions state the source encoding, units, range, enum values and conversion, including raw values when a display conversion loses precision. Unknown parameters remain absent. A file digest identifies the exported bytes; it does not establish that every parameter has been decoded.

16.7 Follow Actions

A Follow Action decides what happens next in a clip's group after it plays. A group is the run of clips in adjacent slots of one track; empty slots separate groups. Scenes have Follow Actions too, in the Scene View.
Controls
Follow Action button — turns Follow Actions on for the selected clip or scene; off by default; Shift+Enter.
Follow Action A and B — two actions to choose between.
Chance A and Chance B — the relative probability of each. A at 100% and B at 0% always picks A; raising B to 90% makes A happen about one launch in ten. The slider between them adjusts both.
Linked/Unlinked (clips only) — Linked fires at the end of the clip, or after the number of loops in the Multiplier field. Unlinked fires after the Follow Action Time.
Follow Action Time — bars-beats-sixteenths from where play starts; one bar by default. A draggable marker shows it in the clip editor.
The ten Follow Actions
No Action — nothing happens, and once chosen, the other action no longer gets a chance.
Stop — stops the clip after the Follow Action Time, overriding its loop settings.
Play Again — restarts the clip.
Previous — plays the clip above.
Next — plays the clip below, wrapping from the last to the first.
First and Last — play the top or bottom clip of the group.
Any — plays any clip in the group.
Other — like Any, but never repeats the current clip while there are others.
Jump — plays a chosen slot or scene, set with the Jump Target slider.
Clips and scenes with Follow Actions show a striped launch button.
Follow Actions bypass global quantization but respect clip quantization other than None or Global.

The Enable Follow Actions Globally button, next to Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View/Button/Back to Arrangement, turns every Follow Action in the Set on or off, which is handy for editing a running clip. It is greyed out when the Set has none.
Clip Follow Actions keep running when a scene Follow Action is scheduled, but scene Follow Actions win once they fire.
Follow Actions let loop-based music repeat yet still surprise; recording the results gives new material.

Arm a track to record its input. Selecting several tracks and arming one arms them all; Cmd-click (Mac) / Ctrl-click (Win) arms several. With Exclusive Arm on, adding an instrument to an empty MIDI track arms it. See .

06.03.22 Vocoder Oscillator (Vocoder)
Vocoder Oscillator Model
This oscillator acts as the Vocoder's carrier and provides waves rich in overtones. Select the waveform with the Wave encoder.

Wave: At 0%, it produces a sawtooth. Around 11%, it becomes a pulse wave with a 50% duty cycle. From there the pulse width increases clockwise until it reaches a 99% duty cycle at 90%. From 91% to 100%, it produces noise.

Timbre: Changes the frequency range used for analysis and resynthesis. Voice formants are frequency peaks; for example, a “U” often has peaks near 330 Hz and 1260 Hz, with variation across speakers and cultures. The synthesis filters recreate the input loudness contour in the selected range. Narrowing the range reduces the frequencies the Vocoder monitors, improving response time and frequency output.
Shape: Sets the bandwidth of the individual bandpass filters. Higher settings narrow the frequency response, emphasizing more pronounced harmonics.

29.24 Limiter

Limiter is a mastering-grade limiter that keeps the output below a set level — a compressor with an infinite ratio. It belongs on the Main track to prevent clipping in the converters. Compression basics are in Ableton/Live/UG/29 Audio Effect Reference/09 Compressor.
Ceiling — the maximum output level; signal that never reaches it is untouched
Gain Reduction meter — current reduction at the ceiling or threshold

Link — how much gain reduction the two channels share (L/R or M/S, per Routing Mode). 100% keeps the stereo image steady; 0% limits each channel separately, for split signals or a deliberate stereo wobble.
Input Gain — level into the limiter
Maximize — turns Ceiling into Threshold, so one control sets loudness: lowering it raises the output by the same amount. Input Gain becomes Output, the target level.
Release — how long limiting continues after the signal drops. Fast is louder and punchier; slow is smoother but can flatten dynamics. Auto sets release from the material and disables Release.
Lookahead — 1.5, 3 or 6 ms. Shorter allows more limiting but can distort, especially bass; longer catches very fast peaks. Longer lookahead adds latency.
Ceiling Mode:
Standard — default
Soft Clip — soft-clips near the ceiling for color and punch; an LED flashes when clipping
True Peak — prevents inter-sample peaks
Routing Mode:
L/R — channels limited separately; more limiting, some stereo image distortion
M/S — limits in mid/side; keeps the stereo image but adds latency
Anything after Limiter can raise the level again. To be sure the output never clips, put Limiter last on the Main track and keep the Main volume below 0 dB.

07 The Filter: sound in close-up
A filter emphasizes or suppresses harmonics in a sound, changing its timbre. It is traditionally paired with an oscillator; the MicroFreak's analog filter shapes the sound of its Digital Oscillator.
The Analogue Filter
Think of the Analog Filter as a searchlight moving over the oscillator's waveform, revealing its harmonic content. Its beam can be broad or focused; the focused width is called Q or resonance.

A sound contains sine-wave frequencies at different loudness levels. These frequencies often form families around a fundamental frequency, with related harmonics above it. The mix of odd and even harmonics largely determines a sound's character. A filter favors some frequencies and attenuates others.

19.2.2. The Perfect Modulator: Your Voice
A useful vocoder sound depends on pairing the modulator with a suitable carrier. Speak or sing with clear, even exaggerated articulation to drive the analysis filters.

Plosives such as “p,” “t,” and “b,” and sibilants such as “s,” “ch,” and “z,” can confuse the filter banks. The vocoder's high-pass filter helps remove them. Its hiss function can add high-frequency energy to help the filters respond.

06.03.05 Karplus-Strong (KarplusStr)
Karplus Oscillator Model

Description: Karplus-Strong is a sound synthesis method developed by Kevin Karplus and Alex Strong at Stanford University. It creates realistic drum and plucked-string sounds by looping a short noise burst through a filtered delay. This physical modeling approach recreates an instrument's physical characteristics digitally, such as string bow position, striking force, and the materials' diffusion and damping.
In physical modeling, an exciter creates vibrations in a resonator. The exciter can be a bow or a strike, and the resonator can emulate many instrument shapes.
Bow: Sets how much bow is added on top of the strike. Bowing creates a continuous tone, while a strike alone creates a decaying tone.
Position: Controls where and how hard the resonator is struck. It does not affect the bowed part of the sound.
Decay: Sets the resonator's resonance by controlling its decay.

3.4 Sound Similarity

Live analyzes sounds to support two features: Similarity Search, which lists Core Library and User Library items that sound like a reference, and Similar Sample Swapping, which replaces samples in Drum Rack, Simpler or Drum Sampler.

Similarity Search works on samples up to 60 seconds long, instrument presets and drum presets. Open it with the Show Similar Files icon next to a selected file, the context menu, or Cmd+Shift+F (Mac) / Ctrl+Shift+F (Win). Results run from most to least similar.
Analysis runs in the background on new user audio files and can be paused from the Status Bar. Core Library content comes pre-analyzed.

19.2.3.1. Timbre Encoder

Timbre selects the frequency range used for analysis and resynthesis. Vowel formants peak at different frequencies: for example, a “u” may have peaks near 330 and 1260 Hz, with variation across voices.

Matching the range to the speaker, or to an instrument used as a modulator, helps the filters respond to the frequencies that matter. Monitoring fewer frequencies can improve response time and output.

31.11.1.1 Classic Playback Mode
The left and right flags bound the usable region. Start and Length are percentages of it; Length 50% plays half. Loop sets how much loops, when the Loop switch is on.
Very short loops turn glitchy or granular, or pitched at audio rates, and can load the CPU heavily, especially in Complex warp modes.
Snap puts markers on zero crossings of the left channel, so stereo samples can still click. Fade crossfades loop end into start, useful for long textures.
Gain — sample level, separate from the final Volume after the filter.
Voices — when exceeded, the oldest voices are stolen.
Retrig — replaying a sounding note cuts it off; off lets copies overlap. Audible only with long releases and more than one voice.
31.11.1.2 One-Shot Playback Mode
Flags set the region; no Loop, Length or Voices, and always monophonic.
Trigger — plays on after note-off, so hold length doesn't matter. Gate — starts fading at note-off over the Fade Out time.
Fade In — time to full volume; Fade Out — starts that long before the region end.
Snap applies to the start and end flags only.
31.11.1.3 Slicing Playback Mode
Slice By:
Transient — at transients; Sensitivity sets how many, up to 64.
Beat — at a beat Division.
Region — a number of equal Regions.
Manual — double-click to add slices.
Playback — Mono plays one slice at a time; Poly plays several, with Voices and Retrig; Thru is monophonic but plays on to the end of the region.
Trigger/Gate as in One-Shot. Fades span each slice in Mono and Poly, or from the triggered slice to the region end in Thru.

Automatic slices are blue and manual ones white. Drag to move, double-click to delete; in Transient mode, Option-click (Mac) / Alt-click (Win) toggles a slice between manual and automatic. Manual slices survive Sensitivity changes.

Creating an instance

Choose the topic namespace first. It is the domain or tool the question is about — Claude Code, git, LangSmith, EdTech/Idea/LearnMark. Infer it from the question when the human did not name one; ask rather than guess when nothing plausible presents itself.
Keep the question's full wording, punctuation included, as the page title. Normalize trailing ? for searching only.
The filing is recorded in today's journal like any other graph edit — a new page under [[Filed]], an edited one under [[Updated]], per .
Commit the drafted question page and its journal entry by default, unless the human asks to leave them uncommitted.
Answering an instance
Filing and answering are one pass: once the page and its journal line exist, research the answer rather than leaving a bare question.
Draw on whatever is at hand — the garden's own pages first, then official documentation, then web search. Prefer a source that can be cited over recollection.
Write the answer into ## [[AI Answer]] per Page shape above, marking it [[Answer/Official]] when it comes from official docs.
When the answer cannot be settled, say so on the page and tell the human what is missing. An honestly open question is worth more than a confident wrong one.
Relationship to other types
Card: [[card]] on the H1 plus [[Logseq/Entity/Card]] in frontmatter when the question page itself is reviewable; distinct from factoring a prompt into a /Card/ namespace page under .
CLI commands / flags: questions about commands link to and instances; they are not substitutes for command reference stubs.
Legacy instances
Older ___Q___ pages may lack logseq-entity::, use ## Related for internal links (use see-also:: instead), or use ## [[AI/Response]] as the section heading instead of the correct form.
Do not bulk-migrate unless requested; new pages should follow the rules above.

Natural Minor Scale
Also called Aeolian and pure minor. On C: C D E♭ F G A♭ B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 1 2 2. The sixth mode of Music/Scale/Major.
History
named the mode on A Aeolian in the Dodecachordon ( ). Before that, a D-final piece with a B♭ sounded the same collection while still counting as Dorian.

Common-practice minor was never this collection alone. Cadences raised the seventh, first through musica ficta and later in notation, and melodic lines raised or lowered the sixth as voice leading required. Natural, Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic and Music/Scale/Minor/Melodic are later pedagogical slices of one flexible minor mode.
Use
Aeolian folk song keeps the minor dominant (v) and cadences without a leading tone.
Rock and film music use the Aeolian progressions i–♭VII–♭VI and i–♭VI–♭VII, which treat ♭VII as a dominant substitute. In C: Cm–B♭–A♭.
In jazz the Aeolian chord-scale fits a minor chord functioning as vi in a major key, where Dorian would put the raised sixth against the key.
Quirks

The scale shares its key signature with its relative major. Baroque composers sometimes wrote minor pieces with one flat fewer than the modern signature, a holdover from Dorian notation; see Music/Scale/Dorian.
The ♭6 separates Aeolian from Dorian. Many melodies described as "minor" use only scale degrees 1 through 5 and never decide between them.

The MicroFreak's "Minor" setting is listed in its manual as C D E♭ F G A B♭ B, which lacks A♭, the note that separates natural minor from Dorian, and adds B natural. See Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings and Music/Scale/Dorian/Bebop. The Launchpad's "Natural Minor" setting carries this scale's name; its manual lists no pitches.
29.33.2 Gain Stage Section
Each routing has its own gain stages, each switched on with its Stage toggle. Every stage tab has Shaper Amount, Shaper Bias and Filter Frequency, plus shaper and filter type menus.
Shaper Amount — saturation; also drag the curve in the display. Distortion happens where the signal reaches the curve's bends.
Shaper Bias — offsets the signal for asymmetric distortion; high values sound like a broken circuit, extreme values silence it
Shaper Type — twelve curves:
Soft Sine — smooth, warm, analog-like even when pushed
Digital Clip — hard clipping with harsh upper harmonics

Bit Crusher — amplitude quantization like Ableton/Live/UG/29 Audio Effect Reference/30 Redux; more Amount means fewer bits and a stronger compander. Good with bias modulation; very audible on quiet signals.
Diode Clipper — virtual analog clipping circuit; like Soft Sine with softer highs
Tube Preamp — soft tube saturation that keeps transients and dynamics
Half Wave Rectifier — fully asymmetric; adds crunch to drums
Full Wave Rectifier — raises the signal an octave; adds harmonics to synths
Polynomial — shifts from a sine curve to more complex shapes; good for modulation and metallic sounds
Fractal — lots of high harmonics

19.1. An Introduction to Vocoding

Bell Labs patented the first vocoder in 1939 to speed up telephone connections. Musical vocoders appeared about forty years later and became known for their robotic sound. Artists have since used them in many ways, from Kraftwerk's “Autobahn” to Imogen Heap's “Hide and Seek.”

A vocoder transfers qualities of one sound to another. Speech vowels have characteristic frequency peaks called formants; a vowel commonly has one to three prominent peaks, F1 through F3. The positions of these peaks vary with the speaker and the sound being made.

The modulator, usually your voice, supplies the changing formants. A bank of tuned filters analyzes them and applies them to a carrier, such as an oscillator wave. The carrier takes on the shape of your voice.
Speech also has a changing loudness contour. The vocoder tracks this contour along with the formants, so the carrier follows the way you articulate a word.

33.3.4 MPE Control

MPE Control reshapes incoming MPE data with curves, usually ahead of a device that uses that data. It can also turn MPE into ordinary channel-wide MIDI so an MPE controller can play instruments without MPE.

11.3.2 Bend
Pitch bending raises or lowers a note. Press the Bend icon to enable bending.
The Bend Strip
The center is neutral. Moving left lowers the pitch; moving right raises it. Touching another point jumps directly to that pitch.

In standard mode, pitch follows the strip's absolute position. In relative mode, finger movement is added to or subtracted from the current pitch, regardless of where the finger first touches. Enable relative mode at Utility > Misc > Relative bend.
The default bend range is 24 chromatic steps: 12 to either side of center. Utility > Preset > Bend range sets the range, up to 48 steps (four octaves).

Music Scale Discussion
Why scale pages put the family noun first, nest by the scale's name, carry no fixed tonic, and leave ragas to pages of their own.
The family noun comes first

Variants nest under the noun they qualify: Music/Scale/Minor/Natural, Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic, Music/Scale/Minor/Melodic and Music/Scale/Minor/Hungarian sit together under Music/Scale/Minor, and the two pentatonic scales under Music/Scale/Pentatonic. The namespace view of a family then lists every variant of it, and the variants sort next to each other.

Music theorists treat natural, harmonic and melodic minor as one family: Music/Scale/Minor/Natural describes them as teaching forms of a single minor mode from the common-practice period, and the Minor segment in their paths keeps them together.

The alternative was to name each page in English word order directly under Music/Scale, as Music/Scale/Natural Minor. It matches how device menus print the names, and it splits the minor family across the alphabet: Harmonic Minor, Melodic Minor and Natural Minor sort under H, M and N.

Live handles two kinds of signal. Audio is a series of numbers approximating a waveform; MIDI is a series of commands, like "play a C4 at mezzo piano", closer to a written score.
An instrument turns MIDI into audio. Simpler plays one sound chromatically; Impulse assigns a different drum sound to each key.

4. Launchpad Pro Interface
Hungarian Minor Scale
Also called Gypsy minor and double harmonic minor. On C: C D E♭ F♯ G A♭ B. Steps in semitones: 2 1 3 1 1 3 1. Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic with a raised fourth.
History

The name comes from the style hongrois: the verbunkos idiom that Romani bands played in Hungarian cities, which , and borrowed. Liszt's book on the subject, Des Bohémiens et de leur musique en Hongrie ( ), credited that music to the Roma.

and 's fieldwork after found that older Hungarian peasant song was largely pentatonic. The "Hungarian" in the scale's name therefore names an urban, Romani-performed popular style rather than Hungarian village song. See Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor.
Use
Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsodies and the "alla zingarese" finales of Brahms and draw on the idiom, usually as melodic color over functional harmony in harmonic minor.
Its two augmented seconds, ♭3–♯4 and ♭6–7, make it a quick shorthand for Eastern Europe in film and game scores.
Quirks
It has two leading tones: F♯ leads to G and B leads to C. A melody can cadence on the dominant as strongly as on the tonic.
The step pattern 2 1 3 1 1 3 1 read backward is a rotation of itself, so the collection maps onto itself under inversion.
It is the fourth mode of the double harmonic major scale (C D♭ E F G A♭ B), which Arabic theory associates with maqam Hijaz Kar.

08.2 LFO Rate
The Rate knob sets the LFO speed from 0.06 Hz to 100 Hz.
The LFO does not follow the MicroFreak clock by default. Press the Rate encoder to enable Sync.

With Sync off, the display shows the rate in hertz. With Sync on, the LFO follows the MicroFreak clock, a DAW clock, or an external MIDI clock, and the display shows divisions from 8/1 to 1/32: 8/1, 4/1, 2/1, 1/1, 1/2, 1/2t, 1/4, 1/4t, 1/8, 1/8t, 1/16, 1/16t, and 1/32.

The displayed ratio sets how the LFO cycle relates to the clock. At 8/1, the slowest rate, a cycle completes in eight pulses. Each step up doubles the LFO speed, except the 1/2t, 1/4t, and 1/8t triplet settings. At 1/4, one LFO cycle equals a quarter note.
Matching the LFO rate to the MicroFreak sequencer, a DAW, or another clock source can create rhythms at multiples or divisions of the clock.
Turning Sync off uncouples the LFO from the MicroFreak tempo and restores its 0.06 Hz to 100 Hz range.

Assign1, Assign2, and Assign3 are user-defined destinations. They can turn nearly any MicroFreak knob into a modulation destination.

29.1.1 Amp Tips
Amp behaves like analog hardware, so results are not always predictable.
29.1.1.1 Amps and Cabinets

Guitar amps are made to drive speaker cabinets, so the companion Ableton/Live/UG/29 Audio Effect Reference/06 Cabinet belongs after Amp for an authentic chain. Using either one alone gives other, less conventional sounds.
29.1.1.2 Electricity

An amp's circuits share a fixed amount of power, so raising one control can take energy from another. Turning up Treble can reduce bass and mids, so getting a sound may mean adjusting controls that seem unrelated.

1. Introduction
Launchpad Pro is a grid controller for producing and performing with Ableton Live or external MIDI hardware.
Its 64 velocity- and pressure-sensitive RGB pads can launch clips, play notes, and sequence steps. The four-track, 32-step sequencer provides probability and mutation controls for evolving patterns.
Eight Custom Modes can send MIDI to software or hardware. The two MIDI output ports extend control to external instruments.
The unit can operate without a computer when powered through its USB-C port by the included wall adapter.

A preset can contain monophonic or paraphonic patterns. In paraphonic mode, the sequencer can play up to four voices; with Paraphony off, it plays only the lowest note of each step.

10.2 Keyboard Responsiveness
Set the keyboard to send aftertouch or velocity at Utility → Preset → Press Mode. This choice changes how the keyboard responds to touch.
Utility → Preset → Velo Amp Mod sets how strongly velocity affects the patch volume, from 0 to 10.

Hearing is more sensitive to pitch changes than to volume changes, so pitch can help when adjusting keyboard responsiveness. On an empty preset, assign pressure to pitch in the Matrix at the maximum amount. Hold one finger at a 90° angle against the upper edge of a key, then lower it so more skin touches the key. The increased contact sends more pressure and raises the pitch.
Pressing hard while keeping the finger at 90° will not reach maximum pressure because of the touch-plate design.
15. Using Tuning Systems
Loading tuning systems other than twelve-tone equal temperament and how MIDI tracks follow them.
Live's default tuning is 12TET: twelve equal steps per octave. A tuning system can divide an octave, or a pseudo-octave that repeats at another interval, differently.
Live 12 loads Scala (.scl) files. The Core Library's tunings, under the Tunings label in the browser, use ASCL, Ableton's extension of the Scala format.
The Info View describes a tuning, including its notes per octave, when you hover over it in the browser or over a loaded tuning's name.
Your own .scl or .ascl files in any folder of Live's Places appear under the Tunings label with the User tag.

All of Live's built-in instruments follow a tuning system. MPE-enabled plug-ins and Max for Live instruments follow it when their pitch bend range is 48 semitones; other instruments will likely play out of tune.

Harmonic Minor Scale
On C: C D E♭ F G A♭ B. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 1 3 1. Music/Scale/Minor/Natural with a raised seventh.
History
The raised seventh came from cadential practice: musica ficta supplied a leading tone at cadences in modal polyphony long before any theorist listed the result as a scale.
"Harmonic minor" is a pedagogical name. It collects the pitches of the chords of a minor key, with the dominant and leading-tone chords built on the raised seventh.
Use
Common-practice harmony uses the collection for V, V7 and vii°7 in minor. Its melodies avoid the augmented second between ♭6 and 7, or fill it in, or turn it into a deliberate effect.
exoticism made that augmented second a marker of the East, Spain or Romani music.
Its fifth mode, C D♭ E F G A♭ B♭ on C, is Phrygian dominant. Flamenco, klezmer (where it is called Freygish or Ahava Rabbah) and Middle Eastern pop use it, and the maqam Hijaz is close to it.
Its fourth mode is Music/Scale/Dorian/Ukrainian.
Quirks
The collection contains a fully diminished seventh chord (B D F A♭) and an augmented triad (E♭ G B). Those two symmetrical chords give it more harmonic ambiguity than the diatonic modes.

The MicroFreak manual lists its "Harmonic Minor" setting as C D E F G A♭ B. With E natural, that collection is harmonic major, 's name for a major scale with a lowered sixth. The manual page is Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings; which collection the firmware plays is not documented there.

35.15 Push 1 Control Reference
What each section and control does.
35.15.0.1 Focus/Navigation Section

Note — on an instrument track the pads play notes, and further presses switch between real-time playing and the melodic sequencer. On a Drum Rack track the lower-left 16 pads play, the lower-right 16 set loop length, and the top four rows step-sequence; press again for 64-pad mode.
Session — pads launch Session View clips.
Shift — hold for second functions.
Arrow keys — move around the Set in Session Mode, or between tracks and scenes in Note Mode.
Select — hold and press a clip to select it without launching and show its name, or a drum pad to select its notes silently.
35.15.0.2 Add Section
Add Effect — opens Browse to add a device right of the selected one; Shift adds it to the left. For a MIDI effect, select the instrument and use Shift + Add Effect.
Add Track — adds a MIDI track to the right; hold to choose Audio, MIDI or Return. Inside a Group Track, the new track joins the group.
35.15.0.3 Note Section
Scales — on an instrument track in Note Mode, picks the key and scale, with Fixed Y/N, In Key/Chromatic and scale type. No effect on Drum Rack tracks or in Session Mode.
User — turns off Push's built-in functions so it can be remapped; hold for configuration. Relative encoders work best as "Relative (2's Comp.)"; turn the encoder slowly left while mapping to get it.
Repeat — holding a pad retriggers it at the Scene/Grid rate.
Accent — every note plays at full velocity; hold for temporary accent.
Octave Up/Down — shift pads by octave on instrument tracks, by 16 pads on Drum Racks, and by eight scenes in Session Mode. Unlit when no further range exists.
35.15.0.4 State Control Section

For tracks, the eight left buttons stop clips, mute or solo, depending on which of Stop, Mute or Solo is active. For devices they turn devices on and off. Other modes reuse them, for example for scale selection. Shift + Stop stops all clips.
35.15.0.5 Selection Control Section
Chooses what the encoders and display edit. In and Out reach devices in Racks or more parameter banks, and in Browse shift the columns.
35.15.0.6 Display/Encoder Section

Six buttons beside the display set the encoder mode; hold one to switch temporarily. The ninth encoder is Main track volume, or Pre-Cue volume with Shift. Shift with any of the first eight encoders gives fine control.
Volume — eight track volumes.
Pan & Send — pans, then each send in turn.
Track — one track's volume, pan and first six sends; Master selects the Main track.
Clip — for MIDI clips: Loop Start (or Clip Start), Position, Loop Length (or Clip End), Loop on/off. Audio clips add Warp Mode, Detune, Transpose and Gain.
Device — parameters of the selected device.
Browse — scroll devices and presets.
35.15.0.7 Tempo Section
Tap Tempo — the Set's tempo follows your taps. With "Start Playback with Tap Tempo" on in the Record, Warp & Launch Settings, four taps in 4/4 also start playback.
Metronome — toggles Live's metronome.
Left encoder sets tempo in 1 BPM steps, or 0.1 BPM with Shift. Right encoder sets swing for Quantize, Record Quantize and Repeat.
35.15.0.8 Edit Section
Undo — Live's own Undo, including actions not made on Push; Shift + Undo redoes.

Delete — in Note Mode deletes the selected clip; in Session Mode hold and press a clip. Hold with a Selection Control button to delete a device or track, or touch an encoder to clear its automation or reset it.
Quantize — press to quantize selected notes, or the whole clip; hold with a drum pad for that pad only. On audio clips it moves transients. Hold for settings.
Double — doubles the loop and its contents.
35.15.0.9 Transport Section
Fixed Length — new clips get a set number of bars; hold to choose.
Automation — toggles Live's Automation Record for playing Session clips. Shift + Automation re-enables overridden automation; Delete + Automation clears all automation in a clip.
Duplicate — captures a scene in Scene Workflow or copies the selected clip in Clip Workflow; with a drum pad, copies that pad.
New — stops the selected clip and readies new recording. On an armed MIDI track, Record + New triggers Capture MIDI.
Record — record, then play, then overdub.
Play/Stop — Live's play button; Shift + Play/Stop returns to 1.1.1 without playing.
35.15.0.10 Touch Strip

On instrument tracks it is pitch bend (default) or mod wheel while playing live, and the note range while step sequencing; Select + tap the strip toggles bend and mod. On Drum Rack tracks it picks the pad bank.
35.15.0.11 Pad Section
Session Mode launches clips. Note Mode plays notes on instrument tracks or splits into play, loop length and sequencer areas on Drum Rack tracks, with 64-pad mode one Note press away.
35.15.0.12 Scene/Grid Section
In Session Mode these launch scenes; hold Select to select a scene without launching. In Note Mode they set step size and Repeat rate.
35.15.0.13 Using Footswitches with Push 1
Two jacks take momentary footswitches. Footswitch 1 is sustain. Footswitch 2 toggles Record on a single tap and acts as New on a double tap.

17.5 About MIDI channels
A central synthesizer or MIDI controller can control several instruments. MIDI has 16 channels so one device can send separate parts to other instruments on different channels.

The MicroFreak can transmit on all 16 channels at once or on a selected channel. By default, it transmits on all channels. To send a performance or sequence to a particular synthesizer or drum machine, set the MicroFreak's output channel to match; drum machines commonly use channel 10. Change the channel in Utility or MIDI Control Center.
MIDI input works the same way. To have a controller such as an Arturia BeatStep Pro control the MicroFreak on channel 2, set its input channel to 2 in Utility.

9.1.4 Clip Tempo Followers and Leaders

Warped clips follow the Set's tempo by default. In Arrangement View, the Lead/Follow toggle in Audio Utilities makes a clip a tempo leader: the Set follows the clip's Warp Markers and the tempo field is disabled.
Many clips can lead, but only one sets the tempo at a time: the playing clip on the lowest track.

15.2 The Scale Root

Starting a scale on a different note changes its mood because the intervals are heard in a different order. Starting C major on C follows tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. Keeping that interval pattern and making D the root gives D, E, F♯, G, A, B, C♯, D.
Changing the Root is an intelligent transpose: it preserves the scale's interval structure. A simple transpose shifts every step by a semitone or whole tone.

3.6 Arrangement and Session
Clips are Live's building blocks: a melody, a drum pattern, a bassline, or a whole song.

The Arrangement lays clips out on a linear timeline; the Session is a launching base where each clip has its own play button and can start at any time in any order. See Ableton/Live/Mode/Arrangement and .

11.1 Using MIDI Tools

MIDI Tools live in the Clip View's Transform and Generate panels. Transformations need selected notes and replace them; MPE tools are transformations that add or change note expression, visible in the MPE Editor. Generators need no input and create notes.
Native tools are built in and fixed; Max for Live tools can be edited, built, or installed from other makers, and show under the browser's MIDI Tools filter group or the MIDI Tool tag.

Pick a tool from the panel's selector and adjust it. Auto Apply, on by default, applies changes immediately; turn it off, which restores the original notes, to adjust first and then press Apply. Cmd+Enter (Mac) / Ctrl+Enter (Win) applies from the editor.
Transformations act on the time selection, the note selection, or the whole loop. Generators fill the time selection or loop, keeping existing notes they don't overlap and replacing those they do.
With a clip scale, pitch parameters use scale degrees.
Undo and Redo affect notes, not tool settings; Reset returns a tool's parameters to default without touching notes.

06.03.07 Waveshaping Oscillator (Waveshaper)
Waveshaper Oscillator Model

Description: Combines a waveshaper and a wavefolder. The waveshaper changes a wave's rising and falling stages: it can steepen a triangle's rise into a falling saw, or change the curves of either stage. These changes affect the number and amplitude of harmonics, with more harmonics producing a richer, sometimes sharper, sound. The original model was based on a feature of the Serge waveshaper.
A wavefolder folds a wave back on itself. Unlike boosting a digital waveform until its top clips off, folding preserves the waveform by turning it back on itself.
Wave: Sets the waveshaper waveform.
Amount: Sets the wavefolder amount.

11.3.1 Spice & Dice
Spice and Dice work together, though their musical effect can be enjoyed without knowing the details.
Dice changes the gates and triggers of the playing Arpeggio or Sequence. It varies their timing and can shorten, lengthen, or omit gates.
Activate the Arpeggiator or Sequencer first. Select Dice, then touch the strip to set the amount of randomness: the left end adds none and the right end adds the most.

The Dice setting is silent until Spice is added. Select Spice and move right on the strip to increase the variation's intensity. Spice and Dice can be set in either order. With Spice held at a chosen amount, each Dice touch generates a different trigger variation at that intensity.
Spice and Dice also subtly vary octaves, velocity, and the Amp envelope's release time. Spice sets how far a parameter deviates from its normal value; Dice updates the random value per step.
Pattern randomizes chord pitches; Spice and Dice randomize gates and triggers. Together they can make an Arpeggio or Sequence sound very different from its starting pattern.
A Sequence's Status is its series of gate lengths. New sequences start at a default gate length of 45%; Utility > Preset > Default gate length sets it from 5% to 85%.
A gate length of 0 is silent; 100 is a tie that continues into the next step without a noticeable pause. Values between them set the gate length percentage.
Spice moves gate lengths from the default toward the current Status. At maximum Spice, the gate lengths follow the Status exactly.

When Dice is lit, touching the strip changes the Status by adding a bipolar value to each step's gate length. A touch near the left makes small changes; a touch near the right can reshuffle the Status.
When the finger lifts, the last gate-length pattern heard becomes the new Status, which can then change again with another Dice touch.

Mixolydian Mode
Also called the tetrardus authentic mode or Mode 7. On C: C D E F G A B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 2 1 2 2 1 2. The fifth mode of Music/Scale/Major.
History
The ancient Greek Mixolydian octave species ran from B to B, the collection now called Locrian. The medieval G mode inherited the name in the Carolingian renaming; see Music/Scale/Dorian.
In polyphony the G mode's seventh was routinely raised to F♯ at cadences, so much "Mixolydian" Renaissance music cadences as if in G major.
Use

Folk traditions that end tunes without a leading tone favor it. Irish and Scottish dance tunes are often Mixolydian, and the Great Highland bagpipe chanter plays a Mixolydian scale on A with a flat seventh.
Rock uses its ♭VII as a third functional chord beside IV and V. The progression I–♭VII–IV–I closes "Hey Jude", and the Beatles' "Norwegian Wood" is Mixolydian throughout.
In jazz chord-scale theory it is the default scale over an unaltered dominant seventh chord.
Quirks
The tonic triad is major, the triad on 5 is minor (G B♭ D on C), and the subtonic chord ♭VII is major. Cadences come from ♭VII–I or IV–I instead of V–I.
Inverting its step pattern gives Music/Scale/Minor/Natural.

31.9.1 General Overview

A central display sits between two sides of shell. The left shell has the four oscillators; the right has LFO, filter, pitch and global. Touching a shell control shows that section in the display, so levels and frequencies are reachable together while envelopes and waveforms sit in each display.
The triangle at the top left folds the display away.

Each oscillator either outputs audio or modulates another. Eleven algorithms, picked in the global display, set the connections; signal flows top to bottom in each icon. The algorithm can be mapped, automated and modulated.
Beyond the usual FM sines, Operator offers other waveforms, two noises and a drawable partial editor. Ableton suggests exploring FM without the filter first, since many classic FM synths had none.

Paste Bounced Audio bounces whatever you copied in its current state at the moment you paste, so you can change the source and paste again without recopying. Handy for variations with different effects, or for gathering bits of several tracks into one.

On the panel, V.Analog puts Detune on the Wave knob (CC 10), Shape on the Timbre knob (CC 12) and Wave on the Shape knob (CC 13). In the session codekiln worked this out by ear: "So timbre is the shape."
Detune: 0.013. Shape: 0.024. Wave: 0.175. The saved sound starts almost undetuned, with a narrow pulse and a mostly triangular wave.

Filter
Low-pass filter. Saved cutoff: 0.099; resonance: 0.000. Cutoff and resonance are normalized settings, not hertz or display values. Microfreak/UG/07 Filter/01 Modifying Sound/01 Low Pass Filter

The main envelope opens the low-pass cutoff from its low saved setting. The cycling envelope changes resonance independently, emphasizing the cutoff region as the note develops (see the modulation matrix).
Envelopes

Main envelope: attack 0.431, decay/release 0.672, sustain 0.996. Amp Mod is on, so the main envelope controls loudness: notes swell in and hold at nearly full level. Microfreak/UG/09 Envelope Gen/03 Envelope Stages

Cycling Envelope mode: Loop. Stored RiseLvl 0.000, RiseSlp 0.500, FallLvl 0.211, FallSlp 0.500, Hold 0.000, Amount 0.695. These are normalized stored fields; rise and fall times in milliseconds remain unverified. Microfreak/UG/09 Envelope Gen/06 Cycling Envelope
LFO

Sample-and-Hold, clock sync off, so the free rate applies. Stored normalized rate: 0.764; stored division code: 5. The rate is not a hertz reading. Microfreak/UG/08 LFO/01 LFO Shape · Microfreak/UG/08 LFO/02 LFO Rate
Modulation matrix
Amounts use the signed normalized range −1…+1. The Assign columns resolve to the destinations shown.
PRESSURE → Timbre (V.Analog Shape): +0.669. Pressing harder widens the pulse toward square and sync formants.
ENV → Cutoff: +0.605. The main envelope opens the filter as each note swells in.
Cycling Envelope → Assign 1 → Filter Resonance: +1.000. The looping envelope keeps changing the resonance.
PRESSURE → Assign 2 → LFO Rate: +0.180. Pressure speeds up the Sample-and-Hold steps slightly.
LFO → Assign 3 → Wave: +0.199. Sample-and-Hold steps the saw/triangle morph.
All other saved matrix amounts are zero; nothing routes to pitch.
Performance and session context
Play the saved sound with sustained notes and varying pressure. Pressure changes the pulse shape and the LFO speed, while the cycling envelope keeps resonance moving underneath.
Paraphonic mode is on in the saved export. The PRESSURE row uses pressure or velocity according to the instrument's global Utility setting; the export does not establish which one was active.

29.22 Grain Delay
Grain Delay chops the input into tiny grains and delays each one, optionally at a different pitch. Randomizing pitch and timing creates textures that may barely resemble the source.
Any parameter can be put on the X-Y controller: pick the X parameter from the row below it and the Y parameter from the row at its left. Delay time can go on X and dry/wet on Y.
Sync on — delay in sixteenths from numbered buttons (4 is one beat); the Delay Time percentage nudges it for swing. Sync off — delay in ms.
Spray — random delay-time changes; low values smear and add noise, high values break the source into rhythmic chaos
Frequency — sets grain size and length, and so shapes how Pitch and Spray sound
Pitch — transposes the grains, like a rough pitch shifter
Random Pitch — random pitch per grain; low values give a warped chorus, high values make the original pitch unrecognizable
Feedback — output fed back into the delay; very high values can run away into loud oscillation
Dry/Wet — balance of processed and dry signal

UI Control Kind
A proposal for describing how a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control changes its value, apart from the protocol that carries it. Not yet a preference.
Two separate questions
Form — what the control is physically or on screen: knob, button, pad, fader, field. The <Kind> segment of a control's page name records the form, in the product's own word.
Behavior — what happens to the value when the control is operated. The same form can behave in different ways: a Launchpad pad can be a toggle, a momentary button or a trigger, as in .
MIDI is one way to carry a control's value to another device. A behavior describes the control itself; a MIDI CC number or a MIDI mapping goes under the control's Remote control block.
Proposed behaviors
Buttons
Momentary — on while held, off when released.
Trigger — fires one event when pressed and keeps no state, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View/Button/Set Locator.
Toggle — alternates between two states on each press, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Button/Arrangement Record.
Multi-state toggle — steps through three or more states in a fixed cycle on each press.
Continuous controls
Unipolar — a value from zero up to a maximum, such as 0–127 or 0–100%.
Bipolar — a value centered on zero that runs from a negative minimum to a positive maximum, such as Length on Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/Sample/Length, from -100 to 100.
Relative (endless) — sends increments and decrements with no fixed end; the device keeps the value.
Stepped controls
Selector — moves through a fixed list of named positions, such as Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type.
Numeric field — holds a number typed in or dragged, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Field/Arrangement Position.
Combined controls
Encoder with push — a rotary control whose press acts as a separate button.
Pressure — adds a continuous value to a pad or key while held, such as aftertouch.
Position on a surface — a fader, slider or touch strip whose value follows a position along a line, or an XY pad that gives two values at once.

Garden notes:
07.01 Modifying sound
The MicroFreak has a Low Pass Filter (LPF), a Band Pass Filter (BPF), and a High Pass Filter (HPF). The Type button switches between them.
A low-pass filter attenuates frequencies above its cutoff; a high-pass filter attenuates frequencies below it; a band-pass filter attenuates frequencies on both sides of the cutoff.

With a low-pass filter open at maximum cutoff, all frequencies pass. Lowering the cutoff removes the highs first, then the midrange; closing it completely leaves silence. In high-pass mode, maximum cutoff removes all frequencies; lowering it lets frequencies above the cutoff pass. In band-pass mode, frequencies near the cutoff remain audible, and resonance sets the width of that range.
Musical Work
In this garden, Musical Work pages model identifiable compositions, songs, and separately named movements or other parts of a larger composition.
What counts
A musical work is an abstract composition or song, independent of any one performance, recording, or release.
A movement may have its own page when it is useful to track or discuss it separately. It remains related to its larger work through part-of::.
An album is a release or collection of recordings, not a musical work. Model an album under Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording and connect its tracks to their works.
An arrangement with a distinct identity may have its own work page, with based-on:: linking to the source work.
Naming and placement

Place a work under its primary credited as <Identity>/Music/Work/<Title> when Logseq/Frontmatter/created-by-identities is present. Without a separate credited identity, use Person/<Creator>/Music/Work/<Title>. A recording artist credit alone does not establish authorship of the underlying composition.
For a movement, continue below its parent work with a two-digit position and the movement's title, such as .../01 Grave - Allegro di molto e con brio.
Use the creator who gives the work its clearest home in the garden; list every creator whose page exists in created-by::.
Use the work's familiar title as the H1. Keep punctuation and diacritics from the established title.

Write a sharp or flat in a key as -sharp or -flat in both the page name and the H1, as Prelude in C-sharp Minor and Elegie in E-flat Minor. In Logseq # starts a tag, and ♯ and ♭ are hard to type into a link.
Relationships
Use part-of:: on a movement or section page to link to its parent work.
Use appears-on:: on a work page to link to a known album recording or release. The album page lists its tracks in order as bullets, linking each work.
Use based-on:: for an adaptation or arrangement and cover-of:: on a cover recording to link the covered work.
A work page may link to performances and recordings, but those entities do not replace the work page.
Use music-form:: to link the Logseq/Entity/Music/Form pages a work belongs to, as music-form:: [[Music/Form/Prelude]].
Examples
Person/Madonna/Music/Work/Vogue is the song; Person/Madonna/Music/Recording/I'm Breathless is its album, whose ordered track list links to .
Person/Ludwig van Beethoven/Music/Work/Piano Sonata No. 8 in C Minor Op. 13 Pathétique/01 Grave - Allegro di molto e con brio is the first movement, nested beneath the sonata.
Person/John Cage/Music/Work/4'33" is a complete work with no movement pages required.
Person/Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart/Music/Work/Piano Concerto No. 23 in A Major K. 488/02 Adagio and .../03 Allegro assai are sibling movements under one concerto.
Person/Stevie Nicks/Music/Work/Landslide is the song. A Smashing Pumpkins recording of it is filed under that performer and links to the Stevie Nicks work with cover-of::.
Instance shape
Start each work page with logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Music/Work]] and one H1 containing the work's familiar title.
Add created-by:: links when the creator pages exist, and date-created:: when a reliable composition or publication date is known.
Add only relationships that are known and useful; leave unknown movement lists and release associations unstated.

38.1 Managing the CPU Load
Live performs a large number of calculations every second to keep audio flowing. When the processor falls behind, playback and recording get gaps or clicks.
What affects CPU performance:
Clock speed — instructions per second, in GHz.
Architecture — how efficiently the CPU runs instructions and talks to other parts.
Cache memory — how fast the CPU fetches data.
System bus bandwidth — how fast data moves between components.
Temperature — an overheating CPU throttles itself.
Live needs a multi-core processor and spreads instruments, effects and I/O across the cores.

06.03.08 Two operator FM (Two Op.FM)
Two operator Oscillator Model
Description: FM synthesis began with Dr. John Chowning's work at Stanford University in the late 1960s. The first FM synthesizer ran on a mainframe computer—roughly a room full of refrigerators.

Chowning found that modulating a waveform with others tuned to the harmonic series could emulate many acoustic instruments. Inharmonic relationships produced bell-like tones and other intricate sounds that were difficult for analog synthesizers of the time to reproduce.
This oscillator uses two sine-wave oscillators, each modulating the phase of the other, to create a wide range of sounds.
Ratio: Sets the frequency ratio between the oscillators.
Amount: Sets the modulation index.
Shape: Sets feedback, with operator 2 modulating its own phase.

Hirajoshi Scale
From hirajōshi, "even tuning", a standard tuning of the Japanese koto. On C, in the form most Western references give: C D E♭ G A♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 4 1 4.
History
Hirajōshi is a tuning for the thirteen strings of the koto, credited to in the . It became the standard tuning for solo koto music of the Edo period, including his Rokudan no shirabe.
Western scale catalogues and guitar method books lifted the tuning's pitches out as a five-note scale in the . Japanese theory treats the same pitches as the miyako-bushi or in scale.
Use
In Western rock, metal and film music, the scale stands in for Japan.
Quirks
Western references disagree about which note is the tonic: 0 2 3 7 8 and 0 4 6 7 11 both appear in print. They are rotations of one pitch set, the same set as the miyako-bushi scale 0 1 5 7 8.

It is a hemitonic pentatonic, the opposite of : two of its five steps are semitones, each followed by a major third. That pairing gives it a sound unlike the semitone-free Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major.
The Launchpad manual names a "Hirajoshi" setting without listing its pitches.

Each engine's two macro knobs change with its oscillator type. All four can be mapped to a MIDI controller, driven by an LFO device, or modulated in the matrix.
Macros by oscillator type:
Basic Shapes — Shape (sine → triangle → saw → square), Tone (pulse width).

Square Sync — Freq 1, Freq 2 of two synced squares.

Sub — Tone (sine toward square), Aux (adds a lower subharmonic sine).
Swarm Sine / Triangle / Saw / Square — Motion (modulates the swarm), Spacing (moves through more complex chords).
Harmonic Fm — Amount, Ratio.
Fold Fm — Amount, Shape (carrier shape).

Simple Fm — Amount, Ratio.
Chip — Tone (pitch and pulse width), Rate (speed of the chip interval).
Shepard's Pi — Rate (below 50 falls, above 50 rises, 50 still), Width (octaves used).
Tarp — Decay, Tone.
Extratone — Pitch, Env Amount.
Noise Loop — Rate (how often noise-loop fragments change; high values become plain noise), Fade (graininess).

Bitgrunge — Freq (square frequency), Mult (number of sub-octaves; maximum gives none, minimum many).
Crackle — Density, Intensity (spread of loudness and brightness).

29.23.4.1 Dark Hall
A smooth, classic hall for medium to long halls.
Damping — high-frequency filtering; higher is darker
Mod — movement in the tail; more gives chorusing and fewer resonances
Shape — from small and resonant to large and diffuse
Bass X — crossover for the low end of the tail; Bass Mult scales its decay time
Long decays with a very small Size give metallic, gong-like resonances.
29.23.4.2 Quartz
A hall-like reverb with audible echoes in the tail and clear early reflections; suits voices, drums, transient material and echo effects.
Damping — high-frequency filtering; higher is darker
Lo Damp — low-frequency filtering; higher is brighter
Mod — movement in the tail
Diffusion — density of the tail
Distance — how far away the reflections are; closer is denser, farther spaces the echoes out
29.23.4.3 Shimmer
Dense diffuse delays with a pitch shifter in the feedback; tails rise or fall in pitch. Low diffusion is a plain delay, high diffusion a lush reverb.
Damping — high-frequency filtering
Mod — movement in the tail
Pitch — pitch shift in the feedback, in semitones
Diffusion — density; below 10% gives dub-style delays, good on drums
Shimmer — amount of pitch-shifted signal; 100% on melodic material gives harmonies
Here Size sets the spacing of echoes on percussive material.
A smooth reverb whose output is modulated by a multiband filter, giving rippling bands.
Damping — high-frequency filtering
Wave — modulation shape from noise (0%) through sine (50%) to square (100%)
Tide — strength of the texture
Phase — left/right offset; 180° is fully opposite
Rate — modulation rate in beat divisions, with triplet, 16th and dotted variations

A bright, clearly artificial diffuse reverb based on spectrally flat "velvet" noise. It adds depth without getting in the way, suits short non-linear decays on drums, and gives a clean digital sound on longer decays.
Low Mult and High Mult — scale the decay of the low and high parts of the tail
X over — crossover between those parts
Small Decay and Size give a classic 1980s gated snare reverb.
29.15 EQ Eight
EQ Eight has up to eight parametric filters per channel.
Modes:
Stereo — one curve for both channels
L/R — separate curves for left and right
M/S — separate curves for mid and side
In L/R and M/S both curves are drawn, but only the one chosen with Edit can be changed.

Each band's chooser offers, top to bottom: low cut (48 or 12 dB/octave), low shelf, peak, notch, high shelf, high cut (12 or 48 dB/octave). Each band has an on/off switch; turn unused bands off to save CPU. Stacking identical bands gives very steep filtering.
Editing:
drag a dot: sideways for frequency, up and down for gain; Option-drag (Mac) or Alt-drag (Windows) for Q
for low cut, notch and high cut, vertical dragging sets Q, since they have no gain
drag a box around several dots to move them together, with the mouse or arrow keys
or click near a band's number and use Freq, Gain and Q
The title bar button moves the display into Live's main window, where all eight bands can be edited at once.
Analyze — shows the output spectrum behind the curves; turn it off to work by ear
Adaptive Q — Q rises with the amount of boost or cut, like classic analog EQs, for steadier output level
Audition (headphone icon) — click and hold a dot to hear only that band
Gain — overall output level
Scale — scales the gain of every band that has gain

Each loop length pad is a page of steps; page length depends on step size. Drums at 16ths show two pages (two bars); the Melodic Sequencer shows one page of eight steps (two beats).
Hold one pad and tap another to set the loop; double-tap a pad for a one-page loop.

Pages follow the playhead by default. Single-tap a page to lock the view there without changing the loop; tapping a page outside the loop sets the loop to it. Page Left/Right step through pages; reselect the loop or hold Page Left/Right to follow again.
Loop length pad colours: unlit outside the loop; grey in the loop but not shown; white shown but not playing; green playing; red recording.
Hold Duplicate, press a page's pad, then a destination's, to copy notes onto it (adding to what's there). Hold Delete and tap a page to clear it first.

Book Section
In this garden, Book Section pages model one headed part of a book or manual as a navigable Logseq page.
What counts

A section has a distinct heading in the source and enough content to read or navigate independently. A caption, callout, paragraph, or table row stays inside its section rather than becoming a section page.

Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 1, Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 2, Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 3, and Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 4 specify the depth. The instance declares its most specific level in logseq-entity::; the level page points here for the shared shape.
Identity and names

A section is identified by its source work and its place in the heading tree. Search the intended path, aliases, and existing section content before creating a page; a changed heading or shortened title does not make a second section.

Nest each section under its parent page. Prefix each segment with a two-digit sibling order from the source, followed by a short, recognizable heading. Shorten long heading words where the meaning stays clear. The full source heading belongs in the page's H1, with its source number where useful.
Number siblings in source order, including unnumbered headings that qualify as sections. Keep the number local to the parent: 06 Dig Osc/02 Param Controls, then 02 Param Controls/01 Knob Speed.
Page shape

Use the level-specific logseq-entity:: marker. up:: links to the parent page; prev:: and next:: link to adjacent siblings when those pages exist. The first and last sibling need only the available direction. See Logseq/Frontmatter for shared frontmatter conventions.

Begin with one bullet-wrapped H1. Put the section's own content under it in source order. Embed each imported child page once at the point where its heading occurs. The child page holds the text; the parent does not repeat it.
Only embed L1 -> L2 -> L3

The Logseq user interface becomes messy-looking and sluggish when more than two levels of pages are embedded and are visible on a single page. It's okay if page MyPage has {{embed [[MyPage/MySubPage]]}}, and if MySubPage has {{embed [[MyPage/MySubPage/MySubSubPage]]}}, in it. It could be okay if there's only a single embed goes deeper and it's a very small page. But if the nesting goes deeper than that, it's usually a poor experience for the page viewer. As a convention, we permit embeds of L2 in L1 and L3 in L2, and use typical logseq wikilinks to L4.
A top-level Logseq/Entity/Book entity or a parent page of a Level 1 page has links to Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 1 sections, not embeds.

Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 1 has an embed of Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 2, and Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 2 has an embed of Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 3. Beneath that, it uses links to Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 4.
Use Block References deeper than Level 4

A newly available child appears in its parent's embed list, and adjacent sibling pages link in both directions through prev:: and next:: once both exist.

Turn the source's paragraphs, bullets, callouts, figures, and tables into readable nested blocks. Preserve the information needed to use the material, not the PDF's line wrapping or table grid. Use > [[Note/Info]] or > [[Note/Warning]] for corresponding callouts.

Place a figure under its caption block. Represent the image with a Logseq/Entity/Asset/B2 page beneath its owning section; Logseq/Entity/Asset defines its page-derived filename. Embed the verified remote URL with the caption as alt text. Keep the full PDF outside the graph.

Replace page-number references with a link to the corresponding section when it exists and its identity is clear. Otherwise, name the destination in prose without a speculative link. Do not preserve a bare PDF page number as navigation.
Source check

Compare the extracted text and images against the source pages: heading order, callout scope, figure/caption pairing, and cross-references can be lost in PDF extraction. The imported page should read naturally in Logseq and nvim.

Collecting copies external files into the Project folder so moved originals can't break the Set.

File → Collect All and Save asks which locations to collect from. Packs and the User Library need collecting only if you plan to move or uninstall them; collecting multisampled instruments can make the Project much larger. Files go into the Project's Samples or Presets folders.

Pitch — shifts pitch by Coarse semitones and Fine cents
Freq — shifts every frequency by a set number of Hz. Small shifts give tremolo or phasing; large ones dissonant, metallic sounds.

1.1 A fascinating adventure

Learning the MicroFreak comes through experimenting, asking questions, and trying ideas. Take time to understand its functions one by one; random tweaking without knowing what is changing can make it harder to stay interested.
