Whole Tone Scale
Also 's first mode of limited transposition. On C: C D E F♯ G♯ A♯. Steps in semitones: 2 2 2 2 2 2.
History
Glinka used a descending whole-tone scale for the sorcerer Chernomor in Ruslan and Lyudmila ( ), and Russian composers after him kept it for the supernatural.
made it a harmonic field. "Voiles" (Préludes, Book I, – ) stays on one whole-tone collection for most of its length and turns pentatonic in the middle.
Messiaen listed it first among his modes of limited transposition in Technique de mon langage musical ( ), and said he avoided it because Debussy and Dukas had used it so thoroughly.
Use
Impressionist harmony, and later film and television, use it for dreams, flashbacks and suspended time.
Jazz uses it over a dominant seventh chord with a ♯5 and 9 (C7♯5, C9♯5), and made descending whole-tone runs a signature.
Quirks

There are only two distinct whole-tone collections, the even and the odd pitch classes. Every rotation of the scale is the same scale, so it has no modes. On a device with root selection, the twelve roots produce only two sets of pitches.
It contains no perfect fifth, no leading tone and no minor or major triad; every triad built from it is augmented. No note can function as a tonic without help from outside the scale.
The French augmented sixth chord (A♭ C D F♯ in C) is a four-note subset of the scale, a pivot between functional and whole-tone harmony.
29.5 Beat Repeat
Beat Repeat captures slices of the incoming audio and repeats them, on a schedule or at random.
When to repeat:
Interval — how often new material is captured, synced from 1/32 to 4 bars
Offset — moves that point later; Interval 1 Bar with Offset 8/16 captures on beat three of each bar
Chance — probability that a scheduled repeat happens; 100% always, 0% never
Gate — total length of the repeats in sixteenths; 4/16 lasts one beat
Repeat — ignores the above and repeats right away until switched off
What repeats:
Grid — slice length; large values give rhythmic loops, small ones give glitchy artifacts. No Triplets keeps the grid binary.
Variation — randomizes the grid size around Grid. Its mode sets when: Trigger (each time repeats start), 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 (at regular intervals) or Auto (after every repeat, the most varied).

Pitch — lowers the repeats by resampling, which also stretches them, so high values blur the rhythm. Pitch Decay makes each repeat lower than the last; the manual calls it the most obscure control in the device.
Filter — a combined low-pass and high-pass with center frequency and width
Mix mode:
Mix — original plus repeats
Insert — original muted while repeats play
Gate — repeats only; suits a return track
Volume sets the output and Decay fades successive repeats.
39.2.4 Summing at Single Mix Points
Live sums signals in 64-bit double precision at every mix point: clip and return track inputs, the Main track and Racks. Mixing at a single point is therefore neutral.
Internal processing stays 32-bit, so a signal mixed across several summing points can lose a very small amount of quality.

29.35.6.1 Pitch-shifted Drum Layers

Duplicate a drum track and put Shifter after its Drum Rack. In Pitch mode, move or automate Coarse with Delay on: high shifts give crisp metallic echoes, low shifts long drawn-out delays. Keep the copy quieter for movement in the background.

UI Control Setting
In this garden, UI Control Setting pages model one mode a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control selects, one parameter that exists only in such a mode, or one gesture that gives the control another function.
What counts
A mode: one named position of a selector, such as the oscillator model Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/VAnalog.
A parameter: the name another control takes while that mode is active, such as Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/VAnalog/Detune, which the Wave knob sets.

A gesture: a way of operating the control other than its plain use, such as pressing a knob, holding a button, or using the control while Shift is held: Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/06 Save Button/Hold.
A plain value along a range, such as 64 on a knob, is not a setting page.
Identity and names
A mode sits at <Control>/<Mode>, beneath the control that selects it; a parameter sits at <Control>/<Mode>/<Parameter>.
A gesture sits at <Control>/<Gesture>, named Press, Hold or Shift. A gesture that combines two nests the second beneath the first: Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/02 Paraphonic Button/Hold/Shift.
Use the names the display or manual shows.
Page shape
Frontmatter: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/UI/Control/Setting]] and up:: to the control or mode above it; prev:: and next:: follow the order of modes in the manual when the modes are numbered.
One bullet-wrapped H1, then one sentence on what the setting does.
A parameter page names the control that sets it, with a link.
A Source line links the user guide or manual section.

11.2.3 Connect
Fills the gaps between notes with new notes at random positions.

Spread limits how far their pitch can stray from the originals; Density sets what share of each gap is filled, all of it at 100%. Rate sets their length; Tie is the chance a note extends to the next original note.
Minor Pentatonic Scale
Also called la-pentatonic in solmization and yu mode in Chinese theory. On C: C E♭ F G B♭. Steps in semitones: 3 2 2 3 2. The fifth mode of Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major.
History

and Kodály's fieldwork after found that the oldest layer of Hungarian peasant song is in a minor pentatonic, often with a melody that repeats a fifth lower in its second half. Bartók set out that finding in The Hungarian Folk Song ( ). It overturned the assumption that Hungarian music meant the style hongrois of Music/Scale/Minor/Hungarian.
The scale is also the foundation of blues and rock melody, where Music/Scale/Blues adds a ♭5 to it.
Use
Rock and blues guitar organize improvisation around five fingerboard patterns of this scale, the "boxes".
Over a dominant seventh chord, the ♭3 grates against the chord's major third. Blues players treat that clash as the idiom.
Kodály pedagogy uses la-pentatonic for early minor-mode songs.
Quirks
Every note of the scale is a chord tone or tension of a minor eleventh chord on the tonic (C E♭ G B♭ F), so the scale can be played over that chord with no avoid notes.
11.2.2 Chop
Divides notes into 2 to 64 Parts, and builds division patterns of up to 16 parts that repeat.

Gaps adds rests: a positive value puts a gap after that many notes, a negative value puts that many gaps after each note. Pattern toggles show the result and let you add or remove gaps by hand, which sets Gaps to a dash.
Emphasis toggles pick notes or gaps to lengthen by the Stretch Chunk(s) factor, 2 to 8 times. Variation randomizes note starts and ends.

31.1.4 Filters
Two multi-mode filters with independent settings, flexible routing, saturation and modulation.
Fil 1 / Fil 2 — on switches; the chooser beside each picks 2nd- or 4th-order low-pass, band-pass, notch, high-pass or formant.
Freq and Reso — cutoff and resonance. With a formant filter, Reso moves between vowel sounds. Filter 1's Freq:
To F2 (Filter 1) — how much of Filter 1's output feeds Filter 2.
Follow (Filter 2) — Filter 2's cutoff tracks Filter 1, including its modulation; Filter 2's Freq then sets the offset.
Freq Mod and Res Mod — modulation of cutoff and resonance by LFO, note pitch and filter envelope; negative values lower them.
Drive — saturation after the filter: Off, three symmetrical Sym modes, or asymmetrical Asym modes; higher numbers distort more.
34.1.2 Manual Control Surface Setup
A controller that is not in the Control Surface chooser can still be mapped by hand from the MIDI Ports section of the Link, Tempo & MIDI tab.
To use an input port for remote control, set its Remote switch to On. Any number of ports can be on; Live merges their MIDI.
For a controller with motorized faders or LEDs, also turn on Remote for its output port so Live can send changed values back to it.
To test, send MIDI from the controller: the Control Bar's MIDI indicators flash when Live receives a message.
The manual suggests choosing a Takeover Mode before leaving Settings — Ableton/Live/UG/34 MIDI and Key Remote/01 MIDI Remote Control/03 Takeover Mode. Mapping then happens one parameter at a time.
31.2.4 Resonator Tabs
The resonators define most of the sound. Each tab has an on switch; with both off there is no sound.
Resonance Type:
Beam — beams of various materials and sizes.
Marimba — a Beam variant with the overtone tuning of arch-cut marimba bars.
String — strings of various materials and sizes.
Membrane — a rectangular membrane like a drum head.
Plate — a flat rectangular plate.
Pipe — a tube open at one end with an adjustable opening at the other.
Tube — a tube closed at both ends.
Quality — Eco to High, trading overtone detail for CPU. Not on Pipe or Tube.
1 → 2 / 2 → 1 — copy one resonator's settings to the other.
X-Y Controller — horizontal sets decay, vertical sets Material or Radius.
Decay — internal damping.

Material — low values let lows ring longer (wood, rubber, nylon); high values let highs ring longer (glass, metal). Pipe and Tube use Radius instead: larger means longer decay and more sustained highs, and at extremes a pitch change.
Ratio (Membrane, Plate) — proportion of the object's two sides.
Brightness — louder highs at higher values. Not on Pipe or Tube.
Inharm — negative compresses partials downward, positive stretches them upward. Not on Pipe or Tube.
Opening (Pipe) — 0% closed at one end, 100% open at both.
Hit — strike point, center at 0% toward the edge at higher values; Rnd randomizes it. Not on Pipe or Tube.
Note Off — how much note-off mutes the resonance; 0% ignores it like a real marimba, 100% mutes at once.
Pos. L / Pos. R — where vibrations are picked up on each side, center to edge. Pipe and Tube are always measured at the open end.
Decay, Material/Radius, Inharm and Opening can be modulated in the MIDI tab.
31.2.4.1 Tuning Section
Tune in semitones and Fine in cents, up to ±50.
Key in the MIDI tab sets keyboard tracking: 100% is equal temperament, 200% makes each half step a whole step, negative values fall in pitch as you play higher.
Pitch Env and Time — a starting pitch that glides to the final pitch; velocity can scale the start.
31.2.4.2 Mixer Section
Gain and Pan per resonator; pan can follow note pitch.
Bleed — mixes in the dry exciter signal, which helps restore highs lost at low tuning or quality.

5.5 Live Projects
A Live Project is a folder for the files of one piece of music: its Set versions, recordings, imported samples, and the clips and presets that belong to it. The File Manager manages it.
11.2.10 Strum
Staggers the start times of a chord's notes, like strumming.

Strum Low offsets from the lowest note and Strum High from the highest, each up to a grid step forward (positive) or back (negative); at least one must be non-zero. Set them in the Strum Position display or by typing.
Tension curves the spacing: positive values start wide and narrow; negative values start tight and widen. At 0 the spacing is even.
7.2 Tracks and Scenes
A track plays one clip at a time, so put alternatives in the same column: song parts, variations of a drum loop.

Drag the edges of a track's title bar to resize it, narrow enough to show only launch buttons and key controls; Option (Mac) / Alt (Win) resizes all tracks. 0 on a selected track header deactivates the track.
Rows are scenes. A Scene Launch button in the Main track column launches the whole row. Cancel Scene Launch in the Main track's context menu cancels a pending one.
After a scene launches, the next one down is selected, unless Select Next Scene on Launch is off in Launch Settings, so you can step down the list. Keys and MIDI can launch and scroll scenes.
Rename scenes with Rename, using Tab to move to the next; add info text and colors from the context menu.
Drag scenes to reorder. Nonadjacent scenes collapse together when dragged; Ctrl+up/down moves them without collapsing. Scene numbers follow position.
See .
10.2.1 Grid Snapping

The grid acts like a magnet: a note moves freely to the first grid line, then snaps. Turn snapping off with the grid settings button, Options → Snap to Grid, or Cmd+4 (Mac) / Ctrl+4 (Win); hold Cmd (Mac) / Alt (Win) to bypass it for one action, or to enable it while it's off.
Notes keep their offset from the grid as they snap, preserving a loose feel.

29.33.6 Sidechain Parameters
By default Roar's own input drives the envelope follower and the feedback pitch. The Sidechain Section toggle at the top left opens external audio and MIDI sidechain controls.
External SC — External Source picks the audio source, External Tapping Point Post FX or Post Mixer. Mix blends internal (0%) and external (100%) as the trigger; SC Gain sets trigger level only.
MIDI > FB Note — incoming MIDI sets the feedback pitch in Note mode. Pick the track under MIDI From and Pre FX or Post FX. Feedback Mode and Feedback Amount are disabled while this is on.
Sidechain Listen — replaces the output with the sidechain signal for monitoring
Band-pass filter
Lets frequencies near the cutoff through and cuts those above and below it.

Timbre (Vocoder)
Set by the Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Timbre while the oscillator model is Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/Vocoder.

Changes the frequency range used for analysis and resynthesis. Voice formants are frequency peaks; for example, a “U” often has peaks near 330 Hz and 1260 Hz, with variation across speakers and cultures. The synthesis filters recreate the input loudness contour in the selected range. Narrowing the range reduces the frequencies the Vocoder monitors, improving response time and frequency output.

Matrix — sources across, targets down. With the tab open, click a parameter to add it as a target, then drag a cell up or down to set the amount. Global Modulation Amount scales everything; X clears all modulation.

25. Instrument, Drum and Effect Racks
Instrument, Drum and Effect Racks: chains, zones, Macro Controls and mixing inside a Rack.

A Rack holds effects, plug-ins and instruments in a track's device chain. Racks can build complex processors, playable performance instruments and stacked synths, while gathering the most important controls in one place. Even a single device gains from a Rack, through new control relationships between its parameters.
Saved Racks are Ableton/File/.adg files.

Software Project
In this garden, Software Project pages model software products: applications for end users, libraries, frameworks, CLIs, desktop or web apps, editors, runtimes, and the like.
Examples in this garden

, , and model the current page shape: a linked H1 title, the repository and star count directly beneath it, then lean descriptive bullets. , , and show the naming instinct—short root-level pages—but predate this shape and lead with prose or an unlinked title; follow them for naming only, not for the first block.
How to name the main page for a software project

ancestors: How to name the main page for a software project
content.text: Give a software entity a root-level one-word or short main page when its primary name is not confusing and it is either reputable or nascent but likely to grow sub-namespaces for shortcuts, config, docs, or related notes. A short main name leaves room; long names (owner/repo or person/project) make every child path longer and harder to work with. Example: rather than Person/Jesse Duffield/GitHub/Lazygit. Aliases can point from other namespaces, such as Programming/Language/Rust or Person/Name/GitHub/Project, to that main page when useful.

ancestors: How to name the main page for a software project
content.text: When the garden is tracking a company or person context, some projects may stay under that sub-namespace for situational awareness. If one of those sub-namespace pages is a software entity and later becomes heavily used in the garden, refactor it: give it a root-level page and add an alias from the old path. Example: this garden originally had Anthropic/App/Claude Code because the focus was on the company; after more content and Claude Code becoming a cultural force, it got its own page with an alias to the old location.

ancestors: How to name the main page for a software project
content.text: Having more than one rule here is intentional but can feel confusing. The aim is to avoid spamming the top level with every similar piece of software, and to use placement as a subtle signal: root-level primacy for software that has "arrived" or is clearly going to grow; under company or person when we're tracking it in context of that entity.
When we treat something as a software project

ancestors: When we treat something as a software project
content.text: Strong signals: GitHub or similar repo links, official project homepages, article or post titles that name a software project, or notes that describe a tool, editor, library, app, CLI, or server. We may infer a software entity from context; when we do, we note that in the report.
Finding and deduplicating

Check in this order: exact main page name, exact alias, partial title match, repo owner and repo name, then page-body mentions of the same homepage, repo, or description. Classify as: existing, similar, new, or blocked.
Frontmatter
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.

To mark a page as a software project instance, add logseq-entity:: pointing at this type page (the namespace uses nested segments: Logseq/Entity/Software/Project). The type page then gets backlinks to all software project pages.
Software-project-specific frontmatter can include created-by:: pointing to a person or company page when the creator entity is clear.
Page shape
File: pages/<ProjectName>.md. In links, use the main page name with forward slashes for namespaces where we use them (e.g. Lazygit/Keyshort/Some action).

The first block is an H1 whose text links to the project: - # [ProjectName](url). The H1 link points to the project's canonical home—its homepage when it has one, otherwise its repository. Descriptive prose never shares the H1 line; the description lives in child bullets below it.

The top-of-page links come first, directly under the H1 and before the description. When the project has both a homepage and a repository, the H1 links the homepage and the first child bullet links the repository. When it lives only on a repository, the H1 links the repository and no separate repository bullet is added.
Each external location appears exactly once. A repository already linked at the top is never repeated in a later "Source repository" or "Links" bullet.
After the links, keep the page lean: a few descriptive child bullets. State the implementation language on its own short bullet (for example, "Written in .") rather than folding it into prose.
When the project is hosted on GitHub, include the count when available: record the count with a dated source-check day on the repository line (or on its own bullet when the repository is the H1).

If the creator is clear and is an individual, create or use a Person/... page and point created-by:: there. If the creator is clearly an organization tracked in the garden, create or use a company entity page and point created-by:: there.

The Clip View has a title bar, clip panels on the left, and an editor on the right: the Sample Editor for audio clips, the MIDI Note Editor for MIDI clips. See .

13.2.1. Step-Time Recording of Modulation
Select a pattern, stop playback, and press Record. Turn Rate/Swing to select the step where modulation should begin.

Turn a control to audition its value. The display shows the step, modulation slot, parameter, and amount. Release the control to store that position with the step. Move to another step with Rate/Swing and set the next value. Repeat across the pattern.
You can fill one control's track across all steps before assigning another control, or set up to four controls at each step before moving on.
The Rate Knob

Turning Rate/Swing through the steps plays their stored notes and modulation, so you can hear and edit each value. Turn its assigned control to replace a stored position. Oct | Mod cycles through active modulation tracks.
Controls available for modulation tracks
Oscillator: Type, Wave, Timbre, and Shape. With sample selection enabled, Type controls sample selection.
Filter: Cutoff and Resonance.
Envelope: Attack, Decay, Sustain, and Filter Amount.
LFO: Rate.
Cycling Envelope: Rise, Fall, Hold, and Amount sent to the Matrix.
Matrix: Modulation amount of a matrix point.
Glide: Glide amount.
To clear a track, press Oct | Mod until its light blinks, then hold Oct | Mod and press Hold. Press Hold repeatedly while holding Oct | Mod to clear further tracks.

05.2 The Matrix and its encoder
The Matrix links control signals from sources to destinations.

A classic synthesizer sends an oscillator through a filter and then an amplifier. The Matrix lets you override those fixed connections and route triggers, gates, LFO waves, and envelopes to the Digital Oscillator and Filter.
The Matrix is the main switchboard for creating, changing, and mixing modulation connections. It has a switchboard and an encoder for selecting connections and setting their modulation amount.
The Matrix and its encoder
Turn the encoder to choose a source–destination point, then press it to create or edit the connection. It scrolls forward or backward and wraps at the end of the Matrix.
The Matrix shows each connection's state:

ancestors: The Matrix shows each connection's state:
content.text: LED on: a connection is active.

ancestors: The Matrix shows each connection's state:
content.text: LED blinking: the connection is selected and its modulation amount is being edited.

The display shows the selected connection and its current modulation amount. Press the encoder to edit the amount; the display inverts and only that connection's LED stays lit. Changes take effect immediately.

Multiple sources can control the same destination. For example, Key/Arp and the LFO can both affect oscillator pitch, and their modulation amounts are added together. With a rectangular LFO wave, this can transpose a sequence up and down at the LFO rate.
Setting a connection's amount to zero turns it off. To clear a Matrix point and reset its amount, hold the encoder for at least 0.5 seconds.

40.3 Live’s MIDI Solutions

Ableton works from two assumptions: latency is better than jitter, because it is predictable, and when playing through while recording you want to record what you hear, even if that is slightly later than what you played.
Recording — the MIDI interface driver timestamps each event on arrival, and Live places the event in the clip by that timestamp.

Playthrough — Live delays events by a constant amount rather than playing them whenever the busy system gets to them. With monitoring on, it adds a delay based on the audio buffer size, so notes land in the clip where you heard them.
Playback to hardware — Live sends timestamps for the driver to schedule outgoing events. Windows MME drivers cannot use timestamps, so Live schedules those events itself.
During audio dropouts Live still receives and records MIDI correctly, even if playthrough sounds wrong; playback is accurate once the system recovers.

use material with clear attacks — notes that swell in may be missed;

12.7 Arpeggiator fun

The Arpeggiator can act as a modulation source. The effect is subtle, so increase the modulation amount and extend the octave range. Routing it to two destinations can make the movement easier to hear.

Set the oscillator type to Waveshaper.

8.2.1 Clip and Loop Region Settings
The region and loop decide what plays when a clip launches. An unlooped clip plays from start to end, or until stopped.

Type start and end values, or press Set Start and Set End during playback to set them at the playhead, quantized to global quantization. Warped audio shows bars-beats-sixteenths; unwarped audio shows minutes-seconds-milliseconds.
The Clip Loop toggle loops the clip over Loop Position and Length, which defaults to the whole clip. Audio clips must be warped to loop.

During playback, Set Loop Position moves the loop start to the playhead and turns looping on; Set Loop Length then ends the loop at the playhead, capturing a loop on the fly. With looping off, Set Loop Length ends the loop at the playhead keeping its length, and turns looping on.
All of these can be MIDI mapped, for example a rotary encoder that walks the loop through a sample by the quantization step.

31.9.4 Envelopes
Seven envelopes: one per oscillator, plus filter, pitch and LFO. All can loop; filter and pitch envelopes have adjustable slopes.

Oscillator envelopes have three rates and three levels: from Initial (often -inf dB) at the attack rate to Peak, at the decay rate to Sustain, and after note-off at the release rate back to silence. Drag breakpoints or nudge selected ones with arrow keys. Copy shapes between oscillators from the context menu.
Slopes (filter, pitch) — positive moves fast then slow, negative slow then fast, zero linear.
Loop — an envelope that reaches sustain while held restarts; Loop Time sets the return. Fast loops give effects you wouldn't expect from an envelope, and are the key to endless evolving FM sounds.
Beat — restarts after the Repeat beat time without quantizing the first note. Sync — quantizes the first repeat to the nearest 16th so repeats follow the song; acts like Beat when stopped.
Looped envelopes restart from their current level at the attack rate, so they don't click.
Trigger — ignores note-off; good for percussion.
Global Time scales all rates except Beat and Sync times; Time < Key speeds envelopes for higher notes; Time < Vel per envelope.
The pitch envelope has Destination A–D and LFO buttons with an amount, an on switch in the shell, and a Dest. B target with Amt. B.
Pitch and filter envelopes add End, the level after release.
Tip from the manual: a looping pitch envelope routed only to the LFO acts as a second LFO on its rate, and the LFO's own looping envelope as a third on its depth.

29.42 Vocoder
Vocoder is not in the Intro and Lite editions.

A vocoder imposes the level contour of one signal, the modulator (usually speech or drums), onto the frequencies of another, the carrier (usually a rich synth such as strings or a pad). The classic result is a talking synth or robot voice.
Both signals pass through banks of band-pass filters; the level in each modulator band sets the level of the matching carrier band.
Put Vocoder on the modulator's track. Carrier options:

ancestors: Put Vocoder on the modulator's track. Carrier options:
content.text: Noise — internal noise; its X-Y display sets downsampling (horizontal, left lowers the sample rate) and density (vertical, down thins it)

ancestors: Put Vocoder on the modulator's track. Carrier options:
content.text: External — any internal routing point; the usual choice for robot voices

ancestors: Put Vocoder on the modulator's track. Carrier options:
content.text: Modulator — the modulator carries itself, a resynthesized version shaped by Vocoder's controls

ancestors: Put Vocoder on the modulator's track. Carrier options:
content.text: Pitch Tracking — a monophonic oscillator that follows the modulator's pitch, limited by High and Low. Saw or three pulse waves, with Pitch for coarse tuning. It holds each detected pitch until it finds a new one, so changing its settings or resetting it (for instance by grouping the track) can change the sound unexpectedly. Best on single melodic lines or voice; unpredictable but interesting on chords and drums.
Enhance — normalizes the carrier's spectrum and dynamics for a brighter sound, useful with external carriers
Unvoiced — level of an extra noise source for pitchless sounds like "f" and "s"; Sens. sets detection (100% always on, 0% off); Fast/Slow how quickly it switches
The center display shows each band's level; click in it to lower bands.
Bands — number of filters; more is more accurate and uses more CPU
Range — frequency span of the filters; narrow it if the sound gets too piercing or boomy
BW — filter bandwidth; 100% is most accurate, other values can be interesting
Precise/Retro — equal gain and width for every band, or narrower, louder bands toward the top
Gate — bands below the threshold are silent
Level — output boost or cut
Depth — how much of the modulator's envelope reaches the carrier; 0% none, 100% classic vocoding, 200% only the loudest peaks
Attack and Release — response speed; very fast keeps transients but can distort
Channel switches — Mono (both mono), Stereo (mono modulator, stereo carrier), L/R (both stereo)
Formant — shifts the carrier's filter bank; small changes on a voice can change its apparent gender
Dry/Wet — balance of processed and dry signal

29.31 Resonators

Resonators is five resonators in parallel that give the input a pitched character, from plucked strings to vocoder-like tones. They tune in semitones, scale degrees or a tuning system — Ableton/Live/UG/15 Tuning Systems.
Input filter first: low-pass, band-pass, high-pass or notch, with Frequency.
Mode — A sounds more realistic; B is interesting with Resonator I set low.
Decay — how long the resonators ring; longer is more sustained and tonal, like an undamped piano string. Low notes ring longer unless Const is on.
Color — brightness
Resonator I takes both channels; II and IV the left; III and V the right.
Tuning:
by default Resonator I sets the root and the others are intervals above it
with scale awareness, Resonator I follows the clip's scale in octave 2
with a tuning system, Resonator I is an absolute pitch from the tuning
Note sets the root — semitones C-1 to C5, scale degrees, or tuning indices; Resonator I Fine Tuning in cents
Each resonator has On/Off (off saves CPU; turning off I does not affect the others) and Gain. II–V follow Note and add their own Pitch (±24 semitones or ±21 scale degrees) and fine tuning.
Output: Width (wet only; 0% folds II–V to mono), Gain (resonated level unless Dry/Wet is 0%), Dry/Wet.

13.3.2. First Experiment: Mixing Pitches

The sequencer controls oscillator pitch directly. Route the LFO to pitch through the Matrix as well, and the two signals add together. A slow rectangular LFO makes the sequence jump between pitch levels. Change the Matrix amount to control the size and direction of the shift.

Variation: Also route the LFO to filter cutoff. With enough modulation to close the filter, some parts of the sequence fall silent. Try different LFO waveforms and amounts to change the rhythm of those gaps.

A random LFO waveform can transpose a running sequence at unpredictable times. Change LFO speed to change when transpositions occur; increase the Matrix amount for wider jumps or use a negative amount to invert the modulation.

Music Scale

In this garden, Music Scale pages model a named collection of pitches ordered from a tonic — a scale, a mode, or a parent scale such as a Hindustani thaat — described apart from any key or instrument.
What counts

A named pitch collection with a tonic: the major scale, the church modes, the minor variants, pentatonic and hexatonic collections, symmetrical scales, and scales from other traditions under the names Western menus give them.
A scale page has no fixed tonic pitch. C major is the major scale on C; a piece or key in C major links to Music/Scale/Major.
A raga has a page of its own, which links to the scale page of its parent thaat.
Chords, tuning systems and a device's scale menu have pages of their own. A device's user guide links each menu entry to its scale page.
Naming and placement
A scale lives at Music/Scale/<Name>, under Music/Scale. Family nouns come first and qualifiers nest beneath them: Music/Scale/Minor/Natural, Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic, Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major.

A scale whose common name qualifies another scale's name nests under that scale. The nesting follows the name even when the scale derives from elsewhere: Music/Scale/Dorian/Ukrainian is the fourth mode of harmonic minor.
The leaf carries the most common English-language name. The first line under the H1 gives the scale's other names: mode names, names from other traditions, and spellings found in device manuals.
A transliterated name uses the standard spelling in the leaf. Music/Scale/Marwa mentions Marva, the Launchpad's spelling.
Finding and deduplicating
One collection often carries several names. Aeolian and natural minor share one page.
Compare scale-semitones-above-tonic:: values before creating a page. A rotation of an existing scale is a different mode and gets its own page.
Sources disagree on the pitches behind some names, such as Hirajoshi, Bebop Dorian and Blues. One page holds the name and describes the variants.
Frontmatter
Logseq/Entity/Music/Scale/Frontmatter/scale-semitones-above-tonic records the pitches as semitones above the tonic.
Other conventions follow Logseq/Frontmatter.
Page shape
One H1 with the scale's common name, followed by a line giving its other names, its spelling on C and its steps in semitones.

Sections ## History, ## Use and ## Quirks. Pages assume formal training in composition and theory: they skip definitions of intervals and modes and spend the space on origins, repertoire and structural properties.
When a device manual spells a scale differently from its standard form, the scale page notes the difference under Quirks and links the manual page.
A mode page links the scale it rotates; a variant links the scale it alters.
Examples
Music/Scale/Major, Music/Scale/Dorian, Music/Scale/Whole Tone, Music/Scale/Todi.

29.38 Spectrum

Spectrum analyzes frequencies in real time and draws level (dB, vertical) against frequency or pitch (horizontal). Peaks stay on the graph until the song restarts. It measures only and never changes the sound.
Block — samples per measurement; more is more accurate and uses more CPU
Channel — left, right or both
Refresh — how often it analyzes; faster is more accurate and uses more CPU
Avg — how many blocks are averaged per update. 1 shows every block, good for finding short peaks; higher values give a smoother view closer to how we hear.
Graph — a smooth line or discrete frequency bins
Max — shows the accumulated maximum; click the display to reset it

18.5 Using Live’s Crossfader
Live's crossfader blends between any number of tracks, returns included. Show it from View → Mixer Controls or the mixer view control menu.
Right-click it to choose one of seven curves.

It maps to any continuous MIDI control. Its far left and right positions can also be mapped separately: a key on one position toggles between the extremes, and keys on two positions give a snap-back move.
Each track's A and B Crossfade Assign buttons decide its response: neither, unaffected; A, full volume across the left half and fading to silence at the right; B, the reverse.
Assignments change only volume at each track's gain stage, not routing — like a VCA group.
Crossfader moves record into the Arrangement. Edit assignments under Mixer → X-Fade Assign in a track's envelope choosers, and the crossfader itself under Mixer → Crossfade on the Main track.

Click a track's Arm button to record-enable it. Session and Arrangement share tracks, so either view works.
Armed tracks are monitored by default ("auto-monitoring"), so you hear the input through the device chain.
Arming a MIDI track locks a natively supported control surface to the track's instrument.
Arming one track disarms the others unless you hold Cmd (Mac) / Ctrl (Windows) or several tracks are selected. Arming also selects the track, showing its devices.

05.1 Control Signals
The Matrix connects control signals from the MicroFreak's modules. These signals move more slowly than audio and are suited to controlling sound.
The MicroFreak Matrix
Control signals usually move between 0 and 100 Hz. They can modulate the Digital Oscillator, Analog Filter, and other destinations. The Matrix encoder sets their amount from -100% to +100%.
The MicroFreak's modules generate control signals in different ways.

ancestors: The MicroFreak's modules generate control signals in different ways.
content.text: The LFO makes slow, regular waves. Routed to oscillator pitch, it makes the pitch rise and fall; it can reach 100 Hz.

ancestors: The MicroFreak's modules generate control signals in different ways.
content.text: An envelope rises once, then gradually fades. Routed to oscillator pitch, it creates a quick rise followed by a descent. The Cycling Envelope can repeat, acting as a second LFO with more complex modulation waves.
A gate rises at Note On and falls at Note Off. The keyboard sends gates that start the MicroFreak's envelope.
Three kinds of control signals are used: triggers, gates, and waves.

ancestors: Three kinds of control signals are used: triggers, gates, and waves.
content.text: Triggers are very short spikes that start an envelope, LFO, or sequencer. Clocks generate triggers.

ancestors: Three kinds of control signals are used: triggers, gates, and waves.
content.text: Gates last longer and keep something active, such as an envelope's hold stage. A keyboard sends a gate while a key is held.

ancestors: Three kinds of control signals are used: triggers, gates, and waves.
content.text: Waves can last any length and usually cycle from high to low and back. The MicroFreak's LFO and two envelopes create slow waves.
Control signals give a MicroFreak performer room to develop a personal style, as color and line do for a painter.

Note for advanced users: Analog synthesizers and modular systems use control voltages for modulation. Mostly digital synthesizers such as the MicroFreak use digital signals that mimic those voltages; this manual calls them control signals.

In this video, we're going to take a look at linked tracks. Using the Link Track feature allows you to adjust multiple tracks to edit or adjust parameters. A great use for this feature is when you've recorded multiple sources at the same time.

So for example, in this case, I have a multi mic recording of some drums in this project. Linking tracks is a very simple procedure in the arrangement view. All I have to do is select the tracks I'd like to link together,

right click to access the context menu and select Link Tracks. When tracks have been successfully linked together, there's a small icon indicating linked tracks in the top right-hand corner of each track.

Now, if I go into my Arrangement View and select any of the clips from the linked tracks, all of the linked tracks are highlighted. With the tracks linked, you can now perform all kinds of edits to all the linked tracks. For example... Splitting and deleting selections.

Reversing selections. Or adding cross-fades and fades. And even renaming selections. You can also manipulate warp markers and warp parameters of all linked tracks. Another great feature of Linked Tracks is the ability to adjust parameters in the mixer section.

By selecting one of the tracks in a Link Track selection, you're able to adjust the mixer parameters of that particular track. In this state, you can continue to work on other individual tracks and adjust their mixer parameters.

If you wish to work on all of the linked tracks at the same time, simply click on the Link Track icon and adjust their parameters. This allows for a great amount of flexibility for you to either adjust individual parameters in the mixer section,

or adjust them all collectively together. Not only can you link together Audio tracks, but you can also link together MIDI tracks. or a combination of MIDI and Audio tracks. As a final technique, Link Tracks can also be used to comp together
several takes from several tracks simultaneously.

The Device tab contains MIDI and configuration settings for the MicroFreak.
Left column of MicroFreak Device Tab in MIDI Control Center
MIDI
MIDI Input Channel: All, 1–16, or None. Sets the receive channel on the MicroFreak's 16-channel MIDI port.
MIDI Output Channel: 1–16. Sets the transmit channel.
MIDI Output Destination: Off, USB, MIDI, or MIDI + USB. USB connects directly to a computer; MIDI cables can run over longer distances.

Dorian Mode
Also called the protus authentic mode or Mode 1. On C: C D E♭ F G A B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 2 1 2. The second mode of Music/Scale/Major.
History

The name is Greek but the scale is not. The ancient Greek Dorian octave species ran from E to E in modern terms, the collection now called Phrygian. Carolingian theorists, most visibly the anonymous Alia musica around , attached the Greek names to the church modes in a different order.
In plainchant and Renaissance polyphony, the D mode was defined by its final, its range and its reciting tone A. B♭ was common, so much Dorian music sounds Aeolian to modern ears.

Baroque composers often wrote D minor with no key signature, a habit inherited from Dorian notation. 's Toccata and Fugue in D minor BWV 538 is called "Dorian" for that reason alone: its notation has no flat, and its music is in D minor.
Use
Modal jazz made Dorian a vamp scale. 's "So What" (Kind of Blue, ) sits on D Dorian with a bridge in E♭ Dorian, and 's "Impressions" uses the same form.
The i–IV vamp, a minor tonic with a major subdominant, is Dorian's signature in rock and Latin music, as in 's "Oye Como Va" and the rock band Santana's cover of it, with on guitar.
English and Celtic folk melodies, among them "Scarborough Fair", are often Dorian.
In jazz chord-scale theory it is the default scale for a minor seventh chord functioning as ii.
Quirks
Its step pattern is a palindrome, so Dorian is the only diatonic mode that inverts to itself about its tonic. D is the center of symmetry of the white-key collection.
The raised sixth makes IV a major triad and puts a tritone between ♭3 and 6. That raised sixth is the note a listener uses to tell Dorian from Aeolian.
Music/Scale/Dorian/Ukrainian and Music/Scale/Dorian/Bebop carry Dorian in their names. Ukrainian Dorian derives from harmonic minor, and Bebop Dorian adds a chromatic passing tone.
The MicroFreak manual spells its "Dorian" and "Minor" settings almost identically; the "Minor" spelling is this scale with an added B natural. See Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings.

29.9 Compressor
A compressor turns down signal above a threshold. Lower peaks leave room to raise the overall level, so the result sounds louder and punchier.
Threshold sets where compression starts. Ratio sets how much: at 3, a 3 dB rise above the threshold comes out as 1 dB. A ratio of 1 does nothing.

The orange Gain Reduction meter shows the current reduction. The manual warns that more than about 6 dB changes the sound a lot and can flatten dynamics in a way that cannot be undone later — especially on the Main track.
Out raises the level again after compression; Makeup does it automatically as Threshold and Ratio change.
Dry/Wet — 0% bypasses, 100% is fully compressed

Knee — how gradually compression starts. 0 dB is a hard knee, which can sound harsh at high ratios. A 10 dB knee with a −20 dB threshold starts gently at −30 dB and reaches full compression at −10 dB.

31.9.2 Oscillator Section
31.9.2.1 Built-in Waveforms

From the Wave chooser: pure Sine, the usual first choice for FM; Sine 4 Bit and Sine 8 Bit for a C64-style sound; Saw D and Square D digital shapes for bass; resynthesized square, triangle and saw whose number (e.g. Square 6) is the harmonic count, with lower numbers mellower and less prone to aliasing; Noise Looped, a noise loop; and Noise White, true random noise.
31.9.2.2 User Waveforms
User, or any built-in wave, can be edited by drawing harmonic amplitudes with the pencil; Shift locks to one harmonic. The status bar shows harmonic number and amplitude.
Edit the first 16, 32 or 64 harmonics. Repeat extends them upward with a fade: low values are brighter, high values roll off more and favor the fundamental; Off truncates.
The context menu limits drawing to even or odd harmonics and toggles Normalize, which keeps level constant; with it off, output can get very loud.

Export as Ableton/File/.ams to Samples/Waveforms in the User Library; drop .ams files back on an oscillator, or into Simpler or Sampler. The Osc Preview's context menu copies waves between oscillators.
31.9.2.3 More Oscillator Parameters
Coarse and Fine set frequency relative to the note. Fixed ignores note pitch and uses Freq times Multi, down to 0.1 Hz; only the timbre changes across keys, as for drums.
Osc < Vel shifts frequency with velocity; Q quantizes the shift to whole ratios, otherwise it detunes into inharmonic tones.
Amplitude comes from Level and the oscillator's envelope, scaled by Vel and Key.
Phase, and R to restart the phase per note or run free.
When modulating, the modulator's level and the frequency ratio set the result. An oscillator nothing modulates can modulate itself with Feedback.
31.9.2.4 Aliasing

Digital synthesis aliases at high frequencies, and FM, with its many harmonics, does so readily; complex waves like Saw 32 more than sines. A little can be useful; too much makes high notes fold to unrelated pitches.
Antialias mode, on by default for new patches, reduces it. Tone in the global section also tames it, sometimes like a low-pass filter. To hear aliasing, turn Tone up and play very high notes.

34.2.4 Mapping to Relative MIDI Controllers

Relative controllers send "increase" and "decrease" messages instead of absolute values, so a parameter never jumps when the hardware and Live disagree. A relative pan knob just moves the pan a little from wherever it is.
Live supports four kinds — Signed Bit, Signed Bit 2, Bin Offset and Twos Complement — each also in a linear version. Some encoders accelerate, sending bigger steps when turned quickly.

For controllers that are not natively supported, Live tries to detect the kind and whether acceleration is used. Turning the control slowly to the left while mapping helps. Live's guess appears in the Status Bar's mode chooser, where it can be changed by hand.
What the messages do:
Session View slots — increase acts as Note On, decrease as Note Off.
Switches — increase turns on, decrease turns off.
Radio buttons — increase steps forward, decrease steps back.
Continuous controls — each kind reads the 0–127 range differently to tell increases from decreases.
34.2.4.1 Relative Session View Navigation

Besides mapping single slots and scenes, controls can be mapped to move the highlighted scene and launch the highlighted clips. In MIDI Map Mode and Key Map Mode a strip of mappable controls appears below the Session grid.

a scene number box, best mapped to an endless encoder, for scrolling through scenes
a button that launches the highlighted scene; with Select Next Scene on Launch on in the Record, Warp & Launch Settings, each press moves on to the next scene
a button that cancels a triggered scene launch
one button per track that launches that track's clip in the highlighted scene
Live keeps the highlighted scene centered in Session View, which helps in large Sets.

23.3 Device Delay Compensation
Live compensates automatically for processing delays from built-in devices and plug-ins, return tracks included, keeping tracks in sync with as little delay as possible between playing and hearing.
It's on by default; Options → Delay Compensation turns it off.

With it on, Reduced Latency When Monitoring (Options menu) skips compensation on input-monitored tracks for the lowest latency, at the risk of those tracks falling out of sync with compensated ones such as returns.
Tempo-synced effects placed after delay-causing devices can sound out of time.

Very large track delays or plug-in latencies can make Live sluggish. Turning compensation off is not usually advised and also disables Track Delay; adjusting track delays may help instead. Compensation can add CPU load.

ancestors: One namespace for kinds of piece and structures
content.text: "Sonata" names two related things. A sonata is a kind of piece, usually in several movements. Sonata form is the plan of a single movement: exposition, development, recapitulation. The second movement of Beethoven's Pathétique Sonata belongs to a sonata and is a rondo; the first movement of Mozart's Symphony No. 40 is in sonata form and belongs to a symphony.

content.text: Alternative: Music/Shape/. "Form" is overloaded and "shape" is not, so Music/Shape/Sonata and Music/Shape/Sonata Form keep the kind of piece apart from the music-theory sense. No one in music uses "shape" this way, so every reader would learn the term from the garden. A nested Music/Shape/Sonata/Form would also imply that sonata form is part of a sonata, which the Mozart example contradicts.

ancestors: One namespace for kinds of piece and structures
content.text: Alternative: Music/Genre/ for kinds of piece, Music/Form/ for structures. Musicologists use "genre" for the symphony, sonata and nocturne: Jim Samson's "Genre" article in Grove Music Online, Jeffrey Kallberg's "The Rhetoric of Genre: Chopin's Nocturne in G Minor" ( ), and Carl Dahlhaus on Gattung. The Library of Congress files "Preludes (Music)" and "Sonatas" among its Genre/Form Terms without choosing between the words. Working musicians call a sonata a form, not a genre, so the split reads as academic jargon.
Genre is not modeled yet
Genre means different things to different readers: a kind of piece to a musicologist, a style such as rock or ambient to most listeners.

codekiln would model a grouping like genre only if it worked the same way across literature, music and other disciplines of expression, and would prefer a neutral word such as "category." Form may face the same question across disciplines.
Works that organize music history by kinds of piece could change this. Dahlhaus's Nineteenth-Century Music and the Samson article are the places to start.
History
— Filed Logseq/Entity/Music/Form and with the first instance, Rachmaninoff's . Weighed Music/Shape/ and a genre/form split, kept Music/Form/ for both senses, and set genre aside.
Open questions
A cross-discipline grouping word for kinds of works, and whether form belongs in it.

Marwa Thaat
Spelled Marva on the Launchpad. In sargam: S r G M' P D N. On C: C D♭ E F♯ G A B. Steps in semitones: 1 3 2 1 2 2 1.
History
classified Hindustani ragas under ten parent scales, or thaats, in the early , and named each after a prominent raga. Marwa is one of the ten.
A thaat is a classification. Ragas live inside it, each with its own phrases, ascent and descent, emphasized notes and performance time; a thaat itself is never performed.
The Carnatic system's equivalent parent scale is Gamanashrama, melakarta 53.
Use
Raga Marwa, a sunset raga, omits Pa entirely and centers on komal Re and Dha.
Ragas Puriya and Sohini use the same notes with different emphasis: Puriya dwells in the lower register around Ni and Ga, and Sohini in the upper register around high Sa.
Quirks
The thaat has both a raised fourth and a lowered second, so the tonic is approached by a half step from either side (N–S and r–S).

Hindustani pitches are tuned by ear against the tanpura drone and do not match equal temperament. The equal-tempered spelling on a Launchpad approximates the collection without its intonation or melodic rules.

Velocity curves
A logarithmic curve rises quickly and slows near its endpoint. An exponential curve rises slowly, then speeds up. A linear curve changes at a steady rate.
An exponential Rise with a logarithmic Fall can make the envelope feel sluggish. A logarithmic Rise with an exponential Fall can make it start more sharply and end more reluctantly.

Ukrainian Dorian Scale
Also called Romanian minor, Dorian ♯4 and, in klezmer, Mi sheberakh or Av harachamim. On C: C D E♭ F♯ G A B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 3 1 2 1 2. The fourth mode of Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic.
History

The scale belongs to the folk and liturgical music of Ukraine, Romania and Moldova and the Ashkenazi Jewish communities that lived among them. Klezmer musicians named it after the Sabbath prayer Mi sheberakh, whose cantorial setting uses it.
The Western names are descriptive labels from scale catalogues. Practitioners name it by its prayer or by the genre that uses it.
Use
Klezmer doinas, the free-rhythm improvisations that open a suite, often sit in this mode, as do many Romanian and Ukrainian dance tunes.
The augmented second ♭3–♯4 is the mode's signature figure. Melodies circle around ♯4 and resolve it up to 5 or down to ♭3.
Quirks

The name says Dorian, and the only change from Music/Scale/Dorian is the raised fourth. Its pitches still come from harmonic minor a fifth below: C Ukrainian Dorian uses the notes of G harmonic minor.
Over a tonic minor triad, the ♯4 and 6 together outline a diminished-seventh sonority (F♯ A C E♭), which gives a static tonic a strong pull toward the dominant.

08.3 Freaky Tips and Tricks

Use the LFO to modulate both the filter cutoff and the envelope attack and decay times. Filter cutoff is a standard Matrix connection; assign the envelope attack and decay destinations explicitly in the Matrix. See Microfreak/UG/05 Connections/02 Matrix and Encoder for details.
Adding some randomness to filter cutoff creates a fuzzy effect. Random modulation of an envelope's decay or sustain adds variety to a rhythmic pulse and can revive a stale sound.

Use the sine or sawtooth wave to modulate an envelope's level. Playing an arpeggio then produces cyclic crescendos and diminuendos. A very slow LFO can also modulate the Cycling Envelope's rise and fall times; route the resulting envelope to other destinations.

Use the rising sawtooth to modulate the decay time of the Standard or Cycling Envelope for more realistic drum or bell sounds. The Cycling Envelope's attack and fall shapes can also change dynamically from linear to exponential. See Microfreak/UG/09 Envelope Gen for details.

To animate a sequence or arpeggio, sync the LFO, select Random, and apply a small amount of modulation to oscillator pitch in the Matrix. Modulate the Matrix amount with a very short Cycling Envelope set to ENV, so the LFO modulation ends after the initial attack.
Assign Glide amount as an LFO destination to switch Glide on and off by setting its amount to zero. With Sync on, the LFO can activate Glide every other or every fourth sequencer step.

Ableton File Types – Conceptual Overview
Overview

Ableton Live uses a variety of proprietary file types to represent sets, clips, presets, and metadata. Some are human-readable (XML or JSON), others are binary. Understanding these formats is essential for workflows involving version control (e.g., Git).
Context

Many Ableton users want to store projects in Git for collaboration, history, and diffs. The challenge is that some file types are opaque binaries, while others can be normalized for text-based diffs. Knowing which is which helps decide what to commit, ignore, or preprocess.
Key Principles
Textual formats (XML/JSON) are git-friendly with proper filters.
Binary formats (analysis files, waveforms, grooves) are not useful to version and can be regenerated.
Archive formats (packs) should be treated as immutable binaries.
Programmatically generated files (e.g., .asd) should be excluded since Live will recreate them.
File Types & Internal Structure
Misconceptions
Myth: All Ableton files are binary and unsuitable for Git.
Myth: .asd files must be backed up.
Recommendations for Git
Store with filters: .als, .alc, .adg, .adv, .amxd, .ask.
Ignore: .asd (auto-regenerated).
Store as binary: .alp, .ams, .agr (no useful diffs).
Use custom diff drivers:
.als/.alc/.adg/.adv: gzip -cd.
.amxd: strip header, parse JSON.
.ask: plain XML diff.

Notes
Phrygian Mode
Also called the deuterus authentic mode or Mode 3. On C: C D♭ E♭ F G A♭ B♭. Steps in semitones: 1 2 2 2 1 2 2. The third mode of Music/Scale/Major.
History
The ancient Greek Phrygian octave species ran from D to D, the collection now called Dorian. The medieval name shifted with the rest of the Greek names; see Music/Scale/Dorian.

In chant and polyphony the E mode was hard to cadence in, because no leading tone rises to the final. Renaissance cadences in the E mode pair F–E in the bass with D–E above it. Heard from A minor, the result sounds like a half cadence.

That cadence outlived the mode. The Baroque "Phrygian half cadence", iv6–V in minor, uses the same half-step bass descent to the dominant. The two-chord Adagio of 's Brandenburg Concerto No. 3 is one.
Use
Flamenco's characteristic sound is usually Phrygian with a major tonic, close to the fifth mode of Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic, over the Andalusian cadence i–♭VII–♭VI–V.
Heavy metal leans on the ♭2 for darkness, often as a riff that alternates the tonic with ♭II.
In jazz chord-scale theory it fits a minor seventh chord functioning as iii, and the sus4♭9 chord voiced over it.
Carnatic music's Hanumatodi, melakarta 8, is this collection. See Music/Scale/Todi for the different Hindustani Todi.
Quirks
It is the inversion of the major scale: the major step pattern read downward from the tonic gives Phrygian.
Phrygian and Locrian are the only diatonic modes with a ♭2. The ♭II triad sits a half step above a minor tonic, the relation the Neapolitan chord borrows in common-practice minor.
The tonic has no dominant: the triad on 5 is diminished (G B♭ D♭).

12.6.2 The MPE/Multi-Channel Settings Dialog
The dialog chooses the MPE zone (lower or upper) and how many note channels it uses, or switches to multi-channel mode with any range of note channels.

Each zone has a global channel for controls that aren't per-note: channel 1 for the lower zone, channel 16 for the upper. The number of note channels sets the zone's polyphony, for example 1–11 for the lower zone and 12–16 for the upper.
A track outputs to one zone only, so using both zones takes two tracks. Zones apply only to MPE output.
Two tracks routed to the same MIDI output, one per zone, can drive two MPE synths chained through MIDI thru, or two sounds in one synth.

Music Recording
In this garden, Music Recording pages model fixed audio or audiovisual recordings and album releases that preserve or publish musical material.
What counts
A recording is a captured rendition or a published collection of captured tracks. It has an identity apart from the musical work and any live performance it may document.

A studio track, a live album, and a video recording of a performance can each be recorded entities. An album page represents the release and its track order; a single-track page represents one captured rendition.
A recording of a cover is a new recording linked to the covered work. The cover does not create a new page for the underlying song.
Naming and placement

Place a recording under its first credited as <Identity>/Music/Recording/<Title> when Logseq/Frontmatter/created-by-identities is present. For a joint release, keep one page under the first credited identity and list all credited identities. Without a separate identity, use Person/<Artist>/Music/Recording/<Title>. Existing group namespaces remain valid until deliberately renamed.
Use the published album, single, track, or video title as the H1. Add a year or release context to distinguish recordings with the same title.

For an album, list known tracks as bullets under a Tracks heading, in listening order. Each track begins with its two-digit, zero-padded position and a hyphen, as 01 - Dis; the padding is two digits even on an album of nine tracks or fewer. A track links to its musical work page when that work is represented in the garden, and is plain text otherwise. Tracks are never page properties.
Relationships
Use work:: for a single-work recording and performance:: when the recording documents a known performance event.
Album pages list tracks as numbered bullets. A work page may point back to an album with appears-on::.
Use cover-of:: to identify a recording as a cover of an existing work.
Use Logseq/Frontmatter/created-by-identities for published artist credits; created-by:: and performer:: retain verified personal credits rather than being inferred from identity membership.
Use record-label:: to link the Logseq/Entity/Music/Label that released the recording.
Instance shape
Start each recording page with logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording]] and one H1 containing its published title.
Add performer::, date-created::, and links to the represented work, performance, or release when those details are known.
Add logseq-created-time-year:: linking the page of the release, as logseq-created-time-year:: [[20/1/8]] for a 2018 album. A recording without a known year links its decade or century.
Keep tracks in the album's listening order; do not create work pages solely to complete an otherwise unknown track list.

One effect at a time, turned on with the Playback Effect toggle and picked from a menu. Each has two parameters, on knobs or an X/Y pad (vertical first, horizontal second).
Stretch — changes length without pitch, with grainy lo-fi artifacts; Factor and Grain Size.
Loop — repeats part of the sample; Loop Offset and Loop Length.
Pitch Env — pitch sweep; Amount ±100% and Decay back to base pitch.
Punch — fixed-attack ducking that brings out the transient; Amount and Release.
8-Bit — filtering plus bit and sample-rate reduction; Sample Rate and the filter's Decay Time.
FM — a sine modulates pitch; Amount and Frequency.
Ring Mod — Amount and Frequency; low frequencies give tremolo, high ones the usual ring-mod artifacts.
Sub Osc — a 30–120 Hz sub layer on the device's envelope; Amount and Frequency.
Noise — a noise layer on the device's envelope; Amount and Color.
Time and frequency controls in most effects follow the played note and global pitch. FM and Ring Mod modulation decays with the global Decay, so short decays touch only the transient.

HARM Oscillator Model
Description: The HARM oscillator creates a waveform by adding harmonics or partials to a fundamental frequency.
Spread: Sets the relation between partials. At zero they are in unison; at maximum they are an octave apart. Intermediate positions interpolate linearly in frequency.

38.1.1 The CPU Load Meter

The CPU meter in the Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar compares the time Live takes to compute one audio buffer with the time that buffer takes to play. 50% means computing runs twice as fast as playback; over 100% is possible.

09.2 Gates and Triggers
An envelope needs a trigger or a gate to start.
A trigger is a very short pulse that can synchronize modules or start the MicroFreak's LFO or envelopes. A gate lasts longer, from a few milliseconds to a few seconds.

The keyboard is the MicroFreak's primary gate source. Touching and holding a key starts the envelope's Attack stage, followed by Decay/Release and Sustain. The envelope stays at the Sustain level while the key is held. Releasing the key ends the gate, and the level falls to zero at the rate set by Decay/Release.

YouTube Playlist
In this garden, YouTube Playlist pages model one identifiable playlist published on YouTube.
Identity and scope
The YouTube list ID is the deduplication key. Search playlist URLs and existing hub pages before creating a second page for a different name for the same playlist.
An informal list of video links without a YouTube playlist ID is a collection or series, but not a YouTube Playlist instance.
Relationship to Logseq/Entity/Series

An ordered playlist declares logseq-entity:: with Logseq/Entity/YouTube/Playlist first and Logseq/Entity/Series second. The playlist hub is the one external work and the named sequence; member videos remain distinct Logseq/Entity/YouTube pages.

Prefer a hub near its member videos, often <creator>/YouTube/Series/<name>; retain a requested or established path when it is already the series hub. Put a published ordinal on members only when the playlist or publisher uses one.
Frontmatter and page shape

Shared property conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter. Add a verifiable date-created:: and creation-year link when the playlist's own creation date is known; the date of its oldest video does not establish the playlist's creation date.
Lead with a bullet-wrapped H1 linked to the playlist URL. Describe the scope briefly and list member video page links in playlist order when known.

29.33 Roar

Roar is a saturation and coloring device with up to three gain stages in several routings. Its shaper curves and filters cover warm saturation, moving harmonics and noisy glitches, and its feedback and built-in compressor add sounds no other Live device makes.
29.19 Filter Delay
Filter Delay has three delay lines, each behind its own linked low-pass and high-pass filters, so only part of the spectrum is delayed. Feedback also runs back through the filters.
Delay 1 takes the left input, delay 2 both channels, delay 3 the right. Each outputs on its source channel unless its Pan control overrides it. Each delay can be switched on and off.
Each filter has an On switch and an X-Y controller: horizontal sets frequency, vertical sets bandwidth.
Sync on — delay in sixteenths from numbered buttons (4 is one beat); the Delay Time percentage nudges it for swing. Sync off — delay in ms, dragged or typed.
Feedback — output fed back into each delay; very high values can run away into loud oscillation, so protect ears and speakers.
Volume per delay, up to +6 dB, makes up for heavy filtering.
Dry — dry level; set to minimum on a return track

29.36.2 Frequency Section

Internal mode: Freq sets the pitch in Hz or as a note (Frequency Control Mode buttons). With Use Current Scale, it follows the clip's scale and Freq becomes SD Shift, transposing by scale degrees; with no scale active it uses the chromatic scale.
MIDI mode: notes set the pitch; Transp. shifts them ±48 semitones, or becomes SD Shift (±28 scale degrees) with scale awareness.
With a tuning system, Freq and Transp. use the tuning's note indices.
Stretch — spacing of the harmonics; below 0% closer, above 0% wider. At 100% only odd harmonics remain, a square-wave sound.
Shift — transposes the input's spectrum ±48 semitones before it reaches the resonator
Decay — how long the resonances last
HF Damp / LF Damp — damping of high and low partials; the ranges move with the current pitch

23.2.6.1 Default Presets

Set a device up and choose Save as Default Preset from its Options or context menu (instruments, MIDI and audio effects, and Racks). It is saved under Defaults in Audio Effects, Instruments or MIDI Effects, and loads every time the device is added — samples included for instruments.
Dragging a device into those folders works too, as long as it keeps the device's own name, such as "Simpler". Saving a new default asks before overwriting.
23.2.6.2 Default Plug-in Configurations

For a VST or Audio Units plug-in, add parameters in Configure Mode and choose Save as Default Configuration. It is saved to Plug-In Configurations → Audio Units or VSTs; VST and AU versions can have separate defaults.
Only the list of parameters is saved, not their values. To keep values too, put the plug-in in a Rack and save the Rack as a default preset.
23.2.6.3 Track Defaults

Set up a track's devices and mixer settings (routing, volume, pan, sends) and choose Save as Default Audio Track or Save as Default MIDI Track from its title bar's context menu. It goes to Creating Tracks → Audio Track or MIDI Track and applies to every new track of that kind.
Dragging a track there also works if it is named Default Audio Track or Default MIDI Track.
23.2.6.4 Sample Dropping Defaults

To choose the instrument made when a sample is dropped into an empty MIDI track's Device View or onto a Drum Rack pad, set up an empty Sampler or Simpler and drag it to Dropping Samples → On Device View or On Drum Rack. A pad's Save as Default Pad adds to On Drum Rack too.
If a folder holds several, the last one added is used.
23.2.6.5 Slicing Defaults

Build an empty Drum Rack with one chain holding an empty Sampler or Simpler, plus any effects and Macro mappings, and drag it into the Slicing folder. It then appears in the Slicing Preset chooser of Slice to New MIDI Track; see Ableton/Live/UG/13 Audio to MIDI.
23.2.6.6 Converting Audio to MIDI Defaults

Custom Racks for Harmony, Melody and Drums to MIDI go in the matching Audio to MIDI folder. Use an Instrument Rack (or a single instrument) for Harmony and Melody; Drums needs a top-level Drum Rack with Sampler or Simpler on its pads, not one nested in an Instrument Rack.
If a folder holds several, the last one added is used.
23.2.6.7 Project-Specific Defaults

A Defaults folder, with the same subfolders, inside the Current Project overrides the User Library defaults for Sets in that Project. Create folders in Finder/Explorer or with New Folder in the browser, then drag devices or tracks in.

Plug-ins can't be dragged into the Project. Instead, create Plug-In Configurations/Audio Units and VSTs folders there, save a configuration as usual, and move its folder with the Default.appc file from the User Library into the Project.
The Save as Default menu commands always save to the User Library, not the Project.

The downsampling controls are on the left. Without filters, downsampling adds inharmonic content that depends on the material and the chosen rate.

05.3 Freaky ideas
Modulation often works best below full strength; the right amount can add subtlety and expression to a patch. The Matrix offers many ways to find unusual sounds.

Change pitch scope: The keyboard and a sequence already modulate oscillator pitch at one volt per octave. Routing Key/Arp to Pitch can widen sequence steps to two or four semitones; negative modulation can shrink them to microtonal intervals.
Sum modulation signals: Combine the Standard and Cycling Envelope outputs at one destination to create a complex control signal for the filter or arpeggiator rate.
Mix the Cycling Envelope and LFO: Combining them at Filter Cutoff creates a composite modulation that can behave in surprising ways.
Modulate the Digital Oscillator: Let an unsynced LFO and Cycling Envelope control Wave, Timbre, and Shape at different speeds to create evolving timbral patterns.
Create regular automatic transpositions: Use the LFO's Random wave to modulate Pitch, or a slow square wave for more regular transpositions. The square-wave approach also works with a sequence.

Modulate modulation: Sequencer modulation tracks can change the strength of a Matrix connection. Hold an Assign button, select a Matrix point, then release the button to set that point as a destination. The LFO and Cycling Envelope can also modulate connection strength.
Modulate Cycling Envelope timing: Use the LFO to control its own rate, or use the Cycling Envelope to control its own rise time, fall time, or amount.

Create circular routings: Let the LFO control the Cycling Envelope's rise or fall time, then let the Cycling Envelope control its own level. The EMS Synthi became known for these distinctive, difficult-to-repeat routings.

Blues Scale
Also called the minor blues or hexatonic blues scale. On C, in its standard textbook form: C E♭ F G♭ G B♭. Steps in semitones: 3 2 1 1 3 2. Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor with an added ♭5.
History

The blues came out of African American vocal music in the Deep South around . Its "blue notes" are inflected regions around the third, fifth and seventh that a singer or guitarist bends into, and they fall between equal-tempered pitches.
's published blues, among them "The Memphis Blues" ( ) and "St. Louis Blues" ( ), had to fit those inflections onto a piano. Notation and keyboards turned the blue notes into fixed lowered pitches.
The six-note blues scale is a later pedagogical summary of that practice, popularized by mid- jazz method books.
Use
Blues harmony is a sequence of dominant seventh chords (I7, IV7, V7). The melody's ♭3 against the chord's major third is the idiom's central dissonance, and players often slide from ♭3 to 3.
Rock guitar improvisation is built largely on minor pentatonic and blues-scale patterns.
A "major blues" scale adds ♭3 to Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major: C D E♭ E G A on C.
Quirks
The chromatic run F G♭ G gives players a fixed-pitch stand-in for a bend through the blue fifth.

The MicroFreak manual lists its "Blues" setting as nine notes: C D E♭ F G♭ G A♭ A B♭. That collection is the hexatonic blues scale plus 2, ♭6 and 6, larger than any standard blues scale. The same manual's introduction to scales says blues scales use six notes. See Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings and Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales.
The Launchpad manual names a "Blues" setting without listing its pitches.

10.8.1 Focus Mode
Focus Mode edits one clip while the others stay visible. Toggle it with the Focus button or N; hold N while editing to switch it temporarily.

On: the active clip's notes and loop bar are in color, the rest gray, with its name below the loop bars. Hover another clip's loop bar to preview it, click to switch. Edits and the displayed scale apply to the active clip; Fold to Notes considers all clips.

Off: every note is active and colored. Clicking a loop bar turns it black so Velocity or Chance randomization targets that clip. Root and scale show only when shared, otherwise an asterisk. 29.32.2 Early Reflections
Early reflections are the first echoes off the walls before the diffuse tail; their level and spacing suggest the room's character.
Spin modulates them; Amount and Rate set it. More Amount gives a more neutral tail. Too high a Rate causes Doppler pitch shifts and odd panning. Turning Spin off saves some CPU.
Shape — low values: reflections fade slowly and overlap the tail, for a smoother decay; high values: they fade fast and the tail starts later, which can help clarity.

29.26.1 Dynamics Processing Theory
Four ways to change dynamics:
Downward compression (common) — loud parts quieter. This is what Ableton/Live/UG/29 Audio Effect Reference/09 Compressor does.
Upward compression (uncommon) — quiet parts louder
Downward expansion (common) — quiet parts quieter. This is what Ableton/Live/UG/29 Audio Effect Reference/20 Gate does.
Upward expansion (uncommon) — loud parts louder
Both kinds of compression shrink the dynamic range; both kinds of expansion widen it.
With three bands and two thresholds each, one Multiband Dynamics can apply six kinds of processing at once.

In this garden, UI Area pages model one named region of a product's interface — a panel section on hardware, or a view or bar in software — and list the controls and smaller areas inside it.
What counts
A region the product's own documentation names and that holds controls: Microfreak/UI/Oscillator, Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar, Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View.
<Item>/UI is the root area for an item and covers its whole interface, the way <Item>/UG holds its Logseq/Entity/Book/User Guide.
A single knob, button, pad or field is a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control, not an area.
A small group of controls stays a heading on its area page rather than becoming a page, even when the documentation names it, such as the Transport Controls section of Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar.
Atomic Design stages
A UI Area corresponds to an ; a root <Item>/UI page or a full view such as Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View corresponds to an .
A Logseq/Entity/UI/Control corresponds to an . A preset or a saved Live Set, which fills the interface with real values, corresponds to an and is modeled by its own entity.

16. Paraphonic Chord Mode
Paraphonic Chord Mode lets you transpose a chord through the current scale.
Initiate Paraphonic Chord Mode
Press the Paraphonic button. It blinks while the mode is active.
Hold the Paraphonic button and play a chord.
Lift your fingers from the keyboard, then release the Paraphonic button. The button stays on and blinks slowly.
Play a key to hear the chord with the same interval structure, transposed to that key and fitted to the current scale.

A chord's intervals come from scale steps. The root is its first note. A third three semitones above the root makes a minor chord; a third four semitones above makes a major chord. Adding notes shapes the chord further. Paraphonic Chord Mode analyzes the intervals in the chord you play, then rebuilds those intervals from each key you play. For example, a minor seventh chord becomes a minor seventh chord rooted at the played key.
Paraphonic Chord Mode can turn scale-quantized chords into fast, intricate arpeggios.
Press the Paraphonic button again to end Paraphonic Chord Mode.

29.34 Saturator

Saturator is a waveshaper that adds dirt, punch or warmth, from soft saturation to heavy coloring. Each sample is mapped to a new value through a curve, so the effect depends on the signal's level at each moment.
Curve Type — eight curves:
Analog Clip — clips smoothly around the clipping point; Digital Clip clips hard. Both stay clean below it.
Soft Sine, Medium Curve, Hard Curve — saturation with different characters
Sinoid Fold — wavefolding: louder input folds back on itself

Bass Shaper — like Analog Clip with smoother harmonics on heavily driven lows; made for 808 kicks and synth bass. Bass Shaper Threshold (0 to −50 dB) goes from soft clipping (low values, best for bass with high Drive) to hard clipping (high values).
Waveshaper — the most extreme, with its own controls in the expanded view (title bar button)
The Shaper Curve display shows the curve and the live input against it.
Post Clip Mode — Soft Clip or Hard Clip keeps the output under the Output level, catching extra boost from negative Color settings. Soft Clip applies an Analog Clip curve to the output.
Color — two color filters: an EQ before the shaper and its inverse after. For example, cut the bass before saturating so only mids and highs distort while the bass comes through intact.

29.10.1 Resonator Parameters
Resonance Type:
Beam — beams of various materials and sizes
Marimba — a beam tuned like arch-cut marimba bars
String — strings of various materials and sizes
Membrane — a rectangular membrane such as a drum head
Plate — a flat rectangular plate
Pipe — a tube open at one end, with a variable opening at the other
Tube — a tube open at both ends
Resonator Quality — fewer overtones (Eco) for less CPU, more (High) for richer resonance; not for Pipe or Tube
Decay — internal damping and so decay time

Material — how damping varies with frequency: low values let lows ring longer (wood, nylon, rubber), high values let highs ring longer (glass, metal). Pipe and Tube show Radius instead: a wider tube rings longer and brighter, and at extremes changes pitch.
The X-Y controller also sets Decay and Material/Radius.
Bright — level of higher frequencies; not for Pipe or Tube
Inharm — squeezes (negative) or stretches (positive) the harmonics; not for Pipe or Tube
Opening (Pipe only) — 0% closed at one end, 100% open at both
Ratio (Membrane and Plate) — proportions of the x and y axes
Hit — strike point, from center (0%) toward the edge; not for Pipe or Tube
Width — stereo spread of the left and right resonators, mono at 0%
Pos. L / Pos. R — where each resonator is "listened to", from center toward edge; Pipe and Tube are always heard at the open end
Tune — resonator frequency in Hz, or coarse offset when MIDI Frequency is on in the sidechain
Fine — fine offset in cents for MIDI Frequency
Spread — detunes the two resonators in opposite directions
