Asset
In this garden, Asset pages represent individual files: recordings, presets, images, PDFs, and other attachments.
Page and filename
An asset page lives beneath its owner at <Owner>/Asset/<Purpose>/<format>. The purpose describes the file; the final segment is its lowercase extension.
Replace namespace separators with Logseq's ___ separator, then turn the final format segment into the file extension. Keep the spelling inside each segment unchanged.
Examples
Diagram: Course/Asset/Diagram/Overview/png corresponds to Course___Asset___Diagram___Overview.png.
Recording: Course/Asset/Audio/First-Lesson/mp3 corresponds to Course___Asset___Audio___First-Lesson.mp3.
Document: Project/Asset/Reference/Setup/pdf corresponds to Project___Asset___Reference___Setup.pdf.
Reverse the mapping by turning the extension back into the final segment and replacing ___ with /. For example, Project___Asset___Reference___Setup.pdf identifies Project/Asset/Reference/Setup/pdf.
Valid names
Namespace separators become ___; an asset filename contains no / or directory structure.

___ is reserved for namespace boundaries and cannot occur inside a page segment. Empty segments, control characters, and filesystem-reserved punctuation (<, >, :, ", \, |, ?, *) are invalid. The format segment contains lowercase letters or digits.
A page name that violates these rules needs a valid name before the asset is stored. Silent punctuation replacement would make the filename ambiguous.

Hyphens keep new multiword asset purposes readable. Spaces already present in an owner's namespace stay intact; a URL percent-encodes them. Replacing spaces with hyphens would prevent exact recovery of the page name.
Frontmatter and body
Logseq/Entity/Asset/Frontmatter/duration-seconds records measured audio or video duration when useful. DVC tracks content identity; podcast feed metadata supplies enclosure size and media type.

The body contains a descriptive heading and the file itself: ![descriptive label](file location) embeds an image, audio recording, or video; [descriptive label](file location) links a downloadable preset or document.
Other technical facts belong in documented frontmatter when the asset needs them. The page contains only information about the represented file.
Principles
: every attachment uses the same relationship between its page and filename.
: the namespace supplies ownership, the page supplies the filename, and the file link supplies its location.
: valid asset names exclude problematic filename characters and reserve ___ for namespace boundaries, so each filename maps back to one page.
29.14 Echo
Echo is a modulated delay with two independent delay lines, envelope and filter modulation, and character controls.
Channel Mode — Stereo, Ping Pong or Mid/Side; Mid/Side replaces the Left and Right knobs with Mid and Side.
Left / Right — delay times, in beat divisions or ms depending on Sync
Sync Mode — Notes, Triplet, Dotted or 16th; only heard while Sync is on
Stereo Link — changes to time, Sync and Sync Mode apply to both sides
Delay Offset — nudges each line slightly for swing; independent even when linked
Input — gain on the dry signal; D distorts it
Feedback — output fed back into the delay lines; Ø inverts the fed-back signal

A Max device can depend on other files: samples, images, other Max patches. Freezing a Max device bundles all of those files into the device.

A wavetable is a set of short looping waveforms. Holding one waveform gives a steady tone; moving through the table while a note plays changes the timbre over time, which suits evolving sounds.

39.2.9 Routing
Routing a signal is neutral: the destination receives the same signal the source sends.
Tapping a signal partway through a chain, such as before a track's effects or from a single Impulse sample slot, gives a different signal than the end of that chain.

13.1.3.3. Real-Time Recording a Sequence
Start playback, then press Record. A blinking Record icon means the sequencer is waiting for notes or knob movements.
During note recording, each pass through the loop replaces notes played at the corresponding steps in the previous pass. Modulation recording runs for one cycle and then stops recording.
Playing a note replaces the recorded note at that point. Pressing Hold while recording replaces notes or modulation events at that point with silence; you can fill the gap on the next pass.
A DAW can play notes into a MicroFreak set to real-time recording. You can later add knob movement to the modulation tracks.

29.13 Dynamic Tube
Dynamic Tube adds tube saturation, with an envelope follower that varies the tone with input level.
Tube models:
A — clean at low Bias, adding bright harmonics once the input passes a threshold
B — between A and C
C — a poor tube that always distorts
Tone — moves the distortion toward the highs or down through the mids and lows
Drive — how much signal reaches the tube; more is dirtier
Bias — tube intensity; very high values make the signal break up
Envelope — lets input level move the Bias. Positive values make loud parts dirtier; negative values clean them up, an expansion effect.
Attack and Release — envelope response; no effect when Envelope is 0
Output — final level

Rate sets the speed, in milliseconds or in tempo-synced divisions depending on the Sync/Free toggle.

Distance and Steps transpose the pattern on each repeat. Distance is the interval in semitones or scale degrees; Steps is how many transposed repeats follow. With Distance +12 st and Steps 2, a pattern starting on C3 plays at C3, then C4, then C5. Negative Distance goes down.
Root and Scale keep the transposition inside a scale. Use Current Scale in the title bar takes the clip's scale instead and disables those two choosers.
Gate sets note length as a percentage of Rate. Over 100% the notes overlap for a legato sound.
Hold keeps the pattern going after the keys are released, until a new key is pressed. Holding keys and adding more builds up the pattern; playing a held note again removes it.
Pattern Offset rotates the start of the pattern by a number of steps. At 1 the second note plays first and the first note plays last.
Groove adds swing from the groove library; the Global Groove Amount in the Groove Pool or Control Bar sets how strong it is.
Retrigger restarts the pattern:
Off — never
Note — on each new note
Beat — every bar or beat set by Interval
An LED next to the Retrigger controls flashes on each restart.
Repeats sets how many times the pattern plays; the default is ∞. Values of 1 or 2 suggest a strummed guitar, and combining Repeats with Retrigger gives patterns with rests between them.

The Velocity toggle shows the velocity controls. Decay is the time to reach the Target velocity; a long Decay with Target 0 fades the pattern out. With Retrigger on, the velocity ramp restarts with the pattern.

Encode PCM (on by default) writes a lossless WAV, AIFF or FLAC file at 16, 24 or 32 bits.

Below 32 bits, choose dithering: No Dither, Rectangular, Triangular (the default), or POW-r 1, 2 or 3. Dither only once. Render at 32 bits if the file will be processed further, and use POW-r only on the final render, never for files headed to mastering.
Encode MP3 writes a 320 kbps CBR MP3, alone or with the PCM file. MP3 export adds a little silence at the start, which can throw off alignment in another DAW.

A 10-second countdown lets external gear fall silent first. Change the seconds, Restart, or Skip.

Auto-Restart on drop-outs re-renders automatically if Live detects glitches. Restart starts over; Cancel stops and deletes the partial file. The dialog counts attempts; closing other CPU-heavy programs helps.

29.2.4 Envelope Follower Controls
These controls set how the envelope follower moves the cutoff.
Envelope Attack — how quickly the envelope follows rising levels; higher values respond more slowly
Envelope Hold — when on, the attack finishes before the release starts
Envelope Release — how quickly it follows falling levels; higher values lengthen the decay
Envelope S&H and Envelope S&H Rate — quantize the envelope to beat values
Envelope (below the display) — direction and amount of envelope modulation

09.7 Freaky Cycling Envelope Suggestions
Use the Matrix to modulate the Cycling Envelope's Rise, Hold, and Fall with the LFO or pressure. Pressure gives direct control over the Rise and Fall stages.
Matrix modulation can be positive or negative. A negative signal to Fall shortens the Fall stage as pressure increases.
Amount controls how strongly the Cycling Envelope affects its destinations. Adjust it carefully, especially when modulating the analog filter. A control that reduces signal strength is an attenuator.

The Matrix can combine the Cycling Envelope with stages of the Main Envelope. For example, modulating Attack changes its slope; modulating Decay changes its length. Further Matrix routings can build longer modulation chains.
Patch ideas:
Use a slow sine LFO to control Cycling Envelope Rise, then use CycEnv to control Main Envelope Sustain.
Use a random LFO to control Cycling Envelope Amount, then use CycEnv to control Main Envelope Decay/Release or Sustain.
9.3.1 Chaining Patterns
Press two Pattern pads at once to set the start and end of a chain. During playback, the Patterns play in order. A chain can span all eight Patterns, for up to 256 steps.
22.2 Separating Audio Files and Clips
Choose Separate Stems to New Audio Tracks from the context menu or Create menu, on a file in the browser or a clip in either view.
In the dialog:
toggles pick which of the four stems to make;
Merge to Single Track combines two or three chosen stems into one;
the quality selector picks High Speed or High Quality;
Separate starts the process and stops playback.
Each stem gets its own track inside a new Group Track, coloured to match the dialog's toggles; the group takes the source track's colour. A single stem, or a merged one, goes on one track instead.
Only the clip's audible region is processed — between its start and end markers, or from the start marker through the loop of a looped warped clip.
In the Arrangement, Separate Stems for Time Selection on a clip splits it at the selection's edges and separates only that part.
Source track effects move to the Group Track; track automation is copied to the group, and clip envelopes and modulation to each stem clip.
The source clip is deactivated to avoid doubling; select it and press 0 to turn it back on.
From the browser, stems land in whichever view has focus. In an empty Set with warping on for samples, the Set tempo follows the source.

Files go to the Project's Samples/Processed/Stems folder (merged stems keep their individual files too), in the File Type from the Record, Warp & Launch Settings, at 44.1 kHz and the source's bit depth.
26.4 Overriding Automation
Moving an automated parameter while not recording overrides its automation without erasing it. The LED turns grey.
The Control Bar's Re-Enable Automation button lights up when anything is overridden; click it to bring all automation back.
Re-Enable Automation in a parameter's context menu restores just that one. Relaunching a Session clip with automation also restores it.

17.5.2 Making Use of Internal Routing
17.5.2.1 Post-Effects Recording

To record a guitar already processed by a gate or amp model, put the effects on a "Guitar" track with Monitor set to In, and record on other tracks whose input is the Guitar track at Post FX (or Post Mixer to include its level and pan). Set those tracks' Monitor to Off.
17.5.2.2 Recording MIDI as Audio
When a complex instrument turns one note into something closer to a passage, record its audio: one MIDI track hosts the instrument, and an audio track taking input from it records the result.
17.5.2.3 Creating Submixes
Route several drum tracks to one submix audio track that goes to Main, so one fader controls the whole kit.
A Group Track sets up the same routing automatically and can fold its tracks away.
Or set each track's Output Type to Sends Only and use a send, so a return track acts as the submix.
17.5.2.4 Several MIDI Tracks Playing the Same Instrument

ancestors: 17.5.2.4 Several MIDI Tracks Playing the Same Instrument
content.text: Point a second MIDI track's Output Type at the instrument track, and choose the instrument itself (not Track In) as Output Channel. Both tracks then play one instrument, so sound changes affect both.

ancestors: 17.5.2.4 Several MIDI Tracks Playing the Same Instrument
content.text: To mute each part separately, move the original clips to a third track and leave the instrument alone on its track, with Input Type set to No Input so it has no Arm button.
17.5.2.5 Tapping Individual Outs From an Instrument

ancestors: 17.5.2.5 Tapping Individual Outs From an Instrument
content.text: Impulse offers each of its eight sample slots as a source for other tracks. An audio track whose input is the Impulse track can choose one slot, which takes that slot out of Impulse's own mix for separate effects. Most plug-ins don't remove the tapped output this way.
17.5.2.6 Using Multi-Timbral Plug-In Instruments

A multi-timbral instrument plays a different part on each MIDI channel. Extra MIDI tracks feed its parts by pointing Output Type at the instrument's track and Output Channel at each part's channel; audio tracks tap its individual outputs.

External Instrument devices on other MIDI tracks can do both at once: set MIDI To to the instrument's track and channel, and Audio From to one of its auxiliary outputs. Several can share one track inside a Rack. The instrument's main outputs stay on its own track.
17.5.2.7 Feeding Sidechain Inputs

A vocoder on a strings track needs a speech signal at its sidechain input: create a "Speech" track whose Output Type is the strings track and whose Output Channel is the vocoder's sidechain. Vocoder plug-ins with their own carrier synth go on a MIDI track and are fed the same way.
Many of Live's built-in devices have their own sidechain choosers, so they don't need this.
17.5.2.8 Layering Instruments

To double a strings part with brass, add a MIDI track with a brass instrument whose Input Type taps the strings track at Post FX. MIDI from another track is tapped after its MIDI effects and just before its instrument, so the brass gets the same notes.

Major Scale
Also called Ionian and natural major. On C: C D E F G A B. Steps in semitones: 2 2 1 2 2 2 1.
History

Medieval theory recognized eight modes on the finals D, E, F and G, defined by final, range and reciting tone. A mode on C circulated in practice, often as a Lydian with B♭, but had no name in the system.
's Dodecachordon ( ) expanded the system to twelve modes and named the C mode Ionian, alongside Aeolian on A. Zarlino later renumbered the modes to start on C, which put Ionian first.

Over the Ionian and Aeolian absorbed the other modes into major-minor tonality. 's Traité de l'harmonie ( ) grounded the major triad in the resonance of a vibrating body and gave major its theoretical priority.
The solmization syllables ut re mi fa sol la come from 's hexachord, taken from the hymn Ut queant laxis in the . The seventh syllable, si (later ti), was added much later.
Use
The reference collection for common-practice tonality, Western pedagogy and most popular music. Every other diatonic mode is described as an alteration of it.
Its association with brightness or happiness is learned. The MicroFreak manual's chapter on scales says as much in Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales.
Quirks

The diatonic collection is a stack of six perfect fifths (F C G D A E B). Its interval-class vector is 254361: each interval class appears a different number of times. Because the tritone appears once, a listener who hears F–B can locate the tonic; resolving that tritone inward to E–C is the core of the dominant-seventh resolution.

In five-limit just intonation the scale needs two sizes of whole tone, 9:8 and 10:9. D–A then comes out a syntonic comma narrow of a pure fifth, so the ii triad is out of tune in a just C major. This is the textbook case for temperament.
Inverting the step pattern about the tonic produces Music/Scale/Phrygian. Inverting Mixolydian produces Music/Scale/Minor/Natural, and Music/Scale/Dorian inverts to itself.
The pitch-class complement of the major scale is Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major: on a piano, white keys against black keys.

Description: Chords mode turns the digital oscillator into four voices that can play and modulate chords.

The first note of a chord is its root. The third determines whether the chord is minor, three half-steps above the root, or major, four half-steps above it. Adding voices further shapes the minor or major feel.
A major chord may sound forceful and happy, while a minor chord may sound sad to listeners raised with Western music. Responses to major and minor scales differ across cultures.

37.1 Synchronizing via Link

Ableton Link keeps beat, tempo and phase in step across apps and devices on a wired or wireless network. Link Audio adds real-time audio streaming between the peers in a Link session, with no extra hardware.

Any peer can start and stop on its own and stay in phase, with playback following the global launch quantization. Any peer can change the tempo for everyone, and peers can join or leave without disturbing the others.
Link can run alongside Tempo Follower or MIDI sync; the Link session then takes its tempo from that external input.
30.7 Scale
Scale remaps each incoming note to an outgoing note through a matrix, so every C can become a D, for example.

The Note Matrix is a 13 × 13 grid: columns are incoming notes in an octave, rows are outgoing notes. Black squares match the keyboard's black keys. Highlighted squares show the mapping, starting from the root in the bottom left.
Base sets the root and Scale Name the scale. Use Current Scale in the title bar takes both from the clip and disables those choosers.
Choosing User in Scale Name allows a custom mapping: drag highlighted squares to move them or click to delete them. A removed note is never output.
Transpose shifts notes by up to ±36 semitones; +7 st moves a C major melody to G major.

Lowest and Range limit which notes are remapped (and transposed); notes outside pass unchanged. Lowest C2 with Range +36 affects only C2 to B4.

06 The Digital Oscillator

The Digital Oscillator is the very heart of the MicroFreak. It's the digital circuit that generates the core sound of this instrument. The other parts of the MicroFreak - the Analog Filter, the Envelopes, and the LFO - exist only to shape/mangle/wobble the sound of the Digital Oscillator.

Oscillators come in two flavors; analog and digital. Digital oscillators have advantages over analog oscillators: they are capable of generating a much broader palette of waveforms and are more flexible and stable than their analog counterparts. Analog filters, on the other hand, have something special to them.
The MicroFreak offers you the best of both worlds: a digital oscillator and an analog filter.

The Oscillator in the MicroFreak is unique in that it can emulate many different synthesis models. In the history of electronic music, many gifted sound engineers developed unique ways of generating sounds. Voltage Controlled Oscillators, the pitch of which could be controlled with an external voltage, FM oscillators that created timbres by modulating two or more oscillators, Harmonic oscillators use combinations of harmonics to create complex

At Arturia, we are fans of Mutable Instruments. They permitted us to implement some of their open-source Oscillator designs in the MicroFreak, for which we are very grateful as they add a lot to the sonic potential of the MicroFreak.

The BASS, SAWX and HARM have been developed by Noise Engineering. The oscillators are special versions of the oscillators included in Noise Engineering's Virt Iter Oscillator Platform. The Virt Iter comes with these same three oscillator models but can be flashed with other models.

36.3.5 Step Sequencing Beats
Tapping a drum pad selects it for step sequencing. Tap steps to place notes; the clip starts playing at the first tap. Steps are 16th notes by default; the Scene/Grid buttons change the step size.
The Tempo encoder changes tempo by 1 BPM per click, or 0.1 BPM with Shift.
A moving green step shows playback (red while recording). Tap a filled step to delete it; hold Mute and tap to deactivate it; hold Solo and tap a pad to solo that sound.
Delete clears the pattern; hold Delete and tap a pad to clear its notes, or its devices if it has no notes in the pattern.
Step colours:
grey — empty;
clip colour — note, brighter for higher velocity;
lighter clip colour — muted note;
unlit — unavailable; with triplet steps only the first six pads of each row are used.

07.01.04 Cutoff frequency

The cutoff frequency is where filtering takes place. Feeding a filter's output back into itself creates a resonance peak around the cutoff. The Resonance knob controls this effect; the LFO or envelopes can also modulate resonance when assigned in the Matrix.

Filters attenuate frequencies gradually above or below the cutoff. This slope, or roll-off, depends on the number of poles: a four-pole filter has a steeper roll-off than a two-pole filter. The MicroFreak filter rolls off at 12 dB per octave.
The Cutoff knob moves the cutoff point from about 30 Hz at its fully counter-clockwise position to above 15 kHz at its fully clockwise position.

19.8.3. How do you set gain?
The useful gain depends on how loudly you sing or speak and your distance from the microphone.
Set the MicroFreak master volume to about 50%, then use a non-vocoder preset to establish an average listening level.
Select the Vocoder Oscillator. Open Utility > Mic Settings > Mic Gain with the Preset encoder. Mic Gain defaults to Auto; turn the encoder left to choose a manual level.

Hold a key and speak or sing while adjusting gain until the vocoder is loud enough without distortion. For chords, enable Paraphonic mode and check the level again. Leave headroom if your voice changes volume widely.

29.21 Glue Compressor

Glue Compressor is an analog-modeled bus compressor made with Cytomic, based on the bus compressor of a famous 1980s mixing console. It works on single tracks but is aimed at the Main track or Group Tracks, to "glue" several sources into one mix.
Threshold and Ratio work as in Ableton/Live/UG/29 Audio Effect Reference/09 Compressor. There is no knee control; the knee gets harder as the ratio rises.
Attack — in ms
Release — in seconds. A (Auto) uses a slow release for the overall level and a fast one for transients; gentle on most material but slow on sudden level changes.
Dry/Wet — 0% bypasses, 100% fully compressed
Range — limits how much compression can happen. −60 to −70 dB behaves like the original hardware; −40 to −15 dB works as an alternative to Dry/Wet; 0 dB does nothing.
Makeup — set it near the needle's reading to get back roughly the original level.

Soft clip — a fixed waveshaper capping output at −0.5 dB to catch loud transients. It colors and distorts the sound, so the manual suggests leaving it off unless that is wanted. With Oversampling, peaks can still pass 0 dB.
The needle shows gain reduction in dB. The Clip LED turns red above 0 dB, or yellow when Soft clip is catching peaks.

With an external keyboard that generates audio, such as an external synthesizer, if you want to record MIDI and audio at the same time into two tracks, one MIDI and one audio, then it's important that you set Ableton Track IO - Monitor set to Off in the MIDI channel.

Oscillator
Model: BasicWaves. Morph moves from square to sawtooth to two sawtooths; Sym changes pulse width or the sawtooths’ relative phase; Sub adds a sine-wave sub-oscillator.
Morph: 0.918.
Filter
Low-pass filter. Saved cutoff: 0.000; resonance: 0.255. Cutoff and resonance are normalized settings, not hertz or instrument display values.
Envelopes
Main envelope: attack 0.000, decay/release 0.185, sustain 0.000. Amp Mod is on, so the main envelope controls loudness.
Cycling Envelope mode: Env. Stored RiseLvl 0.089, FallLvl 0.193, Hold 0.000, Amount 1.000. These are normalized stored fields; rise/fall times in milliseconds remain unverified.
LFO
Sine; clock sync off. Stored normalized rate: 0.148; division code: 0. The rate is not a hertz reading, and the musical division has not been converted.
Modulation matrix
Amounts use the signed normalized range −1…+1. The assignment destinations below resolve the saved Assign columns.
Cycling Envelope → Wave / Morph: −1.000. The envelope moves the waveform morph downward.
LFO → Timbre / Sym: +0.729. The sine LFO changes pulse width or sawtooth phasing according to Morph.
ENV → Cutoff: +0.728. The main envelope opens the filter from its zero base setting.
PRESSURE → Assign 1 → Sub: +1.000. Expression adds sub-oscillator level.
PRESSURE → Assign 2 → Decay/Release: +0.683. Expression lengthens decay/release.
All other saved matrix amounts are zero.
Performance and session context

The saved main envelope has an immediate attack and no sustained level. Expression changes bass weight and note length. The strong envelope-to-cutoff route opens an otherwise closed filter; Morph and Sym modulation change the oscillator spectrum.

Paraphonic mode is on in the saved export. The PRESSURE matrix row uses pressure or velocity according to the instrument’s global Utility setting; the export does not establish which expression source was used in the session.

Base controls use normalized 0…1 values unless a stored choice code is shown; matrix amounts use −1…+1. These describe saved base settings, before modulation, and are not OLED percentages, hertz or milliseconds.
The saved-parameter inspector preserves the original fields. Oscillator interpretation assumes the documented firmware 5 layout; firmware is not detected from the export.

29.16 EQ Three
EQ Three is a DJ-mixer-style EQ with separate level controls for low, mid and high.
Each band's gain goes from −∞ to +6 dB, so a bass line or kick can be removed entirely.
On/Off buttons under each band are handy mapped to computer keys.
An LED per band lights when there is signal in it above −24 dB, even when the band is off.
FreqLo and FreqHi set the crossovers. At 500 Hz and 2000 Hz: low is 0–500 Hz, mid 500–2000 Hz, high above 2000 Hz.
24 dB / 48 dB — crossover steepness; 48 dB is steeper and uses more CPU.

The filters are made to sound like a powerful analog filter cascade, so 48 dB mode colors the sound slightly even with every band at 0 dB. For more neutral behavior use 24 dB mode or Ableton/Live/UG/29 Audio Effect Reference/15 EQ Eight.

31.5.1 Architecture and Interface

A key drives a hammer into a fork, and a magnetic pickup amplifies the fork, much like an electric guitar. The fork has a tine bar, which the hammer strikes, and a tone bar, a tuned resonator. It rings for a long time until the key's release brings a damper down.
Four sections: Hammer, Fork, Damper/Pickup and Global. Click a section, or its icon, to show all its parameters.

MicroFreak Synth Preset
In this garden, MicroFreak Synth Preset pages model individual saved sounds on the Microfreak, following Logseq/Entity/Preset/Synth.
Placement and identity

Pages use Microfreak/Preset/<slot> <name>, with a three-digit slot and the name observed at creation. The filename remains stable so existing music-log links resolve. A newly observed name at an occupied slot needs a new page when continuity is unknown.

Microfreak/Preset/396 Anit and Microfreak/Preset/397 Imit illustrate the frontmatter and notes format. Repeated names or slot numbers alone cannot establish that two observations are the same saved sound.
Frontmatter dictionary
Logseq/Entity/Preset/Synth/Microfreak/Frontmatter/preset-synth-microfreak-number
Logseq/Entity/Preset/Synth/Microfreak/Frontmatter/preset-synth-microfreak-name
Logseq/Entity/Preset/Synth/Microfreak/Frontmatter/preset-synth-microfreak-category
Logseq/Entity/Preset/Synth/Microfreak/Frontmatter/preset-synth-microfreak-initialized
Logseq/Entity/Preset/Synth/Microfreak/Frontmatter/preset-synth-microfreak-on-device
Logseq/Entity/Preset/Synth/Microfreak/Frontmatter/preset-synth-microfreak-oscillator-type
Shared provenance and export properties are defined by Logseq/Entity/Preset/Synth. Unknown origin uses Logseq/Entity/Preset/Synth/Frontmatter/preset-synth-origin/Unknown.
What the sources can capture

The saved-header inventory reads slot, name, category and initialization status. It cannot detect a same-name edit to oscillator, filter, envelope, modulation or sequence settings. The Elektroid header decoder supplies the protocol evidence.

Elektroid’s preset download and serialization retain the preset payload for export: up to 146 blocks of 32 bytes. Supported payloads contain labeled raw parameter records for oscillator, filter, envelopes, LFO, modulation routes and preset settings. Repeated live reads matched the corresponding MIDI Control Center export byte for byte; the parameter inspection documentation records the framing and remaining interpretation limits.

The parameter inspection task reads a saved export with mise run microfreak:inspect /private/path/preset.bin or a computer project with mise run microfreak:inspect /private/path/project.mfprojz --slot 1. It reports exact stored bytes and named raw fields, identifies unsupported layouts, and leaves the input unchanged. Its preserves the distinction between raw values and unverified display conversions.

--interpret-fw5 adds the existing firmware 5 interpretations beside the raw fields: supported oscillator model and control names, normalized or metadata-scaled value domains, and source evidence for each interpretation. The report states the firmware assumption; an export does not establish its firmware version. Unknown models retain generic field names, and unsupported values retain their raw readings. The option leaves the raw report and preset notes intact.

Raw values describe saved base settings; modulation, performance gestures and unsaved edits affect the audible sound. Instrument display units, sequence contents, matrix destination meanings and referenced sample or wavetable identities require further verification. Firmware 5 oscillator indices follow the research cited in the optional interpretation report. A computer project can differ from the current device inventory.

Microfreak/UG/17 Ext Gear/09 MIDI CC Control and Microfreak/UG/21 Appendix D - CC Values describe MIDI control changes. A stream of knob movements is incomplete evidence of a saved sound: parameters that never change remain unobserved. Microfreak/UG/04 Presets/05 Digital Control explains why panel positions may differ from recalled values.

Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/03 Types defines oscillator models. Microfreak/UG/04 Presets/03 Preset Config defines per-preset settings, including voice behavior, scale and sequencer options. These guides describe meanings and ranges; values for a particular saved sound need a read or observation of that sound.

Samples and user wavetables have separate export workflows in Microfreak/UG/14 Config/02 MIDI Control Center/03 Samples Tab/01 Management and Microfreak/UG/14 Config/02 MIDI Control Center/02 Wavetables Tab/01 Management. A preset export alone does not establish that those resources are preserved. Global settings such as tuning and tempo behavior also affect playback; see Microfreak/UG/14 Config/02 MIDI Control Center/01 Device Tab.
Session-linked research

A saved preset referenced by a published session has notes covering Saved export and provenance, Oscillator, Filter, Envelopes, LFO, Modulation matrix, and Performance and session context. These sections explain supported settings and their control meanings, with cited sources and explicit uncertainty.

Provenance identifies the export, capture date, bank or slot when relevant, and file digest. A verified match to an archived factory payload establishes that saved baseline; it does not establish a session-time capture or the instrument's unsaved state.

Values carry verified units or a clearly named normalized or raw domain. Unknown display conversions, matrix destinations, firmware assumptions and resource identities remain qualified. Large raw inventories stay outside the notes unless their numbers help explain the sound.

Performance notes distinguish what the saved patch supports from changes heard or recorded during a session. An unidentified initialized sound is described plainly rather than assigned an invented numbered preset or presumed settings.
Sync
The MicroFreak sync task previews the connected device with mise run microfreak:sync; --apply updates its saved metadata. The sync implementation on GitHub is also available as a .

--save-inventory /tmp/microfreak-inventory.json stores a full inventory; --inventory /tmp/microfreak-inventory.json previews that capture. --garden /absolute/path/to/worktree selects the destination and --port 'Arturia MicroFreak' selects an exact endpoint.

A complete successful inventory updates reported fields, omits initialized slots and marks missing sounds absent. Partial reads write nothing. Handwritten notes, established origin, verified oscillator type and export references survive metadata refreshes. A saved inventory describes its capture time; a new device read is needed to establish current state.
Header sync performs no binary export. File and digest properties are populated only after an export and its destination have been verified.

Major Pentatonic Scale
Also called the pentatonic, gong mode in Chinese theory, and the MicroFreak's "Pentatonic" setting. On C: C D E G A. Steps in semitones: 2 2 3 2 3.
History

Five-note scales without semitones appear in traditions with no historical contact: Chinese, Korean, Japanese, West African, Andean, Scottish and Appalachian music among them. Chinese theory derived its five tones, gong shang jue zhi yu, from a chain of fifths by the third century BCE.

European art music took it up as a marker of the exotic or the rural. heard the Javanese gamelan at the Exposition Universelle in Paris, and "Pagodes" (Estampes, ) is built on pentatonic collections. Javanese slendro tuning divides the octave into five near-equal steps, so the Western pentatonic is only an approximation of what he heard.
Use
Folk melodies such as "Auld Lang Syne" and "Amazing Grace" are pentatonic.
Music education uses it for improvisation because it contains no semitones and no tritone. The Orff Schulwerk and methods start children on it.
Country, gospel and rock guitar use the major pentatonic for major-key soloing. Its five modes include Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor.
Quirks
It is a stack of four perfect fifths (C G D A E).
The pitch-class complement of Music/Scale/Major is a pentatonic collection: the black keys of a piano form G♭ major pentatonic.

The Standard Envelope can control filter cutoff and amplitude. When Amp Mod is off, the envelope controls filter cutoff. When Amp Mod is on, it controls both volume and filter cutoff.

19.2. How Does Vocoder Work?
The MicroFreak analyzes incoming sound with 16 tuned bandpass filters. As with the MicroFreak's own filter in BPF mode, each band emphasizes a limited range of frequencies.

An envelope follower tracks the loudness in each band. The resulting signals control matching filters on the carrier, allowing each formant peak to follow its own changing volume. The vocoder also recreates the overall loudness pattern at the end of the signal path.

3.18 Automation Envelopes
Automation is a control's change over time, stored as a breakpoint envelope you can draw, edit or record. Almost every mixer and device control can be automated, tempo included.
With Automation Arm and Arrangement Record on, control changes are recorded into the Arrangement. With Automation Arm on while Session recording, they go into the clip.
Moving an automated control while not recording overrides its automation until you press Re-Enable Automation or launch a Session clip that carries automation.

22.2.1 Separation Speed vs. Quality
High Speed separates every stem in one pass. It can still take several minutes on older computers.
High Quality gives cleaner results (a higher signal-to-distortion ratio) by running separate passes for Vocals, Drums and Bass, then deriving Others from what remains.
Crop the clip first to save time: Crop Clip Sample to Time Selection in the Sample Editor, or Crop Clip in the Arrangement, both Cmd+Shift+J (Mac) / Ctrl+Shift+J (Windows).
In High Quality, choosing fewer stems saves time unless Others is included, since Others needs all three other passes. Unused stems from those passes are still saved in the Stems folder.
Older Windows computers and Intel Macs separate on the CPU only, so they're slower than Apple silicon Macs, which also use the GPU.
Some sounds land in an unexpected stem, such as hi-hat highs in Others or chorused synths in Vocals. Trying both modes can show which suits the material.

29.12 Drum Buss
Drum Buss is an analog-style processor for adding body and character to a group of drums and holding them together in a mix.
Trim — lowers the input before processing
Comp — a fixed compressor before the distortion, tuned for drum groups: fast attack, medium release, moderate ratio, plenty of makeup gain
Distortion types, increasingly strong:
Soft — waveshaping
Medium — limiting
Hard — clipping with a bass boost
Drive — how hard the input hits the distortion
29.12.0.1 Mid-High Frequency Shaping
For clarity and presence on snares and hats.
Crunch — sine-shaped distortion on the mid-highs
Damp — low-pass filter to remove harsh highs after distortion
Transients — above 100 Hz: positive values add attack and sustain for a fuller, punchier sound; negative values add attack but cut sustain for tighter, drier drums
29.12.0.2 Low-End Enhancement
A resonant filter that strongly boosts the bass, plus a decay control.
Boom — amount of low-end boost; the Bass Meter shows it even when it is hard to hear
Freq — frequency of the boost; Force To Note snaps it to the nearest MIDI note
Decay — how fast the lows decay. At Boom 0% it affects only the incoming (post-distortion) signal; above 0% it also affects the boost.

06.03.01 Basic Waves Oscillator (BasicWaves)
Classic Waveforms Oscillator Model

Description: Every sound consists of a series of harmonics. The first harmonic is the fundamental, which determines the pitch you hear. The second harmonic is twice as high in pitch, the third is three times as high, and so on. On a guitar, touching the exact middle of a string produces the second harmonic; dividing the string into three parts produces the third harmonic.

The second and higher harmonics determine a sound's timbre. The second, fourth, sixth, and eighth harmonics are even; the third, fifth, seventh, and ninth are odd. Odd harmonics can add a more dissonant timbre.

Triangle and square waves contain only odd harmonics; a sawtooth contains odd and even harmonics. A sawtooth can emulate bowed strings: the bow catches the string periodically, then slips to its next position, creating a sawtooth-like wave.

The four basic waveforms developed in the early days of synthesis are sine, triangle, square, and sawtooth. Each has a different mix of even and odd harmonics. The sine wave is the simplest, with only a fundamental. A square wave has only odd harmonics. To some ears, a square wave sounds more musical than a sawtooth, which contains all harmonics.
This oscillator emulates two basic waveforms: square and sawtooth.
Morph: Continuously morphs from a square wave to a sawtooth, then to two sawtooths. It changes waveform symmetry.
Sym: Morphs between square-wave pulse width and phasing between the two sawtooth copies. It has no effect when Wave is at 50 (sawtooth).
Sub: Adds a sine-wave sub-oscillator.
Tip: To get a sine wave, use the filter to remove all harmonics. Alternatively, set filter resonance to maximum; the filter then self-oscillates and produces a pure sine wave.

39.2 Neutral Operations

A neutral operation leaves the audio unchanged. Recorded audio stays identical to what the A/D converter delivered, imported files stay identical to the files on disk, and an export is at least as good as what played back.
Neutral operations usually happen alongside non-neutral ones. Any neutral step that follows an effect or a gain change still carries that change.

26.3 Overwriting Automation
Recording over existing automation for the same parameter replaces it, including on later passes of a looping clip.

In Session View, mouse moves behave like "touch": the value returns to the recorded automation on release. Hardware knobs and faders behave like "latch": the last value holds until the clip or loop ends. A first recording into a clip always latches.

33.2.4 Shaper
A modulator whose output is a breakpoint envelope drawn in its display.
Mapping, Mod, polarity and Min/Max work as described in Ableton/Live/UG/33 Max for Live Devices/02 Max for Live Audio Effects.
Drawing:
click to add a breakpoint; Option-drag (Mac) or Alt-drag (Windows) between points to curve a segment; Shift-click a point to delete it
Clear erases the envelope; six presets next to it start a new one
Grid sets grid divisions; Snap snaps points to the grid
The small display at the top right shows the output like an oscilloscope.
Jitter adds randomness; Smooth softens sudden changes.
Phase — start position in the cycle; R retriggers from there (disabled in Sync time mode)
Offset — moves the center of the output up or down
Trigger modes:
Loop — repeats at Rate
1-Shot — plays once each time the mappable T button is pressed
Manual — the Manual control scrubs through the envelope
Rate — in Hz or synced divisions
Depth — modulation amount for all targets
4.2 Search Bar
Results match all the search terms, not any one of them: "electric bass" finds items with both words.
Cmd+F (Mac) / Ctrl+F (Win) jumps to the All label and puts the cursor in the search field.
Narrow results by clicking tags in the Filter View, or type # and a tag name, such as #Drums, with autocomplete.
The x button clears the search terms only; the Clear button in the Results bar also clears selected tags.
Keyboard-only flow: Cmd+F, type, down arrow into the results, arrows to move, Esc to clear and return to All.
